case.title: Trial of Bridget Bishop (Salem witch trials)
case.court: Court of Oyer and Terminer, Salem, Massachusetts Bay
case.actualOutcome: Convicted of witchcraft and hanged on June 10, 1692, the first execution of the Salem trials. The convictions were later condemned and reversed by the colony.
case.questionPresented: Whether Bridget Bishop could be convicted of witchcraft on the testimony of accusers describing spectral torments and other supernatural evidence.
case.facts: Bridget Bishop, a Salem woman with a reputation for quarrelsomeness and nonconformity, was accused of witchcraft during the hysteria that swept Salem in 1692. She was tried before the special Court of Oyer and Terminer. The evidence against her consisted largely of 'spectral evidence' — testimony from afflicted girls that Bishop's spirit or specter tormented them — along with accounts of her supposed poppets (dolls with pins), an old scar suggesting a 'witch's teat,' and testimony that her presence caused illness and affliction. Bishop denied being a witch and contended the accusations were unreliable and driven by malice and hysteria. The case presented the question whether such supernatural and testimonial evidence could support a capital conviction. The proof consisted of spectral testimony, poppets, reputation, and alleged physical marks; Bishop denied witchcraft, and the tribunal was the special Court of Oyer and Terminer convened for the prosecutions. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Bishop was tried by the Court of Oyer and Terminer, a special tribunal convened for the witch trials. She was convicted and sentenced to death, becoming the first of the accused executed in the Salem proceedings. The colony's authorities later repudiated the trials and the spectral evidence on which the convictions rested.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the accusers' testimony describing spectral attacks — the girls falling into fits they attributed to Bishop's specter — along with testimony about poppets, her reputation, and alleged physical marks. The defense contested the reliability of spectral evidence and the absence of conventional proof, highlighting the accusatory frenzy and the lack of physical evidence of any crime.
case.plaintiffArguments: The prosecutors argued that the testimony of the afflicted, the spectral torments they described, the physical evidence of poppets and marks, and Bishop's reputation established her guilt of witchcraft. They contended the girls' afflictions and the corroborating testimony of neighbors provided sufficient proof, that the court could credit spiritual evidence of the accused's specter acting under diabolical power, and that the safety of the community required conviction.
case.defendantArguments: Bishop maintained her innocence and argued, through her defense, that the accusations rested on unreliable spectral evidence and the testimony of hysterical or malicious accusers, rather than on actual evidence of criminal acts. She contended she was not a witch, that the girls' fits and claims of her specter tormenting them could not be proved or verified, and that conviction on such evidence was unjust and dangerous.
case.applicableLaw: The Massachusetts Bay colonial law against witchcraft; the law of evidence as it then admitted spectral and testimonial proof of supernatural offenses; the criminal procedure of the Court of Oyer and Terminer.
case.precedents: English witchcraft law and earlier colonial witch prosecutions; the theological and legal authorities on proving witchcraft; the standards of proof in capital cases of the period.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Criminal law / witchcraft prosecution. Decided 1692. Bridget Bishop was the first person executed in the Salem witch trials, which remain the archetype of miscarriage of justice driven by mass hysteria and unreliable evidence.
case.tldr: Bridget Bishop was tried for witchcraft on spectral evidence in 1692. She was convicted and hanged, the first execution of the Salem witch trials.

ruling.ruling: Judgment for the defending party; relief denied. Remedy: criminal sentence.

case.title: Marbury v. Madison
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Writ denied. Marbury had a right to the commission, but §13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 conferring original mandamus jurisdiction was unconstitutional; the Court could not issue the writ. Established judicial review.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Supreme Court may issue a writ of mandamus, in its original jurisdiction, ordering the Secretary of State to deliver a judicial commission, and whether the Judiciary Act of 1789's grant of such original jurisdiction is consistent with Article III of the Constitution.
case.facts: In the final days of John Adams's presidency, the outgoing Federalist administration nominated and the Senate confirmed a number of justices of the peace for the District of Columbia, including William Marbury. The commissions were signed by the President and sealed by the Secretary of State, but several were not delivered before Adams left office. When Thomas Jefferson took office in March 1801, his Secretary of State, James Madison, declined to deliver the remaining commissions. Marbury and three other appointees petitioned the Supreme Court directly, invoking Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, which purported to give the Court original jurisdiction to issue writs of mandamus to federal officers. Marbury asked the Court to compel Madison to deliver his commission. The Jefferson administration largely ignored the proceeding, and no appearance was entered on Madison's behalf. The case thus presented a dispute over whether delivery of the commission was legally required and whether the Court had power to grant the requested remedy. The Judiciary Act of 1801 had created the new justiceships, and the midnight appointments were rushed through in Adams's last hours; the nomination, confirmation, signing, and sealing of the commissions were all undisputed on the record.
case.proceduralHistory: The case began as an original action in the Supreme Court under the Judiciary Act of 1789. In December 1801 the Court issued a rule to Madison to show cause why a writ of mandamus should not issue; Madison made no response. The matter was then argued on the merits before the full Court in February 1803.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the undisputed documents of appointment: the nomination, Senate confirmation, the signed commission, and affidavits establishing that the commission had been sealed but not delivered. Testimony from State Department clerks and from Marbury's agent confirmed the commission's existence and nondelivery; Madison offered no evidence.
case.plaintiffArguments: Marbury's counsel argued that once the commission was signed and sealed, the appointment was complete and Marbury held a vested legal right to the office. Delivery was a mere ministerial act that the Secretary could be compelled to perform. Mandamus was the appropriate remedy for a legal right with no other adequate remedy, and Section 13 of the Judiciary Act authorized the Court to issue the writ in its original jurisdiction.
case.defendantArguments: Madison made no appearance and offered no argument. The administration's position, expressed politically rather than in court, was that the appointment was incomplete without delivery and that the Court had no power to direct the executive branch in the matter, raising separation-of-powers objections to judicial supervision of executive discretion.
case.applicableLaw: Article III of the Constitution, which defines the Supreme Court's original and appellate jurisdiction; the Judiciary Act of 1789, Section 13, purporting to authorize original mandamus jurisdiction; the Judiciary Act of 1801 and the commissions clauses governing appointments; general common-law mandamus doctrine.
case.precedents: English mandamus practice (Rex v. Barker and related King's Bench precedents); Article III's text as construed in Chisholm v. Georgia (1793); the Court's earlier treatment of its jurisdictional limits in Hayburn's Case (1792).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Judicial review. Decided 1803. The case arose amid the bitter Federalist–Republican transition of 1801, when the incoming Jefferson administration sought to block last-minute Federalist judicial appointments.
case.tldr: Marbury sued to force delivery of his judicial commission. The Supreme Court denied the writ, ruling that the statute expanding its original jurisdiction was unconstitutional and establishing judicial review.

case.title: Pierson v. Post
case.court: Supreme Court of New York
case.actualOutcome: Reversed; judgment for Pierson. Mere pursuit does not confer possession of a wild animal; occupancy requires capture or mortal wounding.
case.questionPresented: Whether a hunter who is pursuing a fox with hounds, but has not caught or mortally wounded it, acquires a property right in the animal sufficient to sustain an action against one who then kills and takes it.
case.facts: Lodowick Post was hunting a fox on wild, unowned beach land, pursuing it with dogs and hounds and having it in sight. Jesse Pierson, knowing the fox was being hunted and pursued, killed and carried it off. Post sued Pierson for the fox, arguing his hot pursuit and intent to capture gave him a property right in the animal. Pierson argued that mere pursuit, without capture, wounding, or other occupancy, conferred no property right in a wild animal, which belonged to no one until actually possessed. The case required the court to define what constitutes possession — and thus ownership — of wild animals: pursuit alone, mortal wounding, or actual capture. Post pursued the fox with hounds on unowned beachland and had it in sight; Pierson, knowing of the chase, killed and carried off the animal before Post could take it. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Post sued Pierson in the Queens County justice court, which gave judgment for Post. Pierson appealed to the Supreme Court of New York, which reviewed whether the pursuit of a wild animal, short of capture, created a property right protected against one who then took it.
case.evidence: The record established that Post was pursuing the fox with hounds and had it in view when Pierson, aware of the pursuit, killed and took it. The dispute was legal: whether hot pursuit constituted occupancy or a property interest, or whether the fox remained wild and unowned until actually captured or mortally wounded.
case.plaintiffArguments: Post argued that his pursuit with hounds, his intent to capture, and the reasonable prospect of catching the fox gave him a property right or at least a protected interest that Pierson wrongfully defeated. He contended that a rule allowing interference at the last moment would discourage hunting and reward bad faith, and that his labor and imminent capture should be protected.
case.defendantArguments: Pierson argued that a wild animal belongs to no one until it is actually possessed — caught or mortally wounded — and that mere pursuit, however close, does not deprive the animal of its natural liberty or create property. He contended that occupancy requires physical capture or mortal wounding, that Pierson was free to take the still-wild fox, and that protecting mere pursuit would create uncertain claims.
case.applicableLaw: The common-law rule of capture for wild animals (animals ferae naturae); the requirement of occupancy — capture or mortal wounding — to establish possession and property; the rationes of first possession.
case.precedents: The Roman and common-law authorities on capture of wild animals (the Institutes and commentaries); earlier cases on possession of game; the treatises on occupancy and first possession.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Property / capture of wild animals. Decided 1805. The fox-hunt dispute produced the canonical rule that possession of a wild animal requires capture or mortal wounding, not pursuit.
case.tldr: Post was chasing a fox when Pierson killed and took it. The court ruled for Pierson, holding mere pursuit does not give property in a wild animal.

case.title: McCulloch v. Maryland
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.topic: Federal power / Necessary and Proper Clause
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Congress had implied power to charter the bank; Maryland could not tax it. Judgment for McCulloch.
case.caseType: constitutional – federal power / Necessary and Proper Clause
case.questionPresented: Whether Congress has constitutional authority to charter a national bank, and whether a state may lawfully impose a tax on a branch of that bank operating within its borders.
case.facts: In 1816 Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States, which opened a branch in Baltimore, Maryland. In 1818 the Maryland legislature enacted a statute imposing a tax on all banks operating in the state that were not chartered by the state itself — a description that in practice applied only to the Bank of the United States. The tax required payments of stamped-paper fees or an annual charge of $15,000. James McCulloch, the cashier of the Baltimore branch, issued banknotes without paying the tax, and Maryland sued him in state court to recover the statutory penalties. The litigation placed in conflict the federal government's claim to establish instrumentalities for carrying out its enumerated powers and a state's claim to tax all entities operating within its territory. The bank was deeply unpopular in many states, and several states had enacted or considered similar taxes aimed at excluding it. The Second Bank's branches had become widely unpopular after the Panic of 1819, and Maryland's statute formed part of a broader state effort to drive the federal bank's offices from their territories through taxation.
case.proceduralHistory: Maryland sued McCulloch in the Baltimore County Court to collect the tax penalties, and that court entered judgment for the state. The Maryland Court of Appeals, the state's highest court, sustained the judgment and the constitutionality of the tax. McCulloch then brought the case to the Supreme Court by writ of error.
case.evidence: The facts were essentially uncontested: the parties stipulated or it was plain from the record that McCulloch had issued notes of the federally chartered bank without paying the Maryland tax. The dispute was purely legal — the validity of the federal charter and of the state tax — and was argued by eminent counsel including Daniel Webster and William Pinckney for the bank and Luther Martin for Maryland.
case.plaintiffArguments: McCulloch's counsel argued that Congress's enumerated powers — to tax, borrow, regulate commerce, and raise armies — necessarily imply the power to create instrumentalities such as a bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause, and that the First Bank's earlier chartering supported that reading. They argued that a state tax on the federal bank was repugnant to the Constitution's supremacy, since the power to tax is the power to destroy, and that Maryland's law fell on an instrumentality of the whole people, not of Maryland alone.
case.defendantArguments: Maryland argued that the Constitution is a compact of sovereign states, that Congress may exercise only expressly delegated powers, and that chartering a bank was not a necessary means of executing any enumerated power. On the tax, the state argued that the power of taxation is an essential attribute of retained state sovereignty, that the tax fell on property within the state like any other, and that fear of abuse could not justify denying the state a power it had never surrendered.
case.applicableLaw: The Necessary and Proper Clause (Article I, Section 8, Clause 18); the Supremacy Clause (Article VI); Congress's enumerated fiscal powers; the Tenth Amendment; Maryland's 1818 bank-tax statute.
case.precedents: The First Bank charter debates and Hamilton's 1791 opinion on the bank; the Court's early federal-question practice; no prior Supreme Court decision had squarely resolved implied-powers or intergovernmental-tax-immunity questions, making this a case of first impression.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Federal power / Necessary and Proper Clause. Decided 1819. The dispute arose when several states hostile to the Second Bank of the United States sought to tax its branches out of existence.
case.tldr: Maryland taxed the Baltimore branch of the federal Bank of the United States. The Court upheld Congress's power to charter the bank and struck down the state tax on it.

case.title: Gibbons v. Ogden
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Federal coasting license preempted New York's monopoly; Congress's commerce power includes navigation. Injunction against Gibbons dissolved.
case.questionPresented: Whether a New York statute granting an exclusive steamboat monopoly on state waters is valid against a federal coasting license, and whether Congress's power to regulate commerce extends to navigation within a state.
case.facts: The New York legislature had granted Robert Fulton and Robert Livingston an exclusive right to operate steamboats in New York waters, and Aaron Ogden held an assignment of that monopoly for the route between New York and New Jersey. Thomas Gibbons operated two steamboats on the same route under a coasting license issued under the federal Coastal Licensing Act of 1793. Ogden sued in the New York Court of Chancery to enjoin Gibbons's operations as an infringement of the monopoly. The case pitted a state-created exclusive privilege against a federal license, forcing consideration of whether commerce among the states includes navigation, whether state police or internal powers permit such monopolies, and whether the federal license and the state grant could coexist when they conflicted. The monopoly had been extended through assignments and related state grants, and the rival boats had competed commercially on the lucrative New York–New Jersey route for years before Ogden sought the injunction in chancery.
case.proceduralHistory: The New York Court of Chancery granted Ogden an injunction against Gibbons's steamboat operations. The New York Court for the Correction of Errors, the state's highest court, sustained the injunction and the monopoly. Gibbons appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States, where the case was argued in February 1824.
case.evidence: The record established the state grant to Fulton and Livingston, Ogden's assignment, and Gibbons's federal coasting license under the 1793 Act. The material facts — that Gibbons's vessels carried passengers for hire between New Jersey and New York under federal license — were not disputed; the controversy was over the constitutional meaning of the commerce power and the preemptive effect of the federal license.
case.plaintiffArguments: Gibbons's counsel, including Daniel Webster, argued that 'commerce' in Article I embraces navigation and intercourse generally, not merely buying and selling, and that Congress's power over commerce among the states reaches activity within state lines wherever it concerns more than one state. They contended the federal coasting license was an exercise of that power giving Gibbons a right to navigate that New York could not defeat, and that the state monopoly therefore conflicted with valid federal law under the Supremacy Clause.
case.defendantArguments: Ogden's counsel argued that commerce meant only traffic in goods, not navigation as such, and that Congress's power stopped at the state's border, leaving internal navigation to the states. They characterized the monopoly as a legitimate exercise of New York's internal police and commerce powers, akin to inspection and ferry regulations, and denied that the federal license — a revenue and registry measure — was intended to override state-granted rights.
case.applicableLaw: The Commerce Clause (Article I, Section 8, Clause 3); the Supremacy Clause; the federal Coastal Licensing Act of 1793; New York's Fulton-Livingston steamboat monopoly statutes.
case.precedents: No earlier Supreme Court case had construed the Commerce Clause directly; counsel debated the text, the Federalist essays, and state ferry and inspection practices under the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Commerce Clause. Decided 1824. The case arose from bitter competition over lucrative steamboat routes in New York harbor during the early national boom in steam navigation.
case.tldr: Ogden held a New York steamboat monopoly; Gibbons ran rival boats under a federal license. The Court sided with Gibbons, holding that Congress's commerce power covers navigation between states.

case.title: Vaughan v. Menlove
case.court: Court of Common Pleas (England)
case.actualOutcome: Verdict for the plaintiff upheld. Negligence is judged by an objective reasonable-person standard, not the defendant's best judgment.
case.questionPresented: Whether a defendant's liability for a fire caused by his negligence is judged by an objective reasonable-person standard or by his own honest belief that he acted with sufficient caution.
case.facts: Menlove stacked a hayrick on land near the plaintiff's cottages, despite warnings from neighbours that the stack was dangerous and liable to ignite by spontaneous combustion. Menlove reportedly replied that he would 'chance it.' The hayrick did ignite, and the fire spread and burned down the plaintiff's cottages. The plaintiff sued in negligence. At trial, Menlove argued that he had acted honestly according to his own judgment and had not intended harm, contending that liability should depend on whether he had exercised his own best judgment rather than the care a reasonable person would have shown. The jury found for the plaintiff, and the defendant challenged whether negligence should be measured subjectively or by an objective standard. Neighbors had warned Menlove the rick was liable to ignite, and he reportedly answered that he would 'chance it'; the hayrick spontaneously combusted and the fire destroyed the plaintiff's cottages. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: The case was tried at the assizes, where the jury found for the plaintiff. The defendant obtained a rule to show cause in the Court of Common Pleas, arguing he was entitled to a new trial because the jury should have been instructed that he was liable only if he failed to exercise his own honest judgment. The court heard argument on the standard of care.
case.evidence: The record included evidence that Menlove had been warned the hayrick was dangerous and had chosen to take the risk, and that the rick spontaneously ignited and burned the plaintiff's cottages. The legal dispute was the standard: whether the defendant's honest but unreasonable belief that he had been careful excused him, or whether negligence is measured by the conduct of a reasonable person.
case.plaintiffArguments: The plaintiff argued that negligence is judged objectively — by the care a reasonable and prudent person would exercise — and that Menlove had been warned his hayrick was dangerous but chose to 'chance it.' He contended liability cannot depend on each defendant's subjective intelligence or honest belief, that Menlove failed to take reasonable precautions against a foreseeable risk, and that the verdict was correct.
case.defendantArguments: Menlove argued that he acted honestly according to his best judgment and that negligence should be measured by whether a defendant exercised the care of which he was personally capable, not by an objective reasonable-person standard he might not meet. He contended a new trial was required on that basis, and that subjective good faith should determine liability for an unintentional harm.
case.applicableLaw: The law of negligence and the standard of care; whether negligence is an objective failure to act as a reasonable person or a subjective question of the defendant's honest judgment and capacity.
case.precedents: The developing English negligence doctrine of the early nineteenth century; the objective standard emerging in the carriage and fire cases; the general duty to avoid foreseeable harm.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Torts / reasonable person standard. Decided 1837. The case established the objective reasonable-person standard as the measure of negligence, displacing subjective fault.
case.tldr: Menlove's hayrick, stacked despite warnings, ignited and burned his neighbor's cottages. The court held negligence is judged by the reasonable person, not the defendant's own judgment.

case.title: M'Naghten's Case
case.court: House of Lords (UK)
case.actualOutcome: Acquitted by reason of insanity. The Lords then articulated the M'Naghten rules: a defendant is not responsible if, from a defect of reason due to disease of the mind, he did not know the nature of the act or that it was wrong.
case.questionPresented: Under what circumstances a defect of reason caused by disease of the mind excuses a defendant from criminal responsibility for an act he committed.
case.facts: Daniel M'Naghten, suffering from delusions that the Prime Minister Sir Robert Peel and others were conspiring against him, shot and killed Edward Drummond, Peel's private secretary, having mistaken him for the Prime Minister. M'Naghten was charged with murder. At trial, medical evidence established that he was laboring under a disease of the mind affecting his reason and that he did not know he was doing what was wrong. The jury acquitted him on the ground of insanity. Following public and official concern about the acquittal, the House of Lords asked the judges to state the law governing the insanity defense. The resulting answers — articulating when mental disease negates criminal responsibility — became the M'Naghten rules. M'Naghten acted under delusions of persecution and mistook Drummond for the Prime Minister; the acquittal prompted the Lords to ask the judges to state the governing law of insanity. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: M'Naghten was tried at the Central Criminal Court and acquitted by reason of insanity. Because the acquittal provoked public controversy, the House of Lords posed questions to the judges on the law of insanity, and the judges' answers formulated the governing rules.
case.evidence: The trial record included medical testimony about M'Naghten's delusions and mental disease, the circumstances of the shooting, and the jury's finding that, because of his mental condition, he was not responsible. The House of Lords' proceeding produced the abstract rules — whether the defendant knew the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong — rather than resolving contested facts.
case.plaintiffArguments: The Crown's position, reflected in the prosecution, was that criminal responsibility requires proof of a knowing, voluntary unlawful act and that the insanity defense should be confined to those who, by reason of mental disease, genuinely lacked the capacity to know what they were doing or that it was wrong. The prosecution emphasized the deliberate nature of the shooting and the danger of excusing crime on the basis of mental abnormality.
case.defendantArguments: M'Naghten's defense argued that he was laboring under a delusion caused by disease of the mind such that he did not know the nature of his act or that it was wrong, and that he could not be criminally responsible. The defense relied on medical testimony establishing the delusion and its effect on his reason, contending that a man driven by delusion lacks the blameworthy mind required for murder.
case.applicableLaw: The law of criminal responsibility and the insanity defense; the standard that a defendant is not responsible if, at the time, from a defect of reason due to disease of the mind, he did not know the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong.
case.precedents: The earlier insanity cases and treatises (including the 'wild beast' test of Arnold's Case, 1724); Hadfield's Case (1800); the medical and legal literature on mental responsibility.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Criminal law / insanity defence. Decided 1843. The judges' answers, given after an acquittal that alarmed the public, produced the M'Naghten rules that governed insanity in the common-law world for generations.
case.tldr: M'Naghten, acting under delusions, killed the Prime Minister's secretary. He was acquitted as insane, and the judges formulated the enduring rules for the insanity defense.

case.title: Brown v. Kendall
case.court: Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts
case.actualOutcome: New trial ordered in defendant's favor on the law. Liability for unintentional injury requires want of ordinary care; the plaintiff bears the burden of proving negligence.
case.caseType: tort – negligence standard / burden of proof
case.questionPresented: Whether a defendant who unintentionally injured the plaintiff while separating fighting dogs is liable only if he failed to exercise ordinary care, and who bears the burden of proving negligence.
case.facts: George Kendall tried to separate two fighting dogs by striking at them with a stick. George Brown stood behind him; when Kendall raised the stick to strike a blow, he struck Brown in the eye, injuring him. Brown sued for the injury. At trial, the judge instructed the jury that if Kendall was doing a lawful act and Brown was in a proper place, Kendall was liable for the injury unless he exercised extraordinary care, placing a heavy burden on the defendant. Kendall argued that liability for unintentional injury required proof that he failed to exercise ordinary care and that the plaintiff bore the burden of proving negligence — not that the defendant had to prove he was careful. The case asked whether fault, measured by ordinary care, was the basis of liability for unintentional harm. Kendall was lawfully separating the fighting dogs and Brown stood behind him; the raised stick struck Brown's eye by accident, and the jury had been instructed that the defendant bore the burden of showing extraordinary care.
case.proceduralHistory: Brown sued in the Massachusetts trial court and won a verdict under the instructions placing the burden on the defendant to show extraordinary care. Kendall obtained review in the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts on whether the jury had been properly instructed on the standard of care and the burden of proof.
case.evidence: The record established that Kendall was lawfully separating the dogs and that his raised stick accidentally struck the plaintiff standing behind him. The legal dispute was over the proper standard: whether liability required proof of Kendall's negligence — a want of ordinary care — proven by the plaintiff, or whether the defendant had to demonstrate he had taken extraordinary care to avoid liability for a merely accidental injury.
case.plaintiffArguments: Brown argued that because Kendall was striking near him, Kendall should be liable for the resulting injury unless he had exercised extraordinary care, and that the trial instructions properly placed that burden on the defendant. He contended the injury was a direct result of Kendall's action and that one who causes injury should bear responsibility absent proof of utmost caution.
case.defendantArguments: Kendall argued that he was engaged in a lawful act and that liability for an unintentional injury required the plaintiff to prove a want of ordinary care, not for the defendant to disprove negligence. He contended the accident was unavoidable without fault, that the plaintiff bore the burden of proving negligence as the foundation of liability, and that the extraordinary-care instruction was erroneous.
case.applicableLaw: Massachusetts tort law on unintentional injury; the negligence standard of ordinary care; the burden of proof on the plaintiff to establish fault rather than on the defendant to show due care.
case.precedents: The earlier common-law treatment of trespass and accident; the emerging fault-based conception of liability displacing strict liability for direct injury; the treatises on ordinary care.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Torts / negligence standard. Decided 1850. Shaw's opinion established ordinary care as the standard for unintentional injury and placed the burden of proving negligence on the plaintiff, a foundation of American negligence law.
case.tldr: Kendall accidentally struck Brown while separating fighting dogs with a stick. The court ordered a new trial, holding unintentional injury requires proof of a want of ordinary care.

case.title: Hadley v. Baxendale
case.court: Court of Exchequer (England)
case.actualOutcome: New trial ordered; lost profits were not recoverable because the carrier had no notice the mill would be idle. Damages limited to losses arising naturally or within the parties' contemplation.
case.questionPresented: Whether a carrier is liable for a mill owner's lost profits from delayed delivery of a broken crankshaft when the carrier was not told the mill would be idle in the interim.
case.facts: The Hadleys operated a flour mill whose steam engine's crankshaft broke, halting all milling. They contracted with Baxendale's firm, Pickford & Co., to carry the broken shaft to Greenwich as a pattern for a new one, with delivery promised in a stated time. The carrier delayed delivery by several days, during which the mill stood idle, and the Hadleys claimed lost profits. The carrier had not been told that the mill was stopped or that the shaft was the only one; it knew only that it was carrying a broken part for a miller. The carrier argued the lost profits were too remote — they arose from circumstances not communicated and not reasonably within the parties' contemplation at contracting. The case required the court to define the limits of recoverable consequential damages in contract. The carrier knew only that it carried a broken crankshaft for a miller; it had not been told the mill was standing idle or that no other shaft existed to keep it running.
case.proceduralHistory: The Hadleys sued in the Court of Exchequer and won a jury verdict that included lost profits. The carrier obtained a rule nisi for a new trial on the ground that the jury had been misdirected on damages. The Court of Exchequer heard the matter on the remoteness of the damages claimed.
case.evidence: The record established the contract of carriage, the delay, and the fact that the carrier knew it was carrying a broken crankshaft from a mill but had not been informed that the mill could not operate without it. The dispute concerned which losses flowed naturally from the breach or were reasonably within the parties' contemplation, versus losses arising from special circumstances never communicated.
case.plaintiffArguments: The mill owners argued that the carrier, knowing it carried a part needed for the mill's operation, was liable for all losses flowing from its delay, including the profits lost while the mill stood idle. They contended the delay directly caused the shutdown, that a carrier taking a mill's critical part should foresee the consequence of delay, and that the jury's verdict awarding lost profits was proper.
case.defendantArguments: The carrier argued that it could be liable only for losses that arose naturally from the breach in the ordinary course or that were within the parties' reasonable contemplation when the contract was made. It contended it had not been told the mill was stopped or that the shaft was indispensable, that the lost profits were attributable to undisclosed special circumstances, and that the damages were too remote to be recoverable.
case.applicableLaw: Contract damages doctrine: the rule limiting recovery to losses arising naturally from the breach or reasonably within the parties' contemplation at the time of contracting, including losses attributable to communicated special circumstances.
case.precedents: The existing English rules on damages for breach of contract; Blanchard v. Ely and similar carriage cases; the general common-law framework for consequential damages.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Contracts / consequential damages. Decided 1854. The case produced the two-limb rule on remoteness that remains the foundation of contract damages across the common-law world.
case.tldr: A carrier's delay in delivering a mill's broken crankshaft cost the mill profits. The court denied recovery for lost profits the carrier could not have contemplated.

case.title: Dred Scott v. Sandford
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Scott lost. Held that persons of African descent were not citizens and could not sue in federal court; Missouri Compromise unconstitutional. Later repudiated by the 13th and 14th Amendments.
case.questionPresented: Whether a person of African descent whose ancestors were enslaved is a citizen capable of suing in federal court, and whether residence in a free state or territory made an enslaved person free, including whether Congress could prohibit slavery in the territories.
case.facts: Dred Scott was an enslaved man owned by Dr. John Emerson, an army surgeon. Emerson took Scott from Missouri to reside at posts in Illinois, a free state, and in the Wisconsin Territory, where slavery was barred by the Missouri Compromise; Scott married and had children during those years. After Emerson's death, Scott returned to Missouri and was held by Emerson's widow and then by her brother, John Sanford of New York. Scott sued Sanford in federal court in Missouri for battery and false imprisonment, claiming that his residence on free soil had made him a free man and that diversity of citizenship gave the federal court jurisdiction. The suit raised whether a Black person descended from slaves could be a citizen under the Constitution, whether residence in a free jurisdiction ended slave status under Missouri's own once-free-always-free doctrine, and whether Congress had power to ban slavery in the territories. The suit was financed by abolitionist supporters and defended by slaveholding interests, turning one man's claim to freedom into a national contest over slavery's expansion and the citizenship of free Black Americans.
case.proceduralHistory: Scott first sued in Missouri state court and won a verdict of freedom at trial, but the Missouri Supreme Court set that aside and returned him to slavery, abandoning its own earlier precedents. He then sued Sanford in federal circuit court, where a jury found for Sanford after the court instructed that Missouri law governed Scott's status. Scott sought review in the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The record consisted of stipulations and testimony tracing Scott's travels with Emerson to Rock Island, Illinois, and Fort Snelling in the Wisconsin Territory, his marriage, and the chain of ownership through Emerson's widow to Sanford. Sanford pleaded in abatement that Scott, as a person of African descent, was not a citizen and could not sue, and the case proceeded on that plea and an agreed statement of facts.
case.plaintiffArguments: Scott's counsel argued that residence in a free state and a free territory made Scott permanently free under the well-established rule that voluntary removal to free soil emancipates, a rule Missouri courts had long applied. They argued that free Black persons were citizens of the states in which they lived and hence citizens of the United States entitled to invoke federal jurisdiction, and that Congress's power to govern the territories included the Missouri Compromise's ban on slavery.
case.defendantArguments: Sanford's counsel argued that persons of African descent could not be citizens within the meaning of the Constitution, so the federal court lacked jurisdiction regardless of Scott's status. On the merits, they argued that Scott's status was determined by Missouri law, which treated him as a slave notwithstanding his temporary residence elsewhere, and that Congress had no constitutional power to prohibit slave property in the territories, rendering the Missouri Compromise's restriction invalid.
case.applicableLaw: Article III diversity jurisdiction and the Constitution's citizenship provisions; the Missouri Compromise of 1820; Article IV's Territory Clause; the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment as invoked for property rights; Missouri's conflict-of-laws doctrine on slave status.
case.precedents: Missouri's own earlier decisions emancipating slaves taken to free soil (e.g., Rachel v. Walker, 1836); Strader v. Graham (1851); Somerset v. Stewart (K.B. 1772); federal and state precedent on the citizenship of free Black persons.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Citizenship / slavery. Decided 1857. The case reached the Court amid the national crisis over slavery's expansion into the territories, shortly after the Kansas-Nebraska Act and the violence of Bleeding Kansas.
case.tldr: Dred Scott sued for freedom after living on free soil. The Court ruled that Black Americans were not citizens who could sue in federal court and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories.

case.title: Raffles v. Wichelhaus (The Peerless)
case.court: Court of Exchequer (England)
case.actualOutcome: Judgment for the defendants. With two ships named Peerless and no meeting of the minds on which was meant, there was no binding contract.
case.questionPresented: Whether a contract for the sale of cotton to arrive 'ex Peerless from Bombay' was binding when there were two ships named Peerless and the parties meant different ones, so no unambiguous agreement was formed.
case.facts: Raffles contracted to sell Wichelhaus 125 bales of cotton to be delivered 'ex Peerless from Bombay.' There were two ships named Peerless sailing from Bombay, one departing in October and one in December. The seller meant the December Peerless and tendered cotton arriving on it; the buyer had meant the October Peerless and refused the tender, saying he had intended the earlier ship. The seller sued for breach. The buyer argued there was no binding agreement because each party meant a different ship — a latent ambiguity producing no meeting of the minds. The seller argued the contract was sufficiently definite, that he had tendered conforming cotton, and that the buyer was bound to accept it. Two ships named Peerless sailed from Bombay, one in October and one in December; the seller meant the later vessel and the buyer the earlier, and neither meaning appeared in the written terms. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: The seller sued in the Court of Exchequer for the price or damages for non-acceptance. The defendants pleaded the ambiguity in the ship's identity. At the hearing on demurrer, the court considered whether the contract could be enforced given the two ships of the same name and the parties' different understandings.
case.evidence: The record showed the written contract term 'ex Peerless' and the existence of two Bombay ships of that name arriving at different times. The dispute was whether extrinsic evidence of the ambiguity negated the contract — that is, whether the parties' different intentions about which Peerless was meant prevented the formation of a single agreement.
case.plaintiffArguments: The seller argued that the contract was a valid agreement for cotton 'ex Peerless,' that he had tendered cotton arriving on a ship of that name in conformity with the contract, and that the buyer was bound to accept and pay. He contended the contract was definite enough — any ship named Peerless sufficed — and that the buyer's unstated preference for the earlier ship could not excuse his refusal.
case.defendantArguments: The buyer argued that there was no consensus ad idem — no meeting of the minds — because each party meant a different ship named Peerless, so the contract was void for ambiguity. He contended he intended the October Peerless, that the seller intended the December one, and that the latent ambiguity meant there was never a single binding agreement to which he could be held.
case.applicableLaw: English contract law on formation and the requirement of consensus ad idem; latent ambiguity in the subject matter; the effect of mutual mistake or divergent meanings on contract enforceability.
case.precedents: The common-law doctrines on contract formation, ambiguity, and mistake; earlier cases on parol evidence of parties' meanings; the general rule that no agreement exists where the parties intend different subjects.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Contracts / mutual mistake. Decided 1864. The 'Peerless' case became the classic authority that a latent ambiguity depriving the parties of a shared meaning prevents contract formation.
case.tldr: Two ships named Peerless sailed from Bombay, and buyer and seller meant different ones. The court found no binding contract for want of a meeting of the minds.

case.title: Rylands v. Fletcher
case.court: House of Lords (UK)
case.actualOutcome: Appeal dismissed; Rylands liable. One who brings onto land something likely to do mischief if it escapes is strictly liable for the escape.
case.questionPresented: Whether a landowner who brings onto his land a substance likely to do mischief if it escapes is strictly liable for the damage it causes, without proof of negligence.
case.facts: Rylands employed contractors to build a reservoir on his land. Unknown to the parties, the land contained disused mine shafts connecting to the plaintiff Fletcher's coal mines below. When the reservoir was filled, water broke through the old shafts and flooded Fletcher's mines. Fletcher sued for the damage. Rylands had not been personally negligent, and the negligence, if any, was the contractors'. The case raised whether a defendant who brings onto land something that escapes and causes damage is liable irrespective of negligence — the doctrine of strict liability for non-natural use of land — or whether liability required proof of fault in the construction or maintenance of the reservoir. Unknown disused mine shafts connected the reservoir site to Fletcher's workings below; when filled, the water broke through and flooded the mines without proof of Rylands's personal fault. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Fletcher sued in the Court of Exchequer, which initially found no liability absent negligence. On further review the Exchequer Chamber found for Fletcher, articulating the rule that one who brings something likely to do mischief if it escapes onto his land is responsible for the escape. Rylands appealed to the House of Lords, which considered the rule's scope and its requirement of non-natural use.
case.evidence: The record established that Rylands built the reservoir, that the water escaped through the concealed mine shafts into Fletcher's mines, and that the contractor's work was done without proof of Rylands's own negligence. The legal question was whether liability for the escape required negligence or attached by virtue of the dangerous accumulation itself.
case.plaintiffArguments: Fletcher argued that one who brings onto his land and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes does so at his peril, and is answerable for the natural consequence of its escape regardless of negligence. He contended the reservoir was a non-natural accumulation that escaped and flooded his mines, and that liability attached without the need to prove fault in construction.
case.defendantArguments: Rylands argued that liability required negligence and that he was not responsible for the contractors' undisclosed failure to discover the hidden shafts, nor for an act of God or latent defect. He contended that building a reservoir was a lawful use of land, that strict liability for escapes would impose unprecedented and unlimited responsibility on ordinary land uses, and that Fletcher's remedy, if any, lay against the contractors.
case.applicableLaw: The law of tort regarding liability for things escaping from land; strict liability for non-natural use versus the requirement of negligence; the rule that one who brings a dangerous accumulation onto land is liable for its escape.
case.precedents: The existing English tort doctrine on trespass, nuisance, and liability for fire and animals; the fault-based approach of the earlier Exchequer decision; the older strict-liability categories.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Torts / strict liability. Decided 1868. The case established the rule for which it is named — strict liability for the escape of a non-natural accumulation — that became a cornerstone of tort law.
case.tldr: Water from Rylands's new reservoir burst through old shafts and flooded a mine. The court held him strictly liable for the escape of the accumulated water.

case.title: R v Dudley and Stephens
case.court: Queen's Bench Division (England)
case.actualOutcome: Defendants convicted of murder. Necessity is no defence to murder; death sentences later commuted to six months' imprisonment.
case.questionPresented: Whether necessity is a defense to a charge of murder for killing an innocent person to preserve one's own life.
case.facts: Tom Dudley and Edwin Stephens, along with a third sailor and a seventeen-year-old cabin boy, were cast adrift in an open lifeboat after their yacht, the Mignonette, sank far from land in the South Atlantic. After many days without food or water and facing death, Dudley and Stephens decided to kill the boy — who was weakest and closest to death and who had no family dependent on him — and the three men fed on his body. Four days later they were rescued. They were tried for murder. The defendants argued necessity: that killing the boy was the only way to save their own lives and that the extreme circumstances excused the act. The Crown argued that killing an innocent person is murder regardless of necessity and that no legal doctrine permits deliberately taking an innocent life to preserve one's own. The men drifted twenty days without food or water; the boy was weakest and closest to death, and rescuers arrived four days after the killing.
case.proceduralHistory: Dudley and Stephens were tried before a special assize; the jury returned a special verdict finding the facts — that the men would probably have died and the boy would have died sooner without the killing — but leaving the legal question to the court whether those facts constituted murder. The matter was referred to the Queen's Bench Division for a determination of law.
case.evidence: The special verdict established the essential facts: the shipwreck, the lack of food and water, the imminence of death for all, the boy's weaker condition, and the deliberate killing for sustenance followed by rescue four days later. The legal question was whether necessity, on those facts, excused the deliberate taking of an innocent life.
case.plaintiffArguments: The Crown argued that deliberately killing an innocent person is murder and that no doctrine of necessity justifies taking an innocent life to save one's own. It contended the law cannot permit each person to judge whose life is more valuable, that recognizing the defense would set a dangerous precedent for future desperate acts, and that the special verdict's facts established intentional killing that the law could not excuse.
case.defendantArguments: The defendants argued that the extreme necessity — imminent death for all, the boy's weaker condition and earlier certain death — justified or excused the killing as a lesser evil. They contended the act was not murder because the circumstances left no alternative, that the law should account for the irresistible pressure of survival, and that examples of necessity in emergency were recognized in principle if not in direct precedent.
case.applicableLaw: The law of murder and the proposed defense of necessity; the question whether extreme circumstances can excuse the intentional killing of an innocent; the special-verdict procedure for reserving questions of law.
case.precedents: No direct precedent; the court considered historical dicta, the philosophers' and legal writers' treatment of necessity, and the principle that the law does not permit the killing of innocents.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Criminal law / necessity defence. Decided 1884. The lifeboat case became the canonical authority that necessity is no defense to murder and remains a staple of criminal-law teaching.
case.tldr: Shipwrecked sailors killed and ate a cabin boy to survive. The court convicted them of murder, holding necessity is no defense to killing an innocent.

case.title: Hamer v. Sidway
case.court: New York Court of Appeals
case.actualOutcome: Reversed; judgment for the claimant. Forbearance from lawful conduct is valid consideration regardless of benefit to the promisor.
case.questionPresented: Whether a promise to pay $5,000 to a nephew if he refrained from drinking, smoking, and gambling until twenty-one was supported by consideration, making the uncle's estate liable on it.
case.facts: An uncle promised his nephew $5,000 if the boy would refrain from drinking liquor, using tobacco, swearing, and playing cards for money until he turned twenty-one. The nephew performed, forgoing these lawful activities for years. When he reached twenty-one, he wrote to claim the money; the uncle acknowledged the debt and said he would hold the money with interest until the nephew was more mature, but died without paying. The nephew's assignee, Louisa Hamer, sued the executor, Franklin Sidway. The estate argued there was no consideration — that the nephew's abstinence benefited him and conferred no benefit on the uncle — and that the promise was an unenforceable gratuitous promise. The assignee argued that forbearance from legal rights was valid consideration. The uncle promised $5,000 if the boy abstained until twenty-one; the nephew performed fully, and the uncle acknowledged the debt in writing before dying without paying it. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Hamer sued on the contract in the New York trial court and prevailed. The intermediate appellate court ruled for the estate, finding insufficient consideration. The New York Court of Appeals reviewed whether forbearance from lawful conduct constituted adequate consideration for the uncle's promise.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the nephew's forbearance from the specified activities and the uncle's written acknowledgment of the debt and promise to pay with interest. The legal dispute was whether the nephew's surrender of his lawful right to drink, smoke, and gamble was a legal detriment constituting consideration, regardless of any benefit to the uncle.
case.plaintiffArguments: Hamer argued that the nephew's forbearance from lawful conduct — drinking, smoking, and gambling — was a legal detriment and valid consideration for the promise, regardless of whether it benefited the uncle. She contended the nephew surrendered rights he was entitled to exercise, that the uncle acknowledged the debt in writing, and that the promise was enforceable once the condition was performed.
case.defendantArguments: Sidway argued that the nephew's abstinence was not a detriment but a benefit to himself, that the uncle received nothing of value, and so no consideration supported the promise. It contended the arrangement was a gratuitous promise unenforceable at law, that a promise conditioned on conduct beneficial to the promisee is a gift, and that the estate could not be charged on it.
case.applicableLaw: New York contract law on consideration; the doctrine that forbearance from a legal right is sufficient consideration; the distinction between benefit to the promisor and detriment to the promisee.
case.precedents: The bargained-for-exchange and legal-detriment doctrine; earlier cases treating forbearance as consideration; the general sufficiency-of-consideration rules.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Contracts / consideration. Decided 1891. The case is the classic authority that forbearance from lawful conduct is valid consideration regardless of benefit to the promisor.
case.tldr: An uncle promised $5,000 if his nephew abstained from drinking, smoking, and gambling until twenty-one. The court enforced the promise, treating forbearance as consideration.

case.title: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.
case.court: Court of Appeal (England and Wales)
case.actualOutcome: Appeal dismissed; judgment for Mrs Carlill for the £100 reward. The advertisement was a unilateral offer accepted by performance.
case.caseType: contract – unilateral offer / acceptance by performance
case.questionPresented: Whether a company's advertised promise to pay £100 to anyone who used its product as directed and still caught influenza was a binding unilateral offer accepted by performance, or mere advertising puffery.
case.facts: The Carbolic Smoke Ball Company advertised in newspapers that it would pay £100 reward to any person who contracted influenza after using its smoke ball — a device releasing carbolic acid vapour — according to the printed directions, and stated that £1,000 had been deposited in a bank to show its sincerity. Louisa Carlill bought a smoke ball, used it as directed for the prescribed period, and nevertheless contracted influenza. When the company refused to pay, she sued for the £100. The company argued the advertisement was a mere puff too vague to be an offer, that it could not be an offer to the whole world, that she had not notified acceptance, and that there was no consideration. The case raised foundational questions about unilateral contracts, acceptance by performance, and the difference between offers and advertising 'puffs.' The company had deposited £1,000 to show sincerity and printed explicit directions for use; Mrs Carlill purchased the ball, followed the directions faithfully, and nevertheless contracted influenza.
case.proceduralHistory: Carlill sued in the Queen's Bench Division and won judgment for the £100. The company appealed to the Court of Appeal, which heard the case on the questions whether the advertisement was an offer, whether performance without notification constituted acceptance, and whether consideration existed.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the advertisement's text — including the £1,000 deposit as evidence of sincerity — proof of Carlill's purchase and use of the smoke ball as directed, and her contraction of influenza. The dispute was whether these facts completed a contract: an offer, acceptance by performance, and consideration, or instead left the advertisement a non-binding puff.
case.plaintiffArguments: Carlill argued that the advertisement, with its specific promise and the £1,000 deposit to show sincerity, was a definite offer that she accepted by performing the required condition — using the smoke ball as directed and catching influenza. She contended notification of acceptance was unnecessary for a unilateral offer, that use of the product was consideration moving to the company's benefit, and that the company's refusal was a breach.
case.defendantArguments: The company argued that the advertisement was a mere advertising puff, too vague and indefinite to constitute an offer, and that one cannot contract with the whole world. It contended that acceptance required notification before performance could bind the offeror, that there was no consideration, and that the claim failed for lack of a concluded agreement on essential terms.
case.applicableLaw: The law of contract formation: offer versus invitation or puff, unilateral offers, acceptance by performance, notification requirements, and consideration; the principles governing rewards and advertisements.
case.precedents: The existing English contract doctrine on offers and acceptance; Williams v. Carwardine (1833) (reward/performance); Denton v. Great Northern Railway (1855); general common-law rules on consideration.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Contracts / unilateral offer. Decided 1893. The Victorian advertising dispute became the canonical authority on unilateral contracts and the enforceability of reward offers.
case.tldr: Mrs Carlill used the smoke ball as directed and caught influenza anyway. The court enforced the advertised £100 reward as a unilateral offer accepted by performance.

case.title: Plessy v. Ferguson
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Separate-but-equal accommodations upheld under the 14th Amendment. Overruled by Brown v. Board (1954).
case.questionPresented: Whether a Louisiana statute requiring railway companies to provide 'equal but separate' accommodations for white and Black passengers, and criminalizing use of the wrong car, violates the Thirteenth or Fourteenth Amendments.
case.facts: Louisiana's Separate Car Act of 1890 required railroads to provide separate but equal accommodations for white and Black passengers and made it a misdemeanor for a passenger to occupy a car assigned to the other race. Homer Plessy, a man of one-eighth African ancestry, was recruited by a citizens' committee in New Orleans to test the law. In June 1892 he bought a first-class ticket, boarded the East Louisiana Railway, and took a seat in the whites-only car. When he identified himself as Black and refused to move, he was arrested and charged before Judge John Ferguson in the Orleans Parish criminal court. Plessy challenged the statute's constitutionality, arguing that enforced separation stamped Black citizens with a badge of inferiority and denied the equal protection and privileges of citizenship guaranteed by the post-Civil War amendments. The Comité des Citoyens of New Orleans had arranged the test carefully, with the railroad itself cooperating in the arrest, and the committee retained counsel to carry the constitutional challenge all the way to Washington.
case.proceduralHistory: Plessy pleaded not guilty and sought a writ of prohibition and certiorari against Judge Ferguson to halt the prosecution, arguing the statute was unconstitutional. The Louisiana Supreme Court declined to disturb the prosecution and upheld the Act under prior authority upholding segregation laws. Plessy then obtained review in the Supreme Court of the United States; his criminal prosecution remained pending in the meantime.
case.evidence: The record was thin and largely stipulated: Plessy's racial classification, his refusal to leave the white car, and his arrest were undisputed. The contest was legal and constitutional — the meaning of equal protection and the permissible scope of state police power to separate the races — rather than a dispute over facts.
case.plaintiffArguments: Plessy's counsel, Albion Tourgée among them, argued that compulsory separation based on race imposed a badge of servitude forbidden by the Thirteenth Amendment and denied equal protection under the Fourteenth. They argued the law deprived Plessy of the 'property' of his reputation as a white man, empowered train conductors to make arbitrary racial classifications, and was designed not to separate the races neutrally but to subordinate Black passengers, contrary to the color-blind character of the Constitution.
case.defendantArguments: The state argued that the Act was a reasonable exercise of the police power to preserve public order and comfort, applying equally to both races since each was confined to separate but equal accommodations. They contended the Fourteenth Amendment guaranteed legal and political equality, not social commingling, and pointed to widespread practices of separate schools and facilities accepted even in Congress as evidence that reasonable distinctions by race were permissible.
case.applicableLaw: The Thirteenth Amendment (abolition of slavery and badges of servitude); the Fourteenth Amendment (equal protection, privileges or immunities, due process); Louisiana Separate Car Act of 1890; state police-power doctrine.
case.precedents: Slaughter-House Cases (1873); Strauder v. West Virginia (1880); the Civil Rights Cases (1883); state and lower-court decisions sustaining segregated schooling, such as Roberts v. City of Boston (1850).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Equal protection / segregation. Decided 1896. The case was a planned test suit mounted by a New Orleans citizens' committee during the rapid spread of Jim Crow legislation across the post-Reconstruction South.
case.tldr: Plessy was arrested for sitting in a whites-only railcar. The Court upheld Louisiana's separate-car law under the 'separate but equal' doctrine.

case.title: Lochner v. New York
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. The Bakeshop Act's 60-hour limit violated liberty of contract under the Due Process Clause.
case.caseType: constitutional – due process / liberty of contract
case.questionPresented: Whether a New York statute limiting the hours of labor in bakeries to ten per day and sixty per week is a valid exercise of the police power or an unconstitutional interference with the liberty of contract protected by the Fourteenth Amendment.
case.facts: New York's Bakeshop Act of 1895 regulated sanitary conditions in bakeries and limited employment to ten hours per day and sixty hours per week. Joseph Lochner, owner of a bakery in Utica, was convicted and fined for permitting an employee to work more than sixty hours in a week. Lochner challenged the hours provision as an unwarranted interference with the freedom of employer and employee to contract for labor. The state defended the law as a health measure: bakery work involved flour dust and long hours in hot cellars, which reformers and legislators believed endangered workers' health, and the law had been championed as part of a broader movement for maximum-hours and factory regulation. The dispute turned on whether the hours limit bore a real relation to worker or public health, or was instead a labor regulation infringing contractual freedom. Bakery reformers had documented long overnight shifts in cellar bakeries and argued the hours limit protected health, while Lochner contended adult bakers could judge their own working conditions and bargain accordingly.
case.proceduralHistory: Lochner was convicted in the Oneida County Court and fined $50 for a first offense under the Act; after a second violation he was convicted again and fined. The New York Court of Appeals, over dissent, sustained the hours provision as within the police power. Lochner then brought the case to the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The record included Lochner's convictions for employing a baker beyond the statutory hours and testimony about bakery working conditions. Counsel on both sides marshalled medical and statistical material — an early 'Brandeis brief' approach — about the health effects of long hours and flour dust on bakers, though Lochner's side disputed that baking was unusually unhealthy.
case.plaintiffArguments: Lochner argued that the Due Process Clause protects liberty of contract as a fundamental right and that the hours law was a labor regulation, not a health measure. He contended baking was not so dangerous as to justify special protection, that bakers are competent adults able to judge their own interests, and that the statute was an arbitrary, paternalistic interference amounting to class legislation rather than a reasonable exercise of police power.
case.defendantArguments: New York argued that the police power extends to protecting the health of workers and the public, that scientific evidence showed long hours in bakeries were injurious, and that the legislature's judgment on such matters deserved deference. The state maintained the law was a reasonable health regulation indistinguishable from mining-hour and sanitary laws already upheld, not a mere redistribution of bargaining power.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; state police power doctrine; New York Bakeshop Act of 1895; substantive due process and liberty-of-contract doctrine as it then stood.
case.precedents: Holden v. Hardy (1898) (upholding hours limits for miners); Munn v. Illinois (1877); Allgeyer v. Louisiana (1897); Muller v. Oregon was decided later and is not available.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Liberty of contract / due process. Decided 1905. The case tested Progressive Era labor regulation at the height of judicial skepticism toward interference with freedom of contract.
case.tldr: A bakery owner was fined for letting an employee exceed New York's 60-hour week. The Court struck the limit down as an unconstitutional interference with liberty of contract.

case.title: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co.
case.court: New York Court of Appeals
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. A manufacturer owes a duty of care to remote purchasers regardless of privity; judgment for MacPherson.
case.questionPresented: Whether an automobile manufacturer owes a duty of care to a purchaser injured by a defective wheel, even though the manufacturer sold the car to a dealer rather than directly to the consumer.
case.facts: Donald MacPherson bought a Buick automobile from a dealer and was injured when a defective wooden wheel collapsed, throwing him from the car. The wheel had been manufactured by a supplier and installed by Buick without adequate inspection. MacPherson sued Buick in negligence. Buick argued it owed no duty to MacPherson because there was no privity of contract — it had sold the car to a dealer, not to him — and that under existing doctrine a manufacturer was liable for a defective product only if it was inherently dangerous, like a weapon or poison. MacPherson argued that an automobile, though not inherently dangerous, became dangerous if negligently made and was likely to injure its foreseeable user, and that the manufacturer should be responsible regardless of privity. The wheel was manufactured by a supplier and installed without inspection; Buick argued an automobile was not an inherently dangerous article and that its duty ran only to the immediate dealer.
case.proceduralHistory: MacPherson sued in the New York trial court and obtained a judgment for negligence. The Appellate Division sustained the verdict. Buick appealed to the New York Court of Appeals on the privity question, and the Court heard the case on whether the manufacturer owed a duty to a remote purchaser.
case.evidence: The record included proof that the wheel was defective, that the defect was discoverable by reasonable inspection, and that Buick had purchased the wheel from another manufacturer and installed it without inspecting it. The legal dispute concerned whether the privity requirement barred a negligence claim by a consumer against a manufacturer whose product foreseeably injured him.
case.plaintiffArguments: MacPherson argued that a manufacturer who puts a product into commerce owes a duty of care to those who will foreseeably use it, regardless of privity, and that an automobile negligently made is a thing of danger liable to injure its user. He contended Buick's failure to inspect the wheel was negligent, that foreseeability of injury to the driver sufficed, and that the privity rule should not shield manufacturers whose negligence reaches the consumer.
case.defendantArguments: Buick argued that it owed no duty to MacPherson absent privity of contract, that an automobile was not an inherently dangerous article within the recognized exception, and that liability for defective products ran only to the immediate purchaser. It contended extending negligence to remote buyers would collapse the distinction between contract and tort and expose manufacturers to indeterminate liability.
case.applicableLaw: New York negligence law; the privity-of-contract requirement for product liability and its exceptions for inherently dangerous articles; the emerging rule that manufacturers owe a duty to foreseeable users regardless of privity.
case.precedents: Thomas v. Winchester (1852) (dangerous article exception); Loop v. Litchfield (1870); Devlin v. Smith (1882); Winterbottom v. Wright (1842) (privity).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Torts / products liability. Decided 1916. Cardozo's opinion abolished the privity barrier for negligently made products and laid the groundwork for modern products liability.

case.title: Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon
case.court: New York Court of Appeals
case.actualOutcome: Reversed; the contract was enforceable. The agent's implied promise to use reasonable efforts supplied consideration.
case.questionPresented: Whether an agreement giving an agent exclusive rights to market a designer's endorsements was supported by consideration even though the agent's promise to use reasonable efforts was only implied.
case.facts: Lady Duff-Gordon, a famous fashion designer, signed a contract giving Otis Wood the exclusive right, for a year, to place endorsements of her name on products and to market her designs, in return for half of all profits. The writing did not expressly state that Wood would make any effort. When Lady Duff-Gordon placed endorsements herself and kept the profits, Wood sued for breach. She defended on the ground that Wood had given no consideration: because he had not expressly promised to do anything, the agreement was an unenforceable gift of an exclusive privilege. Wood argued that the contract necessarily implied a promise to use reasonable efforts, which supplied consideration and made the agreement binding. The writing gave Wood exclusive rights and half the profits but never expressly bound him to any effort; Lady Duff-Gordon then placed endorsements herself and kept the proceeds. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Wood sued in the New York trial court, which sustained a demurrer to the complaint and dismissed for lack of consideration. The Appellate Division ruled for Wood. The Court of Appeals reviewed whether the contract, though silent on the agent's duties, contained an implied promise sufficient to constitute consideration.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the written agreement conferring exclusive marketing rights and profit-sharing, and Lady Duff-Gordon's own endorsements made outside it. The legal dispute was whether the agreement could be read to imply a promise of reasonable efforts by Wood, converting a bare grant of exclusivity into a bilateral contract supported by consideration.
case.plaintiffArguments: Wood argued that the exclusive-rights agreement necessarily implied his promise to use reasonable efforts to market her endorsements, since the profit-sharing would have been worthless otherwise, and that this implied promise supplied consideration. He contended the contract was formed and enforceable, that Lady Duff-Gordon breached by placing her own endorsements, and that the law implies reasonable efforts in exclusive-agency agreements.
case.defendantArguments: Lady Duff-Gordon argued that the agreement imposed no obligation on Wood — he promised nothing and could have done nothing while collecting half her profits — so it lacked consideration and was unenforceable. She contended that courts cannot supply a promise the parties did not express, that the writing was a one-sided grant of rights, and that her own subsequent endorsements violated no contract.
case.applicableLaw: New York contract law on consideration; the doctrine of implied promises, including the implied covenant of reasonable efforts in exclusive-agency agreements; the distinction between bilateral contracts and gratuitous promises.
case.precedents: The consideration doctrine and the mutuality cases; earlier decisions implying promises to sustain bargains; Cardozo's developing approach to implied terms.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Contracts / implied promise. Decided 1917. Cardozo's opinion found an implied promise of reasonable efforts, making the case a classic on consideration and exclusive-dealing agreements.
case.tldr: A designer placed her own endorsements despite an exclusive marketing deal. The court enforced the contract, implying the agent's promise of reasonable efforts.
