case.title: International News Service v. Associated Press
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed injunction. Appropriating a competitor's fresh news for commercial gain is unfair competition (quasi-property in hot news).
case.questionPresented: Whether a news service's taking of a competitor's published news — fresh 'hot news' gathered at expense — for its own commercial distribution is unfair competition that may be enjoined.
case.facts: The Associated Press gathered news at great expense from its members and correspondents and distributed it to member newspapers. The International News Service, barred from using AP sources and denied access to Allied war news, copied AP's published news from early editions and distributed it to INS's own customers, sometimes before AP's western editions had published. AP sued to enjoin the practice as unfair competition — misappropriation of the product of AP's costly labor. INS argued that news, once published, was public property in the public domain and could be freely copied, that copyright did not protect the facts of news, and that no duty or contract bound it to AP. The case asked whether a quasi-property right existed in fresh news between competitors. INS copied AP's published dispatches from early editions, sometimes reaching western papers before AP's own editions; the news itself was uncopyrighted fact gathered at AP's considerable expense.
case.proceduralHistory: The AP sued in the federal district court, which enjoined INS's copying. The Second Circuit sustained the injunction. INS petitioned the Supreme Court on whether appropriating a competitor's published news for commercial distribution was an enjoinable wrong.
case.evidence: The record established that INS systematically copied AP's news from its published editions and resold it to competing newspapers, sometimes reaching markets ahead of AP. The legal dispute concerned whether the uncopyrighted facts of news could nonetheless be protected against a competitor's misappropriation as a quasi-property interest between rival news services.
case.plaintiffArguments: AP argued that the news it gathered at great expense was, as between competitors, a form of property — quasi-property — that INS misappropriated for commercial gain without bearing the cost of gathering. It contended the practice was unfair competition destroying the incentive to gather news, that the law protected the product of labor against a competitor's free-riding, and that the injunction was a proper remedy regardless of copyright.
case.defendantArguments: INS argued that published news was public property in the public domain, free for anyone to copy, and that no copyright protected facts. It contended there was no contract or duty to AP, that misappropriation doctrine did not extend to publicly disseminated facts, that the injunction would create a monopoly over news, and that the public interest in dissemination outweighed AP's commercial claim.
case.applicableLaw: Federal unfair-competition doctrine; the quasi-property theory of 'hot news' misappropriation; the limited scope of copyright over facts; the law governing a competitor's appropriation of a rival's product.
case.precedents: The unfair-competition and trade-identity cases; copyright doctrine excluding facts; International News Service was decided under the federal common-law framework later reconsidered after Erie.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Unfair competition / misappropriation. Decided 1918. The 'hot news' doctrine created a narrow, enduring quasi-property protection for time-sensitive factual reporting between competitors.
case.tldr: INS copied AP's freshly gathered news and resold it to rivals. The Court enjoined the practice as unfair competition, recognizing quasi-property in 'hot news.'

case.title: Schenck v. United States
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.topic: Free speech / clear and present danger
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Distributing anti-draft leaflets in wartime presented a clear and present danger; conviction upheld.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Espionage Act of 1917, as applied to the mailing of anti-draft leaflets during wartime, violates the First Amendment's protection of speech.
case.facts: Charles Schenck, general secretary of the Socialist Party in Philadelphia, supervised the printing and mailing of some fifteen thousand leaflets to men who had been called to military service during the First World War. The leaflets condemned the draft as involuntary servitude under the Thirteenth Amendment and urged recipients to assert their rights and petition for repeal of conscription, while eschewing explicit advocacy of unlawful resistance. Schenck was indicted under the Espionage Act for conspiring to obstruct the recruiting and enlistment service and for using the mails to transmit nonmailable matter. The case required the Court to consider how far speech critical of war policy could be punished when the government claimed it tended to obstruct military mobilization. The leaflet mixed Thirteenth Amendment argument with calls for lawful petition, and prosecutors relied on its deliberate distribution to drafted men as evidence of intent to obstruct recruiting. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Schenck and a co-defendant were tried in the federal district court in Philadelphia and convicted by a jury on all three counts of the indictment. Schenck appealed directly to the Supreme Court, arguing that his conduct was protected speech and that the Espionage Act could not constitutionally reach it.
case.evidence: The prosecution introduced the leaflets themselves, mailing records showing distribution to drafted men, and evidence tying Schenck to the Socialist Party's printing and mailing operation. The defense did not seriously dispute the mailing; the fight was over whether the leaflet's contents — advocacy framed as appeals to lawful petition — could constitutionally be treated as criminal obstruction.
case.plaintiffArguments: Schenck argued that the leaflet was political advocacy protected by the First Amendment: it urged lawful petition and asserted constitutional objections to conscription without calling for violence or unlawful resistance. He contended that punishing the mailing criminalized dissent, that any obstruction of recruitment was speculative, and that the Thirteenth Amendment claim about conscription was legitimate argument entitled to constitutional protection.
case.defendantArguments: The United States argued that the First Amendment does not protect speech whose natural tendency and intent is to obstruct an essential wartime function. The government contended the leaflets were calculated to encourage resistance to the draft among men already called up, that intent could be inferred from distribution to that audience, and that wartime conditions gave Congress broad power to protect recruitment from obstruction.
case.applicableLaw: The First Amendment; the Espionage Act of 1917, Sections 3 and 4 (obstruction of recruiting, nonmailable matter); the Thirteenth Amendment argument pressed by the defense; criminal-conspiracy doctrine.
case.precedents: No substantial First Amendment jurisprudence yet existed; the Court drew on English common-law and American criminal-attempt doctrine about proximity of speech to unlawful acts; earlier cases like Patterson v. Colorado (1907) had applied a bad-tendency test.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Free speech / clear and present danger. Decided 1919. The prosecution was part of the wartime suppression of dissent under the Espionage Act during and just after World War I.
case.tldr: Schenck was convicted for mailing anti-draft leaflets in wartime. The Court upheld the conviction, announcing that speech posing a 'clear and present danger' can be punished.

ruling.ruling: Judgment for the defending party; relief denied. Decision below: affirmed.

case.title: Dodge v. Ford Motor Co.
case.court: Supreme Court of Michigan
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed in part, reversed in part. Ford was ordered to pay a special dividend (a corporation is run primarily for shareholders' profit), but the injunction against expanding the River Rouge plant was reversed under the business judgment rule.
case.questionPresented: Whether a corporation's refusal to pay substantial dividends in order to reinvest profits for expansion and low prices, and whether its alleged purpose of benefiting employees and the public over shareholders, was lawful against a minority-shareholder challenge.
case.facts: The Ford Motor Company had accumulated a large cash surplus. Henry Ford, the controlling shareholder, announced that the company would reinvest its profits in expanding the River Rouge plant and lowering car prices rather than pay large special dividends, and that he intended the company to benefit employees and customers — 'to spread employment and share profits with the public' — rather than maximize shareholder returns. John and Horace Dodge, minority shareholders (who were financing their own competing automobile venture), sued to compel a special dividend and to enjoin the expansion. Ford argued the decisions were within the business judgment of the board and that a corporation could pursue public benefit. The case asked whether a corporation exists primarily for shareholder profit or may prefer other constituencies. Ford had amassed a large surplus and announced reinvestment, price cuts, and benefits for employees and the public rather than special dividends; the Dodges were minority shareholders building a rival company.
case.proceduralHistory: The Dodges sued in the Michigan trial court, which ordered Ford to pay a substantial special dividend and enjoined the proposed expansion plan. Ford appealed to the Supreme Court of Michigan on whether the withholding of dividends and the expansion plan exceeded corporate authority or abused discretion.
case.evidence: The record included the company's large surplus and history of dividends, Ford's statements about using profits for the benefit of employees and the public rather than shareholders, and the expansion plan. The dispute concerned whether the refusal to declare dividends was an abuse of discretion and whether a corporation may subordinate shareholder profit to employee and public welfare.
case.plaintiffArguments: The Dodges argued that a corporation exists primarily for the profit of its shareholders, that Ford's declared purpose of using profits for public benefit rather than shareholder returns exceeded corporate power, and that the withholding of dividends to finance expansion was an abuse of discretion given the vast surplus. They contended they were entitled to a special dividend and that the company could not lawfully sacrifice shareholder returns to philanthropy.
case.defendantArguments: Ford argued that decisions about dividends and expansion were matters of business judgment committed to the directors, that reinvestment and price reductions were legitimate long-term business strategy benefiting the company, and that courts should not substitute their judgment for the board's. It contended that a corporation could consider employees and customers, and that the Dodges had no right to force a distribution of profits or to veto expansion.
case.applicableLaw: Michigan corporation law; the business judgment rule; the directors' discretion over dividends; the question whether a corporation's purpose is shareholder profit or a broader public benefit.
case.precedents: The business-judgment and dividend-discretion cases; Michigan corporate-law precedents on minority shareholders' remedies; the developing doctrine of corporate purpose.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Corporate law / shareholder primacy. Decided 1919. The case is the canonical statement that a business corporation is run primarily for shareholder profit, while also illustrating the deference given to business judgment.
case.tldr: Ford withheld big dividends to fund expansion and benefit workers. The court ordered a special dividend, ruling a corporation is run primarily for shareholders' profit.

case.title: Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent
case.court: New York Court of Appeals
case.actualOutcome: Reversed; judgment for the builder. The deviation was trivial and innocent; substantial performance entitled the builder to payment less any difference in value.
case.questionPresented: Whether a builder who substantially performed a contract for a country house, but installed a different brand of pipe than specified, could recover payment less the difference in value, or had to pay the cost of replacement.
case.facts: Jacob & Youngs built a country residence for George Kent under a contract requiring all wrought-iron pipe to be of Reading manufacture. After construction, Kent discovered that a substantial portion of the installed pipe was of other brands of comparable quality, not Reading pipe. He withheld the final payment and demanded the pipe be replaced, which would have required tearing into finished walls. The builder sued for the balance due. Kent argued the contract's express specification had not been performed, so payment should be denied or the cost of replacement recovered. The builder argued it had substantially performed, the deviation was trivial and accidental, and that the proper measure was the difference in value — which was nominal — rather than the cost of reconstruction. The installed pipe was of equal quality but a different brand; replacing it would have required tearing into finished walls at a cost far exceeding any difference in value between the brands.
case.proceduralHistory: The builder sued to recover the contract balance in the New York trial court, which excluded evidence of the difference in value between the installed and specified pipe and directed a verdict for the homeowner. The Appellate Division sustained. The Court of Appeals reviewed whether the builder's substantial performance entitled it to payment less only the diminution in value.
case.evidence: The record showed that the installed pipe, though not the specified brand, was of equivalent quality, and that the deviation resulted from the subcontractor's inattention rather than bad faith. The dispute concerned the measure of damages for a trivial, innocent deviation: the cost of completing the contract as specified versus the difference in value between the two.
case.plaintiffArguments: Jacob & Youngs argued that it had substantially performed the contract and was entitled to the contract price less any actual diminution in value caused by the deviation. It contended the installed pipe was of equal quality, the breach was trivial and innocent, and that requiring reconstruction at enormous cost would inflict disproportionate forfeiture and unjust enrichment on the homeowner, contrary to the substantial-performance doctrine.
case.defendantArguments: Kent argued that the contract expressly required Reading pipe, that literal compliance was a condition of payment, and that the builder had not performed as promised. He contended the measure of damages was the cost of completing the contract as specified — replacing the pipe — and that the substantial-performance doctrine could not excuse the failure to install the brand bargained for.
case.applicableLaw: New York contract law on conditions and substantial performance; the measure of damages for trivial or innocent deviations — diminution in value versus cost of completion; the prevention of forfeiture and unjust enrichment.
case.precedents: New York precedents on conditions precedent and substantial performance; the rule distinguishing trivial breaches from material ones; earlier cases on the economic-waste limitation on cost of completion.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Contracts / substantial performance. Decided 1921. Cardozo's opinion and Crane's dissent framed the enduring debate over whether damages should be measured by cost of completion or diminution in value.
case.tldr: A builder installed the wrong brand of equal-quality pipe. The court let it recover the contract price less the trivial difference in value rather than the cost of replacement.

case.title: Gitlow v. New York
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Free speech applies to the states via the 14th Amendment, but the conviction for publishing the Left Wing Manifesto was upheld.
case.questionPresented: Whether New York's Criminal Anarchy Act, as applied to the publication of a revolutionary manifesto advocating socialism through militant means, violates freedom of speech as protected against the states by the Fourteenth Amendment.
case.facts: Benjamin Gitlow, a socialist and former New York assemblyman, was business manager of The Revolutionary Age, the newspaper of the Left Wing Section of the Socialist Party. In 1919 the paper published the 'Left Wing Manifesto,' which called for mass strikes, class struggle, and the establishment of socialism through revolutionary means, though it advocated general doctrine rather than a specific imminent uprising. Gitlow and others were indicted under New York's Criminal Anarchy Act of 1902, which punished advocacy of the doctrine that organized government should be overthrown by force or violence. Gitlow argued that the statute punished the teaching of abstract doctrine unconnected to any concrete danger, and his case forced the Court to decide whether the First Amendment's speech protections bound the states through the Fourteenth Amendment at all. The Manifesto urged mass strikes and revolutionary action by the proletariat, and Gitlow's defense emphasized that it taught abstract doctrine rather than directing any specific imminent act.
case.proceduralHistory: Gitlow was tried in New York County and convicted of criminal anarchy; the trial court instructed the jury that it need only find that the Manifesto advocated violent overthrow doctrine, not that any violence resulted or was imminent. The New York Court of Appeals sustained the conviction. Gitlow obtained review in the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The prosecution relied on the Manifesto itself and on Gitlow's role in its publication and distribution. There was no evidence of any actual attempt at overthrow, riot, or imminent lawless act; the case turned entirely on whether publication of revolutionary doctrine, without more, was a punishable advocacy crime under the statute.
case.plaintiffArguments: Gitlow argued that the statute punished the mere publication and advocacy of political doctrine — abstract teaching of revolution — rather than incitement to any imminent unlawful act, and so violated freedom of speech. He contended the Manifesto was an analysis and exhortation of historical and economic theory, contained no call to immediate violence, and could not be criminalized consistent with a constitutional protection of speech now applicable to the states.
case.defendantArguments: New York argued that the legislature could criminalize advocacy of violent overthrow as a dangerous doctrine without waiting for an imminent attempt, comparing the Manifesto to a spark in combustible conditions. The state maintained the jury found the publication constituted advocacy under the statute, that deference was owed the legislature's judgment about the danger of revolutionary propaganda, and that the First Amendment did not reach state penal laws.
case.applicableLaw: The First Amendment; the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause (liberty including speech, as urged by the appellant); New York Criminal Anarchy Act of 1902.
case.precedents: Schenck v. United States (1919); Abrams v. United States (1919); Patterson v. Colorado (1907); state decisions sustaining criminal-anarchy statutes such as People v. Most (N.Y. 1902).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Incorporation / free speech. Decided 1925. The prosecution grew out of the post-World War I Red Scare and the suppression of radical labor and socialist organizations.
case.tldr: Gitlow was convicted under New York's criminal anarchy law for publishing a revolutionary manifesto. The Court upheld the conviction while holding that free speech binds the states.

ruling.ruling: Judgment for the defending party; relief denied. Decision below: affirmed. Remedy: acquittal.

case.title: State of Tennessee v. John Thomas Scopes (Scopes Monkey Trial)
case.court: Rhea County Circuit Court, Tennessee
case.actualOutcome: Scopes convicted and fined $100. The Tennessee Supreme Court later reversed on the technicality that the jury, not the judge, should have set the fine, but upheld the Act.
case.questionPresented: Whether Tennessee's Butler Act, prohibiting the teaching of human evolution in public schools, was valid and whether a teacher's violation of it could support a conviction.
case.facts: Tennessee's Butler Act made it unlawful to teach in public schools any theory denying the biblical account of creation and teaching instead that man descended from lower animals. John T. Scopes, a high-school science teacher in Dayton, agreed to be the defendant in a test case and was charged with teaching evolution. The prosecution, led by William Jennings Bryan, argued the statute was a valid exercise of the state's power over public-school curriculum. The defense, led by Clarence Darrow, argued the statute violated academic freedom and constitutional rights, that it established religion, and that the state could not dictate scientific truth. The trial became a national spectacle on the conflict between science and religion in education. Scopes agreed to test the Butler Act in Dayton; the prosecution and defense, led by Bryan and Darrow, turned a misdemeanor trial into a national contest over science, religion, and curriculum control. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Scopes was tried in the Rhea County Circuit Court before a jury. The jury convicted him and he was fined $100. He appealed to the Tennessee Supreme Court, which addressed both the statute's validity and a technical defect in the sentence.
case.evidence: The record established that Scopes taught the theory of evolution to his class, which was largely uncontested. The legal dispute was constitutional: whether the Butler Act violated the state and federal constitutions as an establishment of religion or an infringement of free inquiry, and whether the statute was a permissible exercise of the state's control over public education.
case.plaintiffArguments: The state argued that the Butler Act was a valid exercise of the legislature's power to determine the public-school curriculum and to prohibit the teaching of theories offensive to the religious beliefs of the taxpayers who funded the schools. It contended the statute did not establish a religion but simply regulated what could be taught in state-funded schools, that Scopes plainly violated it, and that academic-freedom claims did not limit state authority over public instruction.
case.defendantArguments: Scopes argued that the Butler Act was unconstitutional because it established a particular religious view — biblical creation — in the public schools and infringed freedom of thought and teaching. He contended the statute was vague and discriminatory, that a state could not outlaw the teaching of scientific truth, and that the law violated both state and federal constitutional protections of speech and religion.
case.applicableLaw: Tennessee's Butler Act; the First Amendment's religion clauses and free-speech protections (as argued), and the Tennessee constitution; the state's power over public-school curriculum.
case.precedents: No direct precedent on teaching evolution; the constitutional claims invoked the developing religion-clause and free-speech doctrines of the era.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Criminal law / teaching evolution. Decided 1925. The Dayton 'monkey trial' became an enduring symbol of the conflict between scientific and religious authority in education.
case.tldr: Scopes was tried for teaching evolution in defiance of Tennessee's Butler Act. He was convicted and fined, though the state supreme court later voided the fine on a technicality.

case.title: Buck v. Bell
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Virginia's compulsory sterilization statute upheld; 'three generations of imbeciles are enough.'
case.questionPresented: Whether Virginia's statute authorizing the compulsory sterilization of institutionalized persons adjudged 'feebleminded' comports with the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.
case.facts: Carrie Buck was an eighteen-year-old resident of the Virginia State Colony for Epileptics and Feebleminded, committed as a 'feebleminded' woman after bearing a child out of wedlock. Virginia's 1924 sterilization statute authorized the superintendent of such institutions to order the sterilization of inmates found to be afflicted with hereditary forms of mental deficiency, after prescribed administrative procedures and judicial review. Colony superintendent Dr. Albert Priddy selected Buck — whose mother was also institutionalized and whose infant daughter had been judged mentally slow — for salpingectomy under the statute, and the order was approved through the statutory process. Buck, represented by a guardian who challenged the order, contended that the statute authorized the state to mutilate a competent adult's body to prevent procreation, a deprivation of bodily liberty without adequate justification. The statute's supporters invoked eugenic theories then fashionable in public-health circles; Buck's guardian argued the evidence of hereditary defect was thin and the proposed surgery irreversible.
case.proceduralHistory: After the Colony's board approved the sterilization order, Buck appealed administratively and then challenged the statute's validity in the Virginia courts. The Amherst County Circuit Court and the Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals sustained the statute and the order. Buck appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States.
case.evidence: The record included the administrative findings that Buck, her mother, and her infant daughter were 'feebleminded' and that the condition was hereditary, based largely on institutional records and rudimentary intelligence testing of the era. Her guardian challenged both the sufficiency of that evidence and the constitutionality of subjecting her to irreversible surgery on the strength of it.
case.plaintiffArguments: Buck's counsel argued that the statute authorized an irreversible deprivation of bodily integrity based on doubtful hereditary science, and that the administrative process — conducted by the same officials who sought the operation — denied meaningful due process. They also argued the law violated equal protection because it applied only to institutionalized 'feebleminded' persons and not to similarly situated persons outside state custody, making it an arbitrary and discriminatory exercise of power.
case.defendantArguments: The Colony argued that the statute was a reasonable exercise of the police power to prevent the transmission of hereditary mental defect, a harm the legislature could rationally seek to reduce. Defendants contended the statute's detailed procedural safeguards — notice, hearings, board approval, and judicial review — satisfied due process, and that limiting the law to institutional inmates was a reasonable classification because the state bore responsibility for their care.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment; Virginia's Eugenical Sterilization Act of 1924; police-power doctrine regarding public health measures; Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905) on compulsory health measures.
case.precedents: Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905) (compulsory vaccination); earlier state decisions upholding eugenic sterilization statutes (e.g., the Michigan and Indiana cases of the era), and contrary authority in Smith v. Board of Examiners (N.J. 1913).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Due process / forced sterilization. Decided 1927. The case was a friendly test suit arranged by the Colony's superintendent during the height of the American eugenics movement.
case.tldr: Carrie Buck challenged a Virginia order for compulsory sterilization of the 'feebleminded.' The Court upheld the eugenic sterilization statute.

case.title: Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad Co.
case.court: New York Court of Appeals
case.actualOutcome: Reversed; complaint dismissed. The railroad owed no duty to an unforeseeable plaintiff outside the zone of danger.
case.caseType: tort – negligence / duty and proximate cause
case.questionPresented: Whether a railroad owed a duty of care to a passenger on a platform who was injured when a package of fireworks, dropped by another passenger aided by railroad employees, exploded and caused scales to fall on her.
case.facts: Helen Palsgraf stood on the Long Island Railroad's platform. As a train departed, a passenger carrying a package raced to board; railroad employees helped pull him aboard and push him from the platform, and in the process he dropped the package, which contained fireworks that exploded. The shock of the explosion overturned scales at the other end of the platform, which fell and injured Palsgraf. She sued the railroad for negligence. The railroad argued its employees owed no duty to Palsgraf, an unforeseeable plaintiff far from the boarding, and that the injury was too remote and indirect — caused by the fireworks rather than any act directed at her. The case turned on whether negligence must be measured against a foreseeable plaintiff within a zone of danger. The fireworks' explosion overturned scales at the far end of the platform; Palsgraf stood far from the boarding, and the package's contents were unknown to the employees who assisted the passenger.
case.proceduralHistory: Palsgraf sued in the New York trial court and won a jury verdict; the Appellate Division sustained the judgment. The railroad appealed to the New York Court of Appeals, arguing that no duty was owed to the plaintiff and that the injury was not within the scope of any negligence toward the boarding passenger.
case.evidence: The record included testimony about the boarding, the dropped package, the explosion, and the falling scales at the platform's far end. The dispute was whether the employees' conduct toward the boarding passenger — negligently assisting him in a way that dislodged the package — constituted a breach of any duty owed to Palsgraf, an unforeseeable victim outside the apparent zone of danger.
case.plaintiffArguments: Palsgraf argued that the railroad employees' negligent assistance caused the package to fall and explode, and that her injury, though indirect, was a consequence for which the railroad should be liable. She contended negligence creates liability to anyone injured as a proximate result, that the railroad's conduct was careless regardless of where she stood, and that she was entitled to recover for the injury actually suffered.
case.defendantArguments: The railroad argued that negligence is relational — a breach of duty owed to the particular plaintiff — and that its employees owed no duty to Palsgraf, who was unforeseeably beyond the zone of apparent danger. It contended the explosion was the intervening act of the passenger's concealed fireworks, that the injury was too remote and indirect to be a consequence of any negligence toward the boarding passenger, and that liability cannot attach absent foreseeability of the victim.
case.applicableLaw: New York negligence law: duty of care owed to foreseeable plaintiffs within the zone of danger; proximate cause and the limits of liability for remote, indirect injury; the relational nature of negligence.
case.precedents: The New York and common-law negligence cases on duty and remoteness; the foreseeability doctrine developing in the early twentieth century; analogous liability limits in tort doctrine.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Torts / duty and proximate cause. Decided 1928. Cardozo's majority opinion limiting duty to foreseeable plaintiffs — over Andrews's dissent — became the foundational American statement on the scope of negligence.
case.tldr: Fireworks dropped by a passenger exploded, and falling scales injured Palsgraf down the platform. The court dismissed her claim, holding the railroad owed no duty to an unforeseeable plaintiff.

case.title: Meinhard v. Salmon
case.court: New York Court of Appeals
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed as modified. Co-venturers owe the 'punctilio of an honor the most sensitive'; Meinhard was entitled to share in the new lease opportunity.
case.questionPresented: Whether a joint venturer who obtained a renewal of a lease held by the venture had to share the new opportunity with his co-venturer, or was free to take it for himself after the venture's term ended.
case.facts: Walter Salmon leased a hotel property and brought in Morton Meinhard as a joint venturer who financed much of the operation in return for a share of profits. Near the end of the lease, the landlord offered Salmon — personally, without disclosing it to Meinhard — a new, greatly expanded lease and redevelopment of the property and adjoining parcels. Salmon took the opportunity for himself. Meinhard sued, claiming the renewal opportunity belonged to the joint venture and that Salmon's nondisclosure breached a fiduciary duty. Salmon argued the venture had ended with the original lease, the new lease was a separate and broader transaction he was free to accept, and that he owed no obligation to share an opportunity arising after the venture's term. Near the lease's end, the landlord offered Salmon personally a greatly expanded redevelopment; Salmon accepted without disclosing the opportunity to Meinhard, the venture's principal financier. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Meinhard sued in the New York trial court, which ruled that Salmon had breached his duty and that Meinhard was entitled to share in the new lease. The Appellate Division modified the award. The case reached the New York Court of Appeals on the extent of a co-venturer's fiduciary duty regarding opportunities arising at the venture's end.
case.evidence: The record included the joint-venture agreement, Salmon's acceptance of the expanded lease personally and his failure to disclose the opportunity to Meinhard, and the relationship between the old lease and the larger redevelopment. The dispute was whether the renewal was a venture opportunity Salmon was obliged to share, given the fiduciary standard governing joint venturers.
case.plaintiffArguments: Meinhard argued that Salmon, as a joint venturer and managing partner, owed him the highest fiduciary duty — the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive — and could not take for himself an opportunity that grew out of the venture's leasehold. He contended the new lease was a renewal and expansion of the venture's subject matter, that Salmon's concealment was a breach, and that he was entitled to share in the opportunity.
case.defendantArguments: Salmon argued that the joint venture had a fixed term ending with the original lease, that the new and much larger redevelopment was a different transaction he was free to accept personally, and that no duty required him to share opportunities arising after the venture's obligations ended. He contended Meinhard was a passive investor, that the landlord chose to deal with him alone, and that fiduciary duty does not extend beyond the venture's scope and term.
case.applicableLaw: New York partnership and joint-venture fiduciary law; the duty of loyalty and disclosure between co-venturers; whether an opportunity connected to the venture's asset belongs to the venture.
case.precedents: The partnership fiduciary-duty cases; the trust and agency doctrines on an agent's duty not to profit secretly; earlier New York decisions on co-venturers' obligations.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Fiduciary duty / joint venture. Decided 1928. Cardozo's statement of the fiduciary standard — 'the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive' — became the classic formulation of partners' loyalty.
case.tldr: Salmon took an expanded lease offer personally without telling his co-venturer. The court made him share it, holding partners owe 'the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive.'

case.title: Hawkins v. McGee
case.court: Supreme Court of New Hampshire
case.actualOutcome: New trial ordered on damages only; the surgeon's guarantee was an enforceable promise and the proper measure is expectation damages (value of the promised hand minus the hand as it was).
case.questionPresented: Whether a surgeon's guarantee of a 'hundred percent perfect hand' created an enforceable contract, and how damages should be measured for its breach.
case.facts: George Hawkins, a boy, suffered severe scarring and disfigurement to his right hand after contact with an electrical wire. His family consulted Dr. Edward McGee, who, according to the plaintiffs, solicited the case and promised to make the hand 'a hundred percent perfect' through skin-graft surgery. The operation grafted skin from Hawkins's chest onto his palm, but the graft failed badly: hair grew on the palm and the hand was worsened. The Hawkinses sued for breach of contract, arguing the surgeon's guarantee was a binding promise. At trial, the court instructed the jury that damages could include pain and suffering from the operation itself — a measure the plaintiff contested — and returned a verdict the defendant claimed was excessive. The case went up on exceptions to the damages instruction and the sufficiency of the guarantee evidence. The graft took skin from the boy's chest to his palm; the operation left hair growing on the palm and worsened the hand's condition, and the family contended the promise had induced their consent.
case.proceduralHistory: The case was tried to a jury in the New Hampshire trial court, which entered a verdict for the plaintiff. The defendant excepted to the jury instructions on the measure of damages and to the denial of his motions. The Supreme Court of New Hampshire reviewed the exceptions, addressing whether the guarantee was enforceable and the proper measure of damages.
case.evidence: The record included testimony about the doctor's alleged statement guaranteeing a perfect hand, the circumstances of the surgery and its failure, and medical evidence of the hand's condition. The dispute was whether the guarantee was a binding promise or mere therapeutic encouragement, and whether damages should be measured by the difference between the promised perfect hand and the hand as received, rather than tort-style pain and suffering.
case.plaintiffArguments: The Hawkinses argued that the surgeon's express guarantee of a 'hundred percent perfect hand' was a binding contractual promise, not casual optimism, made to induce them to consent to the surgery. They contended the proper measure of damages was the difference in value between the promised perfect hand and the impaired hand actually delivered, and that pain and suffering from the operation itself should be recoverable as resulting from the breach.
case.defendantArguments: Dr. McGee argued that his statement was a professional expression of opinion and encouragement, not a warranty guaranteeing a result, and that doctors do not contract to cure. He contended the damages instruction erroneously included pain and suffering incident to surgery the plaintiff would have undergone anyway, that the verdict was excessive, and that the correct measure was the difference between the hand's actual condition and its promised condition, not compensation for the surgery's unavoidable discomfort.
case.applicableLaw: Contract formation and enforceability of a physician's guarantee; expectation damages measured by the difference between the promised result and actual result; the rules limiting contract damages to what flows from the breach.
case.precedents: The New Hampshire and general contract doctrine on warranties and express promises; the then-developing rule of expectation damages distinguishing contract from tort recovery; standard treatises on damages.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Contracts / expectation damages. Decided 1929. The 'hairy hand' case became the classic textbook illustration of the expectation measure of contract damages.
case.tldr: A surgeon promised a boy a 'hundred percent perfect hand' and failed badly. The court enforced the promise and measured damages by the difference between the promised and delivered hand.

case.title: Near v. Minnesota
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. The gag law authorizing prior restraint on 'malicious, scandalous' newspapers violated the First Amendment.
case.questionPresented: Whether a Minnesota statute permitting courts to enjoin as a public nuisance any 'malicious, scandalous and defamatory' newspaper, and to suppress future issues, imposes an unconstitutional prior restraint on the press.
case.facts: Jay Near published The Saturday Press, a Minneapolis weekly that ran a series of articles accusing city officials — particularly the police chief and county attorney — of corruption and of protecting gambling, bootlegging, and racketeering controlled, the paper charged, by a Jewish criminal syndicate. The articles were inflammatory and, in part, antisemitic and defamatory. Minnesota's Public Nuisance Law of 1925, known as the 'gag law,' authorized county attorneys to obtain injunctions against periodicals publishing 'malicious, scandalous and defamatory' matter, treating continued publication as a nuisance punishable by contempt. The county attorney sued Near, and the trial court enjoined further publication of the paper as a nuisance. The case asked the Court to decide whether the freedom of the press, applied to the states by the Fourteenth Amendment, forbids judicial suppression of future issues of a publication. The Saturday Press articles mixed accusations of official corruption with antisemitic attacks, and newspaper publishers nationwide watched the case as a test of whether nuisance law could be used to silence hostile journalism.
case.proceduralHistory: Hennepin County obtained an injunction against The Saturday Press in the district court, which adjudged the paper a public nuisance and enjoined Near from publishing it in any form. The Minnesota Supreme Court sustained the statute and the injunction as a permissible abatement of a nuisance rather than censorship. Near appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States.
case.evidence: The record contained the published issues of The Saturday Press, whose charged and defamatory articles about Minneapolis officials were not disputed as publications. The proceeding was equitable: the issue was whether a statute authorizing suppression of a publication as a nuisance, with truth permitted as a defense only if published 'with good motives and justifiable ends,' could stand against press freedom.
case.plaintiffArguments: Near argued that the statute was a classic prior restraint: it suppressed not a particular libelous article but the newspaper itself, barring all future publication under threat of contempt. He contended that freedom of the press, incorporated against the states by the Fourteenth Amendment, forbids preventive censorship of this kind, that the remedy for defamation is a libel action after publication, and that the 'good motives' proviso put the burden on the publisher to justify speech to a court in advance.
case.defendantArguments: Minnesota argued that the statute did not censor content before publication but abated an ongoing public nuisance — a business built on malicious, scandalous defamation — by enjoining its continuation. The state contended the press is not immune from general laws protecting public order, that the procedure allowed truth as a defense, and that states retained power to prevent the systematic publication of defamatory matter that libel actions could not adequately reach.
case.applicableLaw: The First Amendment's press and speech clauses as applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment; Minnesota Public Nuisance Law of 1925; English common-law tradition against prior restraints (Blackstone); equitable nuisance doctrine.

case.title: Donoghue v. Stevenson
case.court: House of Lords (UK)
case.topic: Torts / negligence and duty of care
case.actualOutcome: Appeal allowed. A manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer; the claim could proceed (neighbour principle).
case.jurisdiction: United Kingdom (Scotland appeal to House of Lords)
case.questionPresented: Whether a manufacturer of ginger beer owed a duty of care to the ultimate consumer who allegedly found a decomposed snail in the bottle, despite the absence of a contract between them.
case.facts: May Donoghue consumed a bottle of ginger beer bought for her by a friend at a café in Paisley, Scotland. The bottle was opaque, so its contents could not be inspected; when the remainder was poured into her glass, she alleged a decomposed snail emerged. She claimed to have suffered gastroenteritis and nervous shock. Unable to sue in contract — she had not purchased the bottle — she sued the manufacturer, David Stevenson, in negligence. The defendant argued that, absent a contract, a manufacturer owed no duty to a consumer and that negligence required privity. The case required the House of Lords to decide whether a general duty of care existed between manufacturer and ultimate consumer independent of contract. The bottle was opaque, so its contents could not be inspected before consumption; Donoghue had not purchased it, leaving no contract between her and anyone in the chain of supply. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Donoghue sued in the Scottish courts; the Court of Session dismissed her claim for want of a relevant duty. She appealed in forma pauperis to the House of Lords, which heard the case on the preliminary legal question whether the pleaded facts disclosed a duty of care entitling her to a trial.
case.evidence: At this stage the snail's presence was alleged rather than proved; the appeal proceeded on the assumption the facts pleaded were true. The record consisted of the pleadings asserting that Stevenson manufactured the bottle, that the opaque bottle prevented inspection, and that the snail caused her illness — raising the pure legal question whether a duty of care existed on those facts.
case.plaintiffArguments: Donoghue argued that a manufacturer who places a product into commerce in a form that prevents intermediate inspection owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer, independent of any contract. She contended that privity should not shield a manufacturer whose negligence causes harm to a foreseeable consumer, that the law of negligence should recognize a duty to one's 'neighbour' injured by carelessness, and that she was entitled to prove her case at trial.
case.defendantArguments: Stevenson argued that negligence liability required privity of contract or a recognized category of duty, that no general duty existed between manufacturer and consumer, and that the alleged facts disclosed no basis for liability absent contractual relationship. It contended that extending negligence to manufacturers of goods would open limitless liability, and that the established authorities confined such duties to contract or to inherently dangerous articles.
case.applicableLaw: The law of negligence in Scots and English common law; the privity-of-contract barrier to a manufacturer's duty to remote consumers; the question whether a general 'neighbour' duty of care existed independent of contract.
case.precedents: Winterbottom v. Wright (1842) (privity); Heaven v. Pender (1883) (foreseeability and proximity); the existing categories of negligence duty; the limited exceptions for dangerous goods.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Torts / negligence and duty of care. Decided 1932. Lord Atkin's 'neighbour principle' established the modern general duty of care and founded the law of product liability in the common-law world.
case.tldr: Donoghue fell ill after drinking ginger beer containing a decomposed snail. The House of Lords let her sue the manufacturer, founding the modern duty of care.

case.title: State of New Jersey v. Bruno Richard Hauptmann (Lindbergh kidnapping)
case.court: Hunterdon County Court of Oyer and Terminer, New Jersey
case.actualOutcome: Convicted of first-degree murder and executed in 1936, largely on ransom-money, handwriting and ladder-wood evidence.
case.questionPresented: Whether the circumstantial and physical evidence — ransom money, handwriting, and wood from the ladder — proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Bruno Richard Hauptmann kidnapped and killed the Lindbergh baby.
case.facts: Charles Lindbergh Jr., the infant son of the aviator, was kidnapped from the family's New Jersey home in 1932 and later found dead. A ladder left at the scene had been used to reach the nursery window, and ransom notes demanded money, which was paid through an intermediary; the child was nonetheless found killed. Two years later, Bruno Richard Hauptmann, a German immigrant carpenter, was arrested after spending ransom-marked bills, and a search of his garage found a large sum of the ransom money. The prosecution's case rested on the ransom money in his possession, expert testimony that his handwriting matched the ransom notes, and wood analysis linking the ladder to lumber from his attic. Hauptmann denied involvement, claiming the money was left with him by a deceased associate, and challenged the reliability of the evidence. The case rested on ransom-marked bills found in his garage, expert handwriting matches to the ransom notes, and ladder wood linked to his attic; Hauptmann claimed the money came from a dead associate.
case.proceduralHistory: Hauptmann was tried in the Hunterdon County Court of Oyer and Terminer in a sensationalized trial. The jury convicted him of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to death. His appeals, challenging the evidence and the fairness of the trial, were unsuccessful, and he was executed in 1936.
case.evidence: The prosecution relied on the ransom money found in Hauptmann's possession, handwriting experts' testimony matching his writing to the ransom notes, the wood of the ladder linked to lumber missing from his attic, and testimony placing him near the scene. The defense attacked the eyewitness identifications, the handwriting analysis, and the integrity of the circumstantial case, arguing reasonable doubt.
case.plaintiffArguments: The state argued that Hauptmann's possession of the ransom money, the handwriting match to the ransom notes, the ladder wood traced to his attic, and the other circumstantial evidence proved beyond reasonable doubt that he kidnapped and killed the child. It contended the physical evidence formed an unbroken chain pointing to him, that his explanation for the money was implausible, and that the crime's circumstances — the ladder, the notes, and the money — connected him directly.
case.defendantArguments: Hauptmann argued that the case was entirely circumstantial, that he had no connection to the kidnapping, and that the ransom money had been left with him by a deceased friend. He contended the handwriting and wood-identification evidence was unreliable, that eyewitnesses were mistaken, that police handling of the evidence was suspect, and that the sensational atmosphere and weak proof created reasonable doubt.
case.applicableLaw: New Jersey criminal law on kidnapping and felony murder; the reasonable-doubt standard; the law governing circumstantial evidence, expert handwriting and wood-identification testimony, and eyewitness identification.
case.precedents: The general criminal and evidence doctrines rather than controlling precedent; the case turned on the sufficiency and reliability of the forensic and circumstantial evidence.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Criminal law / kidnapping and murder. Decided 1935. The 'trial of the century' for the Lindbergh baby's kidnapping rested on forensic and circumstantial evidence and led to federal kidnapping legislation.
case.tldr: Hauptmann was tried for kidnapping and killing the Lindbergh baby on ransom-money, handwriting, and ladder evidence. He was convicted of murder and executed.

case.title: Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed and remanded. There is no federal general common law; federal courts in diversity must apply state substantive law (Pennsylvania's rule on trespassers). Swift v. Tyson overruled.
case.caseType: civil procedure – federal common law / diversity jurisdiction
case.questionPresented: Whether a federal court sitting in diversity must apply state common law, or may apply a general federal common law, on a question of substantive tort duty.
case.facts: Harry Tompkins, walking at night along a footpath beside the Erie Railroad's tracks in Pennsylvania, was struck by a passing train and injured. A citizen of Pennsylvania, he sued the railroad, a New York corporation, in federal court on diversity jurisdiction. Under Pennsylvania law, Tompkins was a trespasser or bare licensee to whom the railroad owed only a limited duty; under the 'general law' approach of Swift v. Tyson, the federal court could apply its own view of the common law, under which the railroad owed a duty of ordinary care to a pedestrian on a customary pathway. The district court applied general law, and the railroad argued federal courts in diversity cases were bound by state law. The case required the Court to decide whether federal courts could declare a common law independent of the states. Tompkins walked a customary footpath beside the tracks when the train struck him; Pennsylvania treated him as a trespasser owed limited duty, while the general-law approach allowed ordinary-negligence recovery.
case.proceduralHistory: Tompkins sued in the Southern District of New York and won a verdict under a general-law duty standard, which the Second Circuit sustained. The railroad petitioned the Supreme Court, arguing Swift v. Tyson's general-law regime should be reconsidered and that Pennsylvania's narrower duty rule governed.
case.evidence: The record concerned the accident and the divergent duty rules: Pennsylvania common law treated a pedestrian on the right-of-way path as a trespasser owed limited care, while the general-law approach permitted recovery under ordinary negligence. The constitutional question was whether the federal court in diversity could apply its own conception of the common law rather than the law of the state.
case.plaintiffArguments: The railroad argued that Swift v. Tyson had produced unconstitutional and discriminatory results, that federal courts in diversity cases were bound to apply the law of the state — including its common law — and that there was no federal general common law. It contended the Rules of Decision Act and the Constitution required deference to state law, that Swift had permitted forum-shopping and uncertainty, and that Pennsylvania's trespasser rule should have governed.
case.defendantArguments: Tompkins argued that the federal court could apply a general-law standard of ordinary negligence, that the customary pathway made him more than a trespasser under the prevailing common-law view, and that Swift had long authorized federal courts to declare general commercial and tort law. He contended the verdict for him was proper under the general-law rule and that overturning Swift would unsettle decades of federal practice.
case.applicableLaw: The Rules of Decision Act; the Constitution's division of state and federal judicial power; the Swift v. Tyson doctrine of federal general common law in diversity cases; the substantive-procedural distinction.
case.precedents: Swift v. Tyson (1842) (the doctrine being reconsidered); the Rules of Decision Act's lineage; the constitutional structure of dual sovereignty and diversity jurisdiction.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Civil procedure / federal common law. Decided 1938. The decision abolished federal general common law and made the Erie doctrine — federal courts in diversity apply state substantive law — a foundation of federal practice.
case.tldr: Tompkins won in federal court under 'general' common law that differed from state law. The Court reversed, ruling federal courts in diversity cases must apply state law.

case.title: Wickard v. Filburn
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed in favor of the government. Home-grown wheat, in the aggregate, substantially affects interstate commerce; the quota penalty was valid.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Agricultural Adjustment Act's marketing quotas, as applied to wheat grown on a farm for home consumption and never sold, are within Congress's power to regulate interstate commerce.
case.facts: Roscoe Filburn operated a small dairy and poultry farm in Ohio and grew a modest acreage of winter wheat. Under the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938, the Secretary of Agriculture established acreage allotments and marketing quotas to stabilize wheat prices; Filburn was allotted 11.1 acres but harvested 23 acres, yielding a surplus of about 239 bushels above his quota. Filburn used the excess wheat on his own farm — as feed for livestock, seed, and flour for home use — selling none of it. The government assessed a penalty of 49 cents per bushel on the excess. Filburn sued to enjoin enforcement, arguing that wheat consumed entirely on the farm where grown lay beyond Congress's power over commerce 'among the several states,' and that penalizing it regulated production and consumption reserved to the states. Filburn's excess was only a few hundred bushels, but the government argued that millions of similar farm decisions, taken together, would defeat the quota program's effort to stabilize wheat prices.
case.proceduralHistory: Filburn sued the Secretary of Agriculture in federal district court to enjoin the marketing penalty. A three-judge district court enjoined enforcement of the penalty against him on grounds unrelated to the ultimate constitutional question (defects in the quota-setting process). The Secretary appealed to the Supreme Court, which addressed the commerce power question directly.
case.evidence: The record established the acreage allotment, the excess harvest of 239 bushels, and the stipulated fact that the excess was retained on the farm for feed, seed, and home consumption rather than sold. The legal contest concerned whether such purely intrastate, noncommercial use of wheat, aggregated with that of many farmers, could nonetheless substantially affect interstate commerce and thus be reached by federal price-stabilization quotas.
case.plaintiffArguments: Filburn argued that the wheat at issue never entered commerce of any kind — it was grown, stored, and consumed on a single Ohio farm — so regulating it was regulating production and local consumption, matters reserved to the states. He contended that the marketing quota was in substance an acreage/production control beyond the commerce power, that the effect of one farmer's home consumption on interstate markets was trivial, and that upholding the law would leave no limiting principle to the commerce power.
case.defendantArguments: The government argued that even wheat consumed on the farm substantially affects interstate commerce in the aggregate, because home-consumed wheat supplants wheat the farmer would otherwise buy, reducing market demand and undermining the quota program's price-stabilization purpose. It contended Congress may regulate local activity when failure to do so would defeat a valid regulatory scheme, and that the cumulative effect of thousands of similar farmers made Filburn's excess part of a class Congress could reach.
case.applicableLaw: The Commerce Clause (Article I, Section 8, Clause 3); the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938 marketing-quota provisions; the Necessary and Proper Clause as supporting regulation of intrastate effects on a federal scheme.
case.precedents: NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp. (1937); United States v. Darby (1941); Gibbons v. Ogden (1824); Shreveport Rate Cases (1914) (intrastate rates affecting interstate commerce).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Commerce Clause. Decided 1942. The case arose under New Deal agricultural programs designed to raise crop prices by limiting supply after years of farm depression.
case.tldr: Filburn grew wheat above his federal quota for use on his own farm. The Court upheld the penalty, holding that even home-consumed wheat affects interstate commerce in the aggregate.

case.title: Korematsu v. United States
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Exclusion of Japanese Americans upheld as a military necessity. Repudiated in Trump v. Hawaii (2018).
case.questionPresented: Whether the military order excluding persons of Japanese ancestry from designated West Coast areas during World War II, as applied to a citizen convicted for remaining in his home, exceeded the war powers or violated the Constitution.
case.facts: After the attack on Pearl Harbor, President Roosevelt issued Executive Order 9062 authorizing military commanders to designate exclusion zones. General DeWitt, commanding the Western Defense Command, ordered curfews and then the exclusion of all persons of Japanese ancestry — about 120,000 people, two-thirds of them American citizens — from the West Coast, on the asserted ground of military necessity and the impossibility of rapidly sorting loyal from disloyal individuals. Fred Korematsu, an American-born citizen living in San Leandro, California, refused to leave, was arrested, and was convicted in federal court of violating the exclusion order. Korematsu argued that the order was a racial classification imprisoning citizens in detention camps without individual charges, hearings, or evidence of disloyalty, exceeding any legitimate war power. The exclusion followed curfews and registration orders that had already restricted Japanese Americans, and Korematsu's conviction rested on his remaining in his San Leandro home rather than reporting for removal.
case.proceduralHistory: Korematsu was convicted in the federal district court and sentenced to probation; he was confined at the Tanforan assembly center and later the Topaz internment camp. The Ninth Circuit sustained the conviction, certifying constitutional questions and relying on the Court's earlier curfew decision in Hirabayashi. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the exclusion order's validity.
case.evidence: The record included the text of Executive Order 9062 and General DeWitt's exclusion orders and Final Report, which cited espionage fears, signaling, and the presence of Japanese residents near military installations. Korematsu's loyalty was not individually disputed — no evidence showed he had committed or planned any disloyal act — and the government later conceded errors in DeWitt's report, though that concession postdated the conviction.
case.plaintiffArguments: Korematsu argued that the exclusion was a racial classification subject to the most rigid scrutiny and could not survive it, since the government offered no individualized evidence that he was disloyal or dangerous. He contended the order punished mere presence based on ancestry, that the claimed impossibility of loyalty hearings was belied by the months of delay before removal, and that the war power could not constitutionally authorize the mass imprisonment of citizens without charge.
case.defendantArguments: The United States argued that the exclusion was a military measure under the combined war powers of Congress and the President, justified by the judgment of military authorities that espionage and sabotage risks on the West Coast could not be met by individualized determinations in the time available. It contended the order applied to ancestry as a proxy for risk, not from racial antagonism, and that courts should defer to military necessity judgments in wartime, as in Hirabayashi v. United States.
case.applicableLaw: The war powers of Article I and II; Executive Order 9062 and the Act of March 21, 1942 criminalizing violation of exclusion orders; the Fifth Amendment's due process and equal-protection principles as applied to federal action.
case.precedents: Hirabayashi v. United States (1943) (upholding the curfew); Ex parte Milligan (1866); the Insular Cases and war-powers precedents on military authority.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Equal protection / wartime detention. Decided 1944. The case challenged the largest forced relocation of American citizens in the nation's history, carried out in the two years after Pearl Harbor.
case.tldr: Korematsu was convicted for defying the wartime exclusion order for Japanese Americans. The Court upheld the exclusion as a military necessity.

case.title: International Shoe Co. v. Washington
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Systematic and continuous in-state salesman activity established 'minimum contacts' so that jurisdiction did not offend fair play and substantial justice.
case.questionPresented: Whether a corporation's systematic employment of salesmen in a state, though it maintains no office there, constitutes sufficient 'minimum contacts' to subject it to the state's jurisdiction for a tax on in-state employment.
case.facts: International Shoe was a Missouri corporation that manufactured shoes and employed salesmen who solicited orders in Washington state. The salesmen worked on commission, maintained no permanent office, sometimes rented sample rooms, and transmitted orders to Missouri, where the shoes were made and shipped. Washington sought to collect unpaid unemployment-compensation contributions based on the salesmen's in-state employment. International Shoe argued it was not 'present' in Washington — it had no office, made no sales there, and did no business within the state's borders under the traditional presence test — so Washington lacked jurisdiction to impose the tax. The state argued the systematic and continuous in-state activity created a basis for jurisdiction even absent formal corporate presence. The salesmen solicited orders on commission without a permanent office, transmitting them to Missouri for fulfillment; Washington taxed the in-state employment, and the company disputed its amenability to the state's jurisdiction. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Washington assessed the unemployment contributions and, when the company disputed jurisdiction, prevailed in the state's administrative process and courts, which found the salesmen's activities sufficient for jurisdiction. The company appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States on the due-process limits of state jurisdiction over an out-of-state corporation.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the salesmen's in-state solicitation activities, their commission-based employment, the absence of a permanent office, and the use of rented sample rooms. The legal question was whether such continuous and systematic contacts, without formal presence, satisfied the due-process requirement for jurisdiction over a foreign corporation.
case.plaintiffArguments: International Shoe argued that it was not 'present' in Washington — it had no office, entered into no contracts there, and shipped its shoes from Missouri — so the state lacked jurisdiction under the traditional presence test. It contended that soliciting orders for interstate sales did not constitute doing business in the state, that jurisdiction over a foreign corporation required a substantial corporate presence, and that the tax assessment exceeded the state's power.
case.defendantArguments: Washington argued that the company's continuous and systematic employment of salesmen within the state generated the very employment relationship on which the tax was based, providing sufficient contacts for jurisdiction. It contended the corporation enjoyed the benefit and protection of Washington's laws through its in-state agents, that jurisdiction was consistent with fair play and substantial justice, and that formal corporate presence was not constitutionally required.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment as a limit on state-court jurisdiction; the 'presence' test for corporations and the emerging 'minimum contacts' standard; Washington's unemployment-compensation statute.
case.precedents: Pennoyer v. Neff (1878) (presence); International Harvester v. Kentucky (1914); the corporate-presence cases; the developing doctrine that jurisdiction depends on contacts rather than formal presence.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Civil procedure / personal jurisdiction. Decided 1945. The case replaced the rigid corporate-presence test with the 'minimum contacts' framework that still governs personal jurisdiction.
case.tldr: Washington taxed a shoe company whose salesmen solicited there. The Court upheld jurisdiction, founding the 'minimum contacts' test for personal jurisdiction.

case.title: United States et al. v. Hermann Göring et al. (Nuremberg Trial of the Major War Criminals)
case.court: International Military Tribunal, Nuremberg
case.actualOutcome: Nineteen of 22 defendants convicted (12 sentenced to death), three acquitted. Individual criminal responsibility for aggression, war crimes and crimes against humanity established.
case.questionPresented: Whether individual Nazi leaders could be held criminally responsible, under international law, for conspiracy to wage aggressive war, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.
case.facts: After Germany's defeat in World War II, the Allied powers created the International Military Tribunal by charter to try the major Nazi war criminals. Twenty-two defendants, including Hermann Göring, were charged with conspiracy to wage aggressive war, crimes against peace, war crimes, and crimes against humanity — including the Holocaust and the murder of millions. The prosecution argued that individuals, not only states, bore criminal responsibility for these offenses under international law, and that aggressive war and systematic atrocities were crimes for which leaders could be tried. The defendants raised defenses including superior orders, the novelty of the charges as ex post facto, and the tribunal's legitimacy as victors' justice; the charter barred several defenses, and the tribunal's jurisdiction over individuals was the central legal question. Twenty-two leaders were tried under the London Charter on charges of conspiracy, aggressive war, war crimes, and crimes against humanity, supported by documentary evidence of systematic atrocity.
case.proceduralHistory: The tribunal convened at Nuremberg under the London Charter signed by the four Allied powers, with judges from the United States, United Kingdom, Soviet Union, and France. After a lengthy trial with extensive documentary and testimonial evidence, the tribunal rendered judgments on each defendant, acquitting three and convicting the rest on various counts, including death sentences for twelve.
case.evidence: The record included massive documentary evidence — captured German orders, records, and films — and testimony establishing the systematic planning of aggressive war, the conduct of the war in violation of treaties, and the atrocities including the extermination camps. The legal issues concerned individual responsibility, the criminality of aggressive war, and the application of crimes against humanity.
case.plaintiffArguments: The prosecution argued that international law recognized individual criminal responsibility for war crimes, aggression, and crimes against humanity, and that the defendants — as the architects and executors of Nazi aggression and atrocity — were guilty as principals and conspirators. It contended the charter's charges were not ex post facto but codified existing law (the Kellogg-Briand Pact, Hague Conventions, and the laws of war), and that superior orders and official position were no defense.
case.defendantArguments: The defendants argued that the charges — particularly crimes against peace and conspiracy — were novel and ex post facto, that international law punished states rather than individuals, that they acted under superior orders or in sovereign capacity, and that the tribunal lacked legitimacy as an instrument of the victors judging the vanquished. They also contested the evidence of individual responsibility and the characterization of defensive war.
case.applicableLaw: The London Charter establishing the International Military Tribunal; the Kellogg-Briand Pact and Hague Conventions on aggressive war and war crimes; customary international law; the doctrine of individual criminal responsibility and the rejection of the superior-orders defense.
case.precedents: The Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928); the Hague Conventions; customary international law of war; no direct precedent existed for an international criminal tribunal of this scope.
case.additionalContext: Topic: International criminal law. Decided 1946. The tribunal established the principle of individual criminal responsibility for aggression and atrocity and founded modern international criminal law.
case.tldr: The Allies tried top Nazi leaders for aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. Nineteen were convicted, establishing individual criminal responsibility under international law.

case.title: Summers v. Tice
case.court: Supreme Court of California
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Where two defendants act negligently and only one caused the harm, the burden shifts to each to prove he did not; both held jointly liable.
case.questionPresented: Whether two defendants who each negligently fired a shotgun in the plaintiff's direction may be held jointly liable when it cannot be determined which defendant's shot actually caused the injury.
case.facts: Charles Summers went hunting with Harold Tice and Ernest Simonson. When a quail flew up, both defendants fired at it in Summers's direction, and Summers was struck in the eye and lip by birdshot. It was impossible to determine which of the two guns had fired the pellet that struck him, but both defendants had been negligent in shooting toward him. Summers sued both. Because only one shot could have caused the injury, the defendants argued that Summers could not prove which one was liable — that under ordinary causation rules, neither could be held responsible absent proof that his shot caused the harm. The case required the court to decide whether the burden of proof on causation could be shifted to the two negligent defendants. Both defendants fired negligently toward the quail at the same instant; only one pellet struck Summers's eye, and no evidence could establish which gun had fired it.
case.proceduralHistory: Summers sued both defendants in the California trial court, which entered judgment against them jointly. The defendants appealed to the Supreme Court of California, arguing that the plaintiff had failed to prove which of them caused the injury and that joint liability was improper.
case.evidence: The record established that both defendants fired negligently in the plaintiff's direction at the same time and that a single pellet caused the eye injury, with no way to determine which gun fired it. The dispute was whether the plaintiff's inability to identify the actual source of the pellet defeated his claim or whether the two negligent actors should bear the burden of proof.
case.plaintiffArguments: Summers argued that both defendants were admittedly negligent in firing toward him, that he was injured by one of them, and that it would be unjust to deny recovery merely because he could not prove which. He contended the burden of proof on causation should shift to the two wrongdoers to exculpate themselves, that both should be jointly and severally liable absent such proof, and that leaving the innocent plaintiff without remedy would place the burden of the defendants' negligence on him.
case.defendantArguments: The defendants argued that the plaintiff failed to prove which of them caused the injury, a necessary element of negligence liability, and that joint liability would hold an innocent party responsible. They contended each was entitled to judgment because the evidence could not connect his particular shot to the wound, that shifting the burden departed from fundamental tort principles, and that at most one of them could be liable.
case.applicableLaw: California negligence law on causation; the burden of proof on the cause of injury; the doctrine that allows the burden to shift to multiple negligent defendants when the actual cause cannot be identified (alternative liability).
case.precedents: The common-law rules on causation and burden of proof; the concert-of-action and enterprise-liability cases; analogous precedent on shifting burdens where multiple defendants are negligent.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Torts / alternative liability. Decided 1948. The case established the 'alternative liability' doctrine for cases where two negligent defendants make it impossible to prove which caused the harm.
case.tldr: Two hunters fired negligently and one shot blinded Summers in one eye, with no way to tell whose pellet hit. The court shifted the burden to the defendants and held both liable.
