case.title: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed injunction. President Truman lacked constitutional or statutory authority to seize the steel mills.
case.caseType: constitutional – separation of powers / executive power
case.questionPresented: Whether the President has constitutional or statutory authority to seize and operate the nation's steel mills to avert a strike during wartime, absent authorization from Congress.
case.facts: During the Korean War, collective bargaining between the steel companies and the United Steelworkers broke down, and the union called a nationwide strike. Asserting that a steel shutdown would cripple the war effort and national defense, President Truman issued Executive Order 10340 directing Secretary of Commerce Charles Sawyer to seize and operate most of the nation's steel mills. Congress had considered but declined to authorize seizure in the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947, which instead provided for injunctions and cooling-off periods the President chose not to invoke. The steel companies complied under protest while suing for a declaratory judgment and injunction, arguing the seizure was lawless executive action — legislation, in effect — unsupported by any statute or constitutional grant. The government asserted inherent executive emergency power. The seizure order issued hours before the strike deadline, the companies sued at once, and the dispute moved from the district court to the Supreme Court in a matter of weeks.
case.proceduralHistory: The companies sued in the federal district court for the District of Columbia for injunctive relief. The district court issued a preliminary injunction against the seizure, finding the President had acted without statutory or constitutional authority. The government sought a stay and expedited review; the Supreme Court granted certiorari before judgment in the court of appeals and heard argument on an accelerated schedule.
case.evidence: The record included Executive Order 10340, the President's messages to Congress, the history of the labor dispute and of Taft-Hartley's deliberate omission of seizure authority, and affidavits on the consequences of a steel shutdown for defense production. There was no factual dispute that the seizure had occurred and that Congress had not authorized it; the question was the scope of presidential power.
case.plaintiffArguments: The steel companies argued that the Constitution commits lawmaking to Congress and that the President may act only pursuant to a statute or an express constitutional grant, neither of which supported seizure of private industry. They pointed to Congress's rejection of seizure authority in Taft-Hartley as evidence of legislative intent against the action, and argued that invoking military necessity to seize domestic plants would erase the separation of powers and create unchecked executive power.
case.defendantArguments: The government argued that the aggregate of the President's powers — as Chief Executive, Commander in Chief, and executor of the laws — includes inherent authority to act in a national emergency threatening the war effort, at least where Congress has not forbidden the action. It contended prior presidents had taken extraordinary measures in wartime, that the seizure was temporary and protective rather than a taking of ownership, and that judicial second-guessing of emergency necessity was inappropriate.
case.applicableLaw: Article II executive power (Vesting, Take Care, and Commander in Chief Clauses); the Labor Management Relations (Taft-Hartley) Act of 1947; the Fifth Amendment takings framework; separation-of-powers doctrine.
case.precedents: In re Neagle (1890) (inherent executive protection power); In re Debs (1895); Ex parte Milligan (1866); United States v. Curtiss-Wright (1936) (foreign affairs power).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Separation of powers / executive power. Decided 1952. The dispute erupted during the Korean War when a nationwide steel strike threatened munitions supply and the President claimed emergency authority to keep the mills running.
case.tldr: President Truman seized the steel mills to avert a wartime strike. The Court blocked the seizure, holding the President had no constitutional or statutory authority to take the mills.

case.title: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Racially segregated public schools are inherently unequal and violate the Equal Protection Clause; Plessy overruled as to public education.
case.questionPresented: Whether state laws requiring or permitting racially segregated public schools deny Black children the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment, even where facilities are nominally equal.
case.facts: Oliver Brown and other Black parents in Topeka, Kansas, sued on behalf of their children, including third-grader Linda Brown, who was required to travel past a nearby white school to attend a segregated Black school under Topeka's racial assignment system. The case was consolidated with challenges from South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, and the District of Columbia, all attacking state-enforced school segregation. The plaintiffs argued that separating children by race generated a sense of inferiority affecting educational opportunity, relying in part on social-science evidence — including the doll studies of psychologists Kenneth and Mamie Clark — about segregation's psychological harm. The school boards defended segregation as lawful under the separate-but-equal doctrine, pointing to purported equality of facilities, teachers' salaries, and curricula. The consolidated cases arose from communities where Black schools were markedly inferior or where plaintiffs challenged enforced separation itself, and the plaintiffs marshalled expert testimony on segregation's psychological harms to children.
case.proceduralHistory: In each consolidated case, a three-judge district court or state court denied relief, applying the separate-but-equal doctrine and, in some instances, finding the facilities substantially equal or being equalized. The plaintiffs obtained review in the Supreme Court, which heard argument in 1952, restored the case to the calendar, and ordered reargument in December 1953 on the history of the Fourteenth Amendment.
case.evidence: The record included findings about comparative school facilities and expert testimony from psychologists and educators that segregation itself — regardless of material equality — instilled a sense of inferiority in Black children that impaired learning. The doll-preference studies and the expert consensus of social scientists were contested by the states, which argued such evidence could not displace a settled constitutional doctrine.
case.plaintiffArguments: The plaintiffs argued that the Fourteenth Amendment was intended to abolish caste legislation and that segregated education stamped Black children with a badge of inferiority, denying equal protection regardless of the quality of facilities. They presented social-science testimony showing segregation's detrimental psychological effects, argued that education was the foundation of citizenship and opportunity, and contended that the separate-but-equal doctrine had no legitimate application to public education, where separation was inherently a statement of inferiority.
case.defendantArguments: The states argued that the Fourteenth Amendment did not abolish the states' power over education or require racially mixed schools, pointing to the Amendment's history, the contemporaneous acceptance of segregated schools in Congress and the states, and the long-settled separate-but-equal doctrine. They contended that educational policy was a matter for local democratic control, that facilities were equal or being equalized, and that claims of psychological harm were speculative social science insufficient to overturn generations of precedent and practice.
case.applicableLaw: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment (and, for the District of Columbia case, the Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause); state segregation statutes and constitutional provisions in Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia, and Delaware; the separate-but-equal doctrine.
case.precedents: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896); Sweatt v. Painter (1950) and McLaurin v. Oklahoma (1950) (graduate education); Cumming v. Board of Education (1899); Gong Lum v. Rice (1927).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Equal protection / school segregation. Decided 1954. The consolidated cases were the culmination of a decades-long NAACP Legal Defense Fund campaign against Jim Crow education, argued before a newly constituted Court under Chief Justice Earl Warren.
case.tldr: Black families challenged racially segregated public schools. The Court unanimously ruled that separate schools are inherently unequal and violate the Fourteenth Amendment.

case.title: Lucy v. Zehmer
case.court: Supreme Court of Virginia
case.actualOutcome: Reversed; specific performance ordered. Contract formation is judged by outward manifestations, not secret intent; the Zehmers' claim of a joke failed.
case.questionPresented: Whether a written agreement to sell a farm for $50,000, signed on a restaurant check during an evening of drinking, was a binding contract judged by the parties' outward manifestations rather than undisclosed intent.
case.facts: W.O. Lucy had long wanted to buy the Ferguson Farm from A.H. Zehmer. One evening at Zehmer's restaurant, after considerable drinking, Lucy again offered $50,000. Zehmer wrote a memorandum on the back of a restaurant check agreeing to sell the farm for $50,000 and, at Lucy's insistence, had his wife Ida sign it too. Zehmer later claimed the whole transaction was a joke between drinking companions and that he had no intention of selling. Lucy sought specific performance. Zehmer argued that his secret intent was jest, that he was intoxicated, and that no serious contract existed. The case required the court to decide whether contract formation is judged by outward expressions or by unexpressed mental reservations. Lucy had pursued the farm for years; after an evening of drinking and bargaining, Zehmer wrote the terms on a restaurant check and, at Lucy's insistence, obtained his wife's signature as well. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Lucy sued in the Virginia trial court for specific performance of the written agreement. The trial court dismissed the suit, finding that no enforceable contract had been formed. Lucy appealed to the Supreme Court of Virginia, which reviewed whether the writing and circumstances manifested a serious agreement.
case.evidence: The record included the writing on the restaurant check signed by both Zehmers, testimony about the evening's drinking and conversation, and Zehmer's claim that the deal was a bluff and that he told Lucy it was a joke. The dispute was whether the outward acts — the written, signed memorandum and the bargaining over terms — demonstrated mutual assent regardless of Zehmer's unexpressed intent.
case.plaintiffArguments: Lucy argued that the signed writing manifested a serious agreement judged by its outward terms, and that a party's undisclosed intent does not defeat contract formation. He contended the parties negotiated price and had both spouses sign, that Zehmer was not so intoxicated as to be incapable of contracting, and that he reasonably understood the transaction as genuine, entitling him to specific performance.
case.defendantArguments: The Zehmers argued that the transaction was a jest between drinking companions, that Zehmer never intended to sell, and that no meeting of the minds occurred. They contended Zehmer was intoxicated, that the writing was casual and incomplete, that Lucy knew or should have known the offer was not serious, and that enforcing the paper would make a joke into a binding sale of a valuable farm.
case.applicableLaw: Virginia contract law on formation; the objective theory of assent — that intent is judged by outward manifestations; the effect of intoxication on contractual capacity; specific performance standards for land-sale contracts.
case.precedents: The objective theory of contract formation in the treatises and earlier cases; precedents on intoxication and capacity; Virginia doctrine on specific performance of land contracts.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Contracts / objective theory. Decided 1954. The case became the standard illustration that contract intent is judged by what parties say and do, not by hidden reservations.
case.tldr: Zehmer signed a farm sale on a restaurant check after drinks, then called it a joke. The court ordered specific performance, judging intent by outward acts.

case.title: Mapp v. Ohio
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment is inadmissible in state courts.
case.questionPresented: Whether evidence obtained through a search that violates the Fourth Amendment is admissible in a state criminal prosecution.
case.facts: Cleveland police officers went to Dollree Mapp's home seeking a suspect in a bombing and evidence of gambling equipment. When Mapp, on advice of counsel, refused entry without a warrant, officers forced their way in, waved a piece of paper purporting to be a warrant, handcuffed Mapp, and searched the house, including the basement. The search turned up no fugitive, but officers found materials they described as obscene, and Mapp was convicted under Ohio's obscenity statute for possessing them. No warrant was ever produced at trial. Ohio had previously declined to apply the federal exclusionary rule in state courts, so the illegally seized material was admitted over objection. The case presented whether the Fourth Amendment's guarantee against unreasonable searches, applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, required exclusion of the fruits of an unlawful search. The officers claimed a bombing suspect and gambling evidence might be inside; the forcible entry, the never-produced warrant, and the basement search yielded the materials used to convict her.
case.proceduralHistory: Mapp was convicted in the Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas of possessing obscene materials. The Ohio Supreme Court sustained the conviction, holding that Ohio law did not require exclusion of evidence obtained by an unlawful search. Mapp appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States.
case.evidence: The prosecution's case rested entirely on the materials seized in the warrantless search; no search warrant was produced or shown to have existed. The defense established that officers entered forcibly over Mapp's objection and that the claimed warrant was never proved, making the admissibility of the seized items the decisive issue.
case.plaintiffArguments: Mapp argued that the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment and is meaningless without a remedy. She contended that admitting illegally seized evidence makes the guarantee an empty form, that federal courts already excluded such evidence, and that the only effective deterrent to unlawful police conduct is exclusion, so the seized materials should not have been admitted against her.
case.defendantArguments: Ohio argued that the exclusionary rule was a judicially created remedy, not a constitutional command, and that the Constitution did not require states to adopt it. The state contended that remedies like trespass actions and internal discipline sufficed, that the rule's cost — freeing the guilty — was too high, and that the evidence was reliable and properly admitted under state law regardless of how it was obtained.
case.applicableLaw: The Fourth Amendment (unreasonable searches and seizures); the Fourteenth Amendment (incorporation); Ohio obscenity statute; the federal exclusionary rule of Weeks v. United States and the state-law discretion recognized in Wolf v. Colorado.
case.precedents: Weeks v. United States (1914) (federal exclusionary rule); Wolf v. Colorado (1949) (incorporation without exclusion); Rochin v. California (1952); Boyd v. United States (1886).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Fourth Amendment / exclusionary rule. Decided 1961. The case arose from a heavy-handed police search in Cleveland and became the vehicle for extending the federal exclusionary rule to state prosecutions nationwide.
case.tldr: Police searched Mapp's home without a valid warrant and found obscene materials. The Court suppressed the evidence, extending the exclusionary rule to state prosecutions.

case.title: Overseas Tankship (UK) Ltd v Morts Dock & Engineering Co (The Wagon Mound No 1)
case.court: Privy Council
case.actualOutcome: Appeal allowed; claim failed. Liability in negligence is limited to reasonably foreseeable damage; fire damage from the oil was not foreseeable.
case.questionPresented: Whether a defendant is liable in negligence for damage of a kind that was not reasonably foreseeable, and whether the directness rule of Re Polemis should govern.
case.facts: The ship Wagon Mound, chartered by Overseas Tankship, discharged furnace oil into Sydney Harbour, where it drifted to the plaintiffs' wharf. The wharf workers, welding at the dock, were assured the oil was not flammable on water and continued welding; molten metal ignited floating material, which set the oil alight, and the resulting fire severely damaged the wharf and ships. The wharf owners sued in negligence for the fire damage. At trial it was found that the oil spill was negligent and that fire damage to the wharf was not reasonably foreseeable, though some fouling damage was. The defendants argued that because fire damage was unforeseeable, no liability attached; the plaintiffs argued that once the spill was negligent, they were liable for the direct consequences under the rule that a negligent defendant is liable for all direct damage. The trial court found the spill negligent and fouling damage foreseeable but fire damage unforeseeable, since furnace oil on water was considered difficult to ignite; welding had continued on expert assurances.
case.proceduralHistory: The plaintiffs sued in the Supreme Court of New South Wales; the trial judge found the oil spill negligent but the fire damage not reasonably foreseeable, yet applied the Re Polemis direct-consequence rule to award damages. The appeal reached the Privy Council on whether foreseeability or directness governed remoteness of damage in negligence.
case.evidence: The record included the trial court's findings that the oil discharge was negligent, that oil fouling of the wharf was foreseeable, but that the fire damage was not reasonably foreseeable because the oil was difficult to ignite on water. The legal question was whether liability extended to all directly caused damage or only to damage of a kind reasonably foreseeable.
case.plaintiffArguments: The wharf owners argued that once the negligent oil spill occurred, the defendant was liable for the direct physical consequences — the fire damage — even if its precise extent or manner was unforeseeable. They contended the Re Polemis rule made a negligent defendant responsible for all direct damage, that the fire was a direct consequence of the discharge, and that foreseeability of the exact type of harm was not required.
case.defendantArguments: Overseas Tankship argued that liability in negligence is limited to damage of a kind reasonably foreseeable, and that because the trial court had found the fire damage unforeseeable, no liability attached. It contended the Re Polemis direct-consequence test was unsound and unworkable, that a defendant should answer only for the harms a reasonable person would have anticipated, and that the unforeseeable fire was too remote.
case.applicableLaw: The law of negligence on remoteness of damage; the competing tests of reasonable foreseeability versus direct consequences (Re Polemis); the extent of a negligent defendant's liability for harm.
case.precedents: Re Polemis (1921) (direct-consequence rule); Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932) (duty); the foreseeability cases on the type of damage recoverable in negligence.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Torts / remoteness of damage. Decided 1961. The Privy Council's decision replaced the directness test with reasonable foreseeability and became the governing rule on remoteness in negligence.
case.tldr: Spilled furnace oil ignited and burned a Sydney wharf. The Privy Council denied liability, holding negligence is limited to reasonably foreseeable damage.

case.title: Baker v. Carr
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed and remanded. Legislative apportionment claims under the Equal Protection Clause are justiciable, not political questions.
case.questionPresented: Whether federal courts have jurisdiction to decide a claim that a state's legislative apportionment violates the Equal Protection Clause, or whether such claims are nonjusticiable political questions.
case.facts: Tennessee's constitution required legislative districts to be reapportioned every ten years according to population, but the legislature had not redrawn district lines since 1901 despite massive population shifts to cities. By 1960, urban voters' ballots counted for far less than rural voters'; districts of vastly unequal population elected equal numbers of legislators. Charles Baker and other Tennessee voters sued Secretary of State Joe Carr in federal court, arguing that the gross malapportionment debased their votes and denied equal protection, and seeking to compel reapportionment. The district court questioned whether it had power to grant relief given the doctrine that legislative apportionment presented a nonjusticiable political question. The case forced the Court to decide whether courts could entertain equal-protection challenges to districting at all. The disparities had grown for six decades as population shifted to cities while district lines stayed fixed, leaving some citizens' votes worth a fraction of others'. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: The voters sued in the Middle District of Tennessee under the Civil Rights Act for declaratory and injunctive relief requiring reapportionment. A three-judge district court dismissed the complaint, holding it lacked power to order relief even though the apportionment was invidious. The plaintiffs appealed directly to the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The record consisted of census and apportionment data showing the dramatic population disparities among Tennessee legislative districts after six decades without reapportionment. There was no dispute about the disparities; the controversy was over judicial power — whether federal courts could adjudicate such claims, and under what constitutional standard.
case.plaintiffArguments: The voters argued that diluting urban votes relative to rural votes denied equal protection by giving some citizens' votes a fraction of others' weight, a concrete injury courts could remedy. They contended the political-question doctrine did not bar relief because the claim rested on the Equal Protection Clause rather than the Guarantee Clause, the standards for judging equality were judicially manageable, and constitutional violations are not insulated simply because they touch politics.
case.defendantArguments: Tennessee argued that legislative apportionment was a quintessential political question committed to the political branches and the people, citing the Court's own reluctance in Colegrove v. Green and the Guarantee Clause tradition. The state contended there were no judicially manageable standards for judging district fairness, that the voters' remedy lay at the ballot box or through constitutional conventions, and that judicial intervention would entangle courts in inherently political judgments.
case.applicableLaw: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; the political-question doctrine under Article III; the Tennessee constitutional reapportionment provisions; the Civil Rights Act's jurisdictional grant (42 U.S.C. § 1983 / 28 U.S.C. § 1343).
case.precedents: Colegrove v. Green (1946) (declining to intervene in districting); Luther v. Borden (1849) (Guarantee Clause political questions); South v. Peters (1950); MacDougall v. Green (1948).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Justiciability / apportionment. Decided 1962. The case challenged rural-dominated legislatures that had ignored reapportionment for generations amid rapid urbanization, setting the stage for the 'one person, one vote' revolution.
case.tldr: Tennessee voters challenged legislative districts left unchanged since 1901. The Court held that equal-protection challenges to apportionment are justiciable, opening the door to reapportionment suits.

case.title: Engel v. Vitale
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. State-composed voluntary school prayer violates the Establishment Clause.
case.questionPresented: Whether a state-composed nondenominational prayer, recited voluntarily in public school classrooms at the start of each day, violates the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment as applied to the states.
case.facts: The New York State Board of Regents, a governmental body, composed a brief nondenominational prayer — 'Almighty God, we acknowledge our dependence upon Thee, and we beg Thy blessings upon us, our parents, our teachers and our Country' — and recommended that local school districts adopt it for daily classroom recitation. The Union Free School District in New Hyde Park directed teachers to lead the prayer at the start of each school day, with participation voluntary and students free not to join or to leave the room. Steven Engel and other parents of varied faiths sued the school board, arguing that official composition and sponsorship of prayer in public schools was an establishment of religion, regardless of voluntariness or denominational neutrality. The board defended the prayer as a permissible encouragement of moral and spiritual values rather than religious coercion. The Regents had drafted the prayer to be denominationally neutral, and the district permitted children to abstain; the parents argued that official authorship and classroom sponsorship were themselves an establishment of religion.
case.proceduralHistory: The parents sued in the New York state courts to bar the prayer's recitation. The trial court and intermediate appellate court permitted the practice to continue, and the New York Court of Appeals sustained it, reasoning that the prayer was voluntary and noncompulsory. The parents obtained review in the Supreme Court of the United States.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the Regents' prayer text, the district's adoption and classroom procedure, and the voluntary-participation arrangements. There was no claim that any child was forced to recite the prayer or punished for abstaining; the dispute was over whether official authorship and classroom sponsorship of prayer themselves constituted an establishment of religion.
case.plaintiffArguments: The parents argued that the Establishment Clause bars government from composing, endorsing, or sponsoring prayer, so state authorship of the Regents' prayer was unconstitutional regardless of voluntariness. They contended that classroom recitation under teacher direction carried implicit coercion and governmental endorsement, that the Clause protects minorities from official religion however mild, and that history — from the framers' opposition to established churches — forbade any union of government and prayer.
case.defendantArguments: The school board argued that the prayer was nondenominational, voluntary, and a permissible acknowledgment of the nation's religious heritage rather than an establishment of a church. It contended no child was coerced, that the practice advanced moral values, and that the Establishment Clause prohibited only coercive or sectarian religious exercises, not brief noncompulsory invocations consistent with longstanding American public practice.
case.applicableLaw: The Establishment Clause of the First Amendment, applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment; New York's Regents' prayer regulation; the heritage of church-state separation doctrine.
case.precedents: Everson v. Board of Education (1947); McCollum v. Board of Education (1948); Zorach v. Clauson (1952).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Establishment Clause / school prayer. Decided 1962. The case challenged a state-authored prayer adopted amid mid-century debates over religion's place in public schooling, and it ignited lasting controversy over school prayer.
case.tldr: New York composed a nondenominational prayer for voluntary classroom recitation. The Court struck it down as an unconstitutional establishment of religion.

case.title: Gideon v. Wainwright
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. States must provide counsel to indigent felony defendants; Betts v. Brady overruled.
case.caseType: constitutional – Sixth Amendment / right to counsel
case.questionPresented: Whether the Sixth Amendment right to counsel, as applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, requires states to appoint counsel for indigent defendants in all felony prosecutions.
case.facts: Clarence Earl Gideon was charged in Florida state court with breaking and entering a poolroom with intent to commit a misdemeanor, a felony under Florida law. Unable to afford a lawyer, Gideon asked the trial court to appoint counsel. The court refused, because Florida law provided appointed counsel only in capital cases. Gideon defended himself, and the jury convicted him; he was sentenced to five years in prison. From his cell, Gideon filed a handwritten petition for habeas corpus in the Florida Supreme Court, arguing that the federal Constitution guaranteed him a lawyer. After the Florida court denied relief, Gideon petitioned the Supreme Court, which appointed counsel — future Justice Abe Fortas — to argue whether the Court's special-circumstances rule for appointed counsel should govern or be reconsidered. Gideon conducted his own defense, cross-examining witnesses and addressing the jury, and his handwritten petition argued that a fair trial was impossible for a poor man without a lawyer.
case.proceduralHistory: Gideon was tried and convicted in the Bay County Circuit Court after representing himself, and sentenced to five years. His habeas petition to the Florida Supreme Court was denied without a hearing. The Supreme Court granted his in forma pauperis certiorari petition and set the case for plenary review, inviting briefing on whether Betts v. Brady's case-by-case approach should be revisited.
case.evidence: The trial record included eyewitness testimony placing Gideon near the poolroom, which he unsuccessfully tried to rebut without counsel. The habeas record established his indigence, his request for counsel, and the court's refusal; the constitutional question turned on the trial record's demonstration that an untrained defendant could not adequately defend himself.
case.plaintiffArguments: Gideon argued that a fair trial is impossible for a poor defendant without a lawyer, and that the Sixth Amendment's guarantee, made applicable to the states by the Fourteenth, requires appointed counsel in all felony cases. He contended the Betts special-circumstances rule was unworkable and wrong in principle — counsel is a necessity, not a luxury — and that the disparity between rich and poor defendants denied equal justice under law.
case.defendantArguments: Florida argued that the Constitution required appointed counsel only in capital cases or where special circumstances showed unfairness, under Betts v. Brady. The state contended Gideon's trial was fundamentally fair, that he capably conducted his own defense, that imposing a universal counsel rule intruded on state administration of criminal justice, and that the Fourteenth Amendment did not incorporate the Sixth Amendment wholesale.
case.applicableLaw: The Sixth Amendment right to counsel; the Fourteenth Amendment (incorporation and due process); Florida's rule limiting appointed counsel to capital cases; the Betts v. Brady special-circumstances standard.
case.precedents: Powell v. Alabama (1932); Betts v. Brady (1942); Johnson v. Zerbst (1938) (federal right to counsel); Griffin v. Illinois (1956).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Sixth Amendment / right to counsel. Decided 1963. The case began with an inmate's penciled petition and became the foundation of the modern public-defender system.
case.tldr: Gideon was convicted after being denied a lawyer because he could not afford one. The Court ruled states must appoint counsel for indigent felony defendants.

case.title: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Public officials must prove actual malice to recover for defamation; $500,000 judgment set aside.
case.questionPresented: Whether a public official may recover damages for a defamatory falsehood relating to his official conduct absent proof that the statement was made with knowledge of its falsity or reckless disregard of the truth.
case.facts: In 1960 the New York Times published a full-page advertisement, 'Heed Their Rising Voices,' placed by civil-rights supporters, describing police actions against demonstrators in Montgomery, Alabama. The ad contained several factual errors — minor inaccuracies about dates, songs sung, and the conduct attributed to police. L.B. Sullivan, the Montgomery city commissioner responsible for the police department, was not named in the ad but sued the Times and several ministers for libel under Alabama law, claiming the ad defamed him by implication. Under Alabama law, libel was 'libel per se' — falsity and damages were presumed once publication was shown — and the publisher bore the burden of proving truth. An all-white jury awarded Sullivan $500,000, one of a wave of libel suits southern officials brought against northern media covering the civil-rights movement. The advertisement's inaccuracies concerned details such as the number of arrests and whether students had been padlocked in a lunchroom; Sullivan was not named but claimed the references to police implicated him.
case.proceduralHistory: Sullivan sued in the Montgomery County Circuit Court and won a $500,000 verdict on the presumed-damages theory. The Alabama Supreme Court sustained the judgment, applying state libel rules that placed the burden of proving truth on the defendant and presumed malice from falsity. The Times appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States.
case.evidence: The record contained the advertisement's text and testimony establishing its factual errors — such as the wrong number of times Dr. King had been arrested and inaccuracies about police conduct — alongside Sullivan's claim that references to 'the police' implicated him. The Times's minimal fact-checking of the ad, submitted by an advertiser, was the key evidence on fault.
case.plaintiffArguments: The Times argued that a rule allowing public officials to recover presumed damages for criticism of official conduct would chill debate on public issues at the core of the First Amendment, resurrecting seditious libel. It contended that erroneous statements are inevitable in free debate, that Alabama's rule inverted the constitutional protection of speech by presuming falsity and malice, and that public officials should have to prove the statement was made with knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth.
case.defendantArguments: Sullivan argued that the First Amendment did not protect false and defamatory commercial advertisements, that Alabama law reasonably balanced reputation against speech, and that the jury properly found the ad referred to him and injured his reputation. He contended the Times published with reckless disregard by failing to verify the ad against its own news files, and that libel judgments were a matter of state tort law beyond federal constitutional supervision.
case.applicableLaw: The First and Fourteenth Amendments; Alabama common-law libel rules, including libel per se, presumed damages, and the defendant's burden of proving truth; the emerging constitutionalization of defamation law.
case.precedents: Near v. Minnesota (1931); New York Times v. Sullivan drew on debate over the Sedition Act of 1798's unconstitutionality; Beauharnais v. Illinois (1952); Roth v. United States (1957).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Defamation / First Amendment. Decided 1964. The suit was part of a coordinated effort by southern officials to use libel verdicts to deter national press coverage of the civil-rights movement.
case.tldr: An Alabama official won a libel verdict over a civil-rights ad with minor errors. The Court reversed, requiring public officials to prove actual malice to recover for defamation.

case.title: Heart of Atlanta Motel, Inc. v. United States
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Congress could bar racial discrimination in public accommodations under the Commerce Clause; the motel lost.
case.questionPresented: Whether Congress may prohibit racial discrimination by privately owned motels serving interstate travelers under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as a regulation of commerce.
case.facts: The Heart of Atlanta Motel, a 216-room motel in downtown Atlanta, readily accessible to interstate highways, solicited business through national advertising and served mostly out-of-state guests. It refused to rent rooms to Black customers. Within hours of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 taking effect, the motel sued for a declaratory judgment that Title II — which barred discrimination in places of public accommodation affecting commerce — was unconstitutional as applied to it. The motel argued that its refusal policy was a private choice beyond Congress's reach, that its business was local, and that the Act violated the Fifth Amendment's property protections and the Thirteenth Amendment's limits on compelled association. The government defended the statute as a regulation of commerce aimed at removing burdens on interstate travel. The motel advertised nationally and served mostly interstate travelers, and Congress had compiled findings that discrimination in lodging imposed real burdens on Black travelers and commerce.
case.proceduralHistory: The motel filed a declaratory-judgment action in the Northern District of Georgia; a three-judge district court sustained Title II's constitutionality as applied to the motel and enjoined its continued refusal to serve Black patrons. The motel appealed directly to the Supreme Court under the Act's expedited-review provisions.
case.evidence: The record included the motel's advertising practices, its percentage of interstate guests, its accessibility to interstate highways, and congressional findings about the burden racial discrimination placed on Black interstate travelers — the difficulty of finding lodging and the resulting deterrent to travel and commerce.
case.plaintiffArguments: The motel argued that its discrimination was a private, local business decision that Congress could not reach under the Commerce Clause, since lodging was a local activity and its effects on interstate commerce were incidental. It contended the Act took property without due process and compelled involuntary servitude contrary to the Thirteenth Amendment, and that Congress was using commerce power as a pretext to legislate morality and association.
case.defendantArguments: The United States argued that racial discrimination in public accommodations imposed substantial burdens on interstate commerce — deterring Black travel, depressing commerce, and obstructing the free flow of goods and people — which Congress could regulate. It contended the motel's solicitation of interstate guests put it squarely within the commerce power, that Congress need only have a rational basis to find effects on commerce, and that precedent had long sustained federal reach over local activities affecting interstate commerce.
case.applicableLaw: Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; the Commerce Clause; the Fifth Amendment due process and the Thirteenth Amendment arguments raised by the motel; the Civil Rights Cases (1883) framework on the Fourteenth Amendment's limits.
case.precedents: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824); Wickard v. Filburn (1942); the Civil Rights Cases (1883); Katzenbach v. McClung (Ollie's Barbecue), decided the same day.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Commerce Clause / civil rights. Decided 1964. The case was the leading test of the just-enacted Civil Rights Act's public-accommodations provisions, enacted over a southern filibuster after the Birmingham campaign and March on Washington.
case.tldr: A motel refused Black guests and challenged the 1964 Civil Rights Act. The Court upheld Title II, holding Congress could bar discrimination in public accommodations under the Commerce Clause.

result.title: Heart of Atlanta Motel, Inc. v. United States

case.title: Griswold v. Connecticut
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Connecticut's ban on contraceptive use by married couples violated a constitutional right to marital privacy.
case.questionPresented: Whether a Connecticut statute criminalizing the use of contraceptives, and aiding or counseling their use, violates a constitutional right of marital privacy.
case.facts: Connecticut law since 1879 made it a crime for any person to use a drug or instrument to prevent conception, and a separate statute punished those who aided, abetted, or counseled such use. Estelle Griswold, executive director of Planned Parenthood of Connecticut, and Dr. C. Lee Buxton, a Yale physician, opened a birth-control clinic in New Haven to test the law, counseling married couples on contraception. They were arrested, convicted as accessories, and fined. Griswold challenged the statute as applied to married couples, arguing it invaded a zone of privacy surrounding the marital relationship that no constitutional provision explicitly named but that liberty and the Bill of Rights protected. The state defended the law as within its police power over morality and public health. The clinic was opened deliberately to test the statute after Poe v. Ullman had left the issue unresolved, and the married couples who received counseling were identified in the prosecution's case.
case.proceduralHistory: Griswold and Buxton were convicted in Connecticut state court as accessories to the use of contraceptives and fined $100 each. The Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors sustained the convictions, finding no constitutional barrier. Griswold appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States; the Court had previously declined to reach the merits of a similar challenge in Poe v. Ullman on justiciability grounds.
case.evidence: The record established the clinic's counseling of married couples and the resulting convictions; the facts of 'use' by married patients were undisputed. The legal contest centered on whether a right of privacy could be located in the Constitution — in the penumbras of the First, Third, Fourth, Fifth, and Ninth Amendments, or in due process liberty — rather than on contested facts.
case.plaintiffArguments: Griswold argued that the statute reached into the intimate marital relationship — the very bedroom — and violated a right of privacy implicit in the liberty protected by the Fourteenth Amendment and the penumbras of specific Bill of Rights guarantees. She contended the law was not justified as a health or morality measure, that the use ban affected a fundamental liberty more basic than express enumeration, and that the Ninth Amendment confirmed rights beyond those listed.
case.defendantArguments: Connecticut argued that no enumerated constitutional right barred a state from regulating contraceptives and that the claim of a general 'privacy' right lacked textual foundation. The state contended the law was a legitimate exercise of police power over sexual morality, that courts had no warrant to invalidate it on free-floating notions of liberty, and that any change should come from the legislature.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; the Connecticut anti-contraception statutes of 1879; the penumbral and Ninth Amendment theories of unenumerated rights advanced by the appellants.
case.precedents: Poe v. Ullman (1961) (dismissed on standing); Meyer v. Nebraska (1923) and Pierce v. Society of Sisters (1925) (liberty in family matters); Lochner-era due process cases the Court was wary of reviving.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Privacy / contraception. Decided 1965. The challenge was organized by Planned Parenthood after decades of Connecticut's ban, the strictest such law in the nation, surviving earlier repeal efforts.
case.tldr: Connecticut prosecuted Planned Parenthood staff for counseling contraception. The Court struck down the ban, recognizing a constitutional right to marital privacy.

case.title: Williams v. Walker-Thomas Furniture Co.
case.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit
case.actualOutcome: Reversed and remanded. Courts may refuse to enforce unconscionable contracts; the trial court must consider whether the cross-collateral clause was unconscionable.
case.questionPresented: Whether a retail installment contract containing a cross-collateralization clause was so unfair as to be unenforceable as unconscionable, and whether courts may refuse to enforce such contracts.
case.facts: Ora Williams, a poor District of Columbia consumer on public assistance, bought a series of household items on credit from Walker-Thomas Furniture. Each purchase was made under a standardized installment contract containing an add-on or cross-collateral clause: payments were credited to all prior purchases so that every item remained collateral until the whole balance was paid, meaning default on any payment allowed repossession of all items ever bought. After buying many items, including a stereo she could not afford, Williams defaulted, and the company sought to repossess everything. She argued the contract was unconscionable — a term she alleged she did not understand — and that its enforcement would be unfair. The case asked whether courts could refuse to enforce a contract whose terms were unreasonably favorable to the seller. The standardized clause credited each payment across all prior purchases, so default on the last item permitted repossession of everything ever bought; Williams was a public-assistance recipient of limited education.
case.proceduralHistory: Walker-Thomas sued in the D.C. trial court to enforce the contract and repossess the goods; the court entered judgment for the seller. The District of Columbia Court of Appeals sustained. Williams sought review in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit on the unconscionability defense under the Uniform Commercial Code.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the standardized installment contracts with the cross-collateral clause, Williams's financial circumstances and limited education, and the company's practice of using the clause to secure every purchase by the entire account balance. The dispute was whether the clause was so one-sided and oppressive, and the bargaining inequality so great, as to render the contract unenforceable.
case.plaintiffArguments: Williams argued that the cross-collateral clause was unconscionable — a term so unfair and hidden that no reasonable consumer would have accepted it had she understood it — and that under the UCC courts may refuse to enforce unconscionable contracts. She contended the clause allowed repossession of all goods on any default, that it was imposed on an unsophisticated buyer without meaningful choice, and that enforcement would be oppressive.
case.defendantArguments: Walker-Thomas argued that the contract was a standard, lawful installment agreement and that Williams had signed it and obtained the goods. It contended the clause was a legitimate security arrangement common in consumer credit, that courts should not rewrite contracts or protect parties from bad bargains, and that the UCC's unconscionability provision did not reach this common commercial practice.
case.applicableLaw: The Uniform Commercial Code's unconscionability provision (UCC § 2-302) and the common-law doctrine of unconscionability; contract defenses based on unfairness, oppression, and inequality of bargaining power.
case.precedents: UCC § 2-302 and its official comments; the earlier unconscionability cases in equity and at common law; the developing doctrine on adhesion contracts and consumer protection.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Contracts / unconscionability. Decided 1965. The decision is the leading modern authority on the judicial power to refuse enforcement of unconscionable consumer contracts.
case.tldr: A furniture company used a clause letting it repossess everything on any missed payment. The court said judges may refuse to enforce unconscionable contract terms and sent the case back.

case.title: Miranda v. Arizona
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Suspects must be warned of their rights before custodial interrogation; the confession was inadmissible.
case.questionPresented: Whether statements obtained from a suspect during custodial police interrogation, absent warnings of the right to remain silent and to counsel, are admissible under the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.
case.facts: Ernesto Miranda was arrested at his Phoenix home and taken to a police station, where a witness identified him in a lineup for kidnapping and rape. Two officers interrogated Miranda for two hours in a separate room; he was not told he had a right to counsel or that he could remain silent. Miranda confessed in writing, and the confession — over objection — was admitted at trial, where he was convicted of kidnapping and rape. His case was consolidated with three others (Vignera v. New York, Westover v. United States, and California v. Stewart), all involving confessions obtained during incommunicado interrogation without full warnings. The cases presented whether the coercive atmosphere of custodial questioning compelled self-incrimination and what procedural safeguards the Fifth Amendment required. The four consolidated cases all involved station-house interrogations in which suspects were questioned incommunicado without advice of rights, illustrating the coercive atmosphere the Court was asked to regulate.
case.proceduralHistory: Miranda was convicted in the Maricopa County Superior Court and sentenced to concurrent prison terms. The Arizona Supreme Court sustained the conviction, finding his confession voluntary under the totality of the circumstances. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and consolidated the case with three companion cases raising the same issue.
case.evidence: The central evidence was Miranda's written confession, obtained after two hours of custodial questioning without warnings; the record showed no physical coercion but also no advice of rights. Companion cases similarly involved station-house interrogations where suspects were isolated and questioned until they confessed, illustrating the inherent pressure of custodial interrogation.
case.plaintiffArguments: Miranda argued that custodial interrogation is inherently coercive — the isolation, incommunicado setting, and psychological pressure compel confession — and that the Fifth Amendment requires that suspects be informed of their rights before questioning. He contended his confession was not the product of free choice, that ignorance of rights is no less coercive than physical pressure, and that only prophylactic warnings could protect the privilege against self-incrimination for those unable to invoke it knowingly.
case.defendantArguments: Arizona argued that the confession was voluntary under the traditional totality-of-circumstances test, that no physical coercion or prolonged deprivation occurred, and that the Fifth Amendment barred only compelled confessions, not uncounseled ones. The state contended that mandatory warnings would cripple law enforcement, that many voluntary confessions would be lost, and that the Court had never held warnings constitutionally required in state prosecutions.
case.applicableLaw: The Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination; the Fourteenth Amendment (application to the states); the voluntariness/totality test for confessions; the Sixth Amendment counsel right as it bore on interrogation after Escobedo.
case.precedents: Escobedo v. Illinois (1964); Massiah v. United States (1964); Malloy v. Hogan (1964) (incorporating the Fifth Amendment privilege); Brown v. Mississippi (1936) (coerced confessions).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Fifth Amendment / custodial interrogation. Decided 1966. The consolidated cases were decided amid a national debate over policing and produced the warnings now recited in every arrest.
case.tldr: Miranda confessed after custodial interrogation without warnings. The Court suppressed the confession, requiring police to advise suspects of their rights before questioning.

case.title: Loving v. Virginia
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Virginia's ban on interracial marriage violated the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses.
case.questionPresented: Whether a Virginia statute criminalizing marriage between white and non-white persons violates the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.
case.facts: Richard Loving, a white man, and Mildred Jeter, a Black woman, married in the District of Columbia in 1958 and returned to live in Caroline County, Virginia. Virginia's Racial Integrity Act made it a felony for a white person to marry a non-white person. Indicted on their marriage certificate, the Lovings pleaded guilty and were sentenced to a year in jail, suspended on condition they leave Virginia and not return together for twenty-five years. The trial judge declared that God had separated the races and did not intend them to mix. The Lovings moved to Washington, D.C., and later sought to vacate the sentences and invalidate the statute, arguing that criminalizing marriage on the basis of race was a paradigmatic denial of equal protection and of the freedom to marry. Sixteen states still had anti-miscegenation laws. The Lovings' cause was taken up by the ACLU after they were barred from returning home together, and sixteen states still enforced anti-miscegenation laws when the case was argued.
case.proceduralHistory: The Lovings pleaded guilty in the Caroline County Circuit Court and received suspended one-year sentences conditioned on leaving the state. They moved to set aside the sentences; after that motion was denied, the Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals sustained the convictions and the statute under the equal-application theory. The Lovings appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States.
case.evidence: The record included the marriage certificate, the indictment, and the guilty pleas establishing the fact of the interracial marriage. There was no factual dispute; the case turned entirely on whether a statute criminalizing interracial marriage — applied equally to both races — could satisfy the Fourteenth Amendment.
case.plaintiffArguments: The Lovings argued that the statute rested solely on racial classification — the most suspect basis of legislation — and could not survive the strictest scrutiny absent an overriding state purpose. They contended that 'equal application' to both races did not save the law, which served only to maintain white supremacy, and that the freedom to marry was a fundamental liberty and basic civil right protected by due process, which the state could not condition on race.
case.defendantArguments: Virginia argued that the statute punished both races equally and therefore did not discriminate within the meaning of the Equal Protection Clause, following reasoning in earlier cases like Pace v. Alabama. The state contended marriage regulation was a traditional state power under the Tenth Amendment, that the legislature could rationally conclude interracial marriage posed social harms, and that courts should defer to state domestic-relations policy.
case.applicableLaw: The Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment; Virginia's Racial Integrity Act of 1924 and related anti-miscegenation statutes; the emerging strict-scrutiny doctrine for racial classifications.
case.precedents: McLaughlin v. Florida (1964) (striking interracial cohabitation ban); Pace v. Alabama (1883); Skinner v. Oklahoma (1942) (marriage as a fundamental right); Korematsu's strict-scrutiny language.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Equal protection / interracial marriage. Decided 1967. The case reached the Court during the civil-rights era when a shrinking number of states, all in the South, still criminalized interracial marriage.
case.tldr: The Lovings were convicted for marrying across racial lines. The Court struck down Virginia's anti-miscegenation law under equal protection and due process.

case.title: Katz v. United States
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places; warrantless electronic eavesdropping on a phone booth was an unconstitutional search.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Fourth Amendment protects against warrantless government eavesdropping on a telephone conversation in a public phone booth, absent physical trespass into a constitutionally protected area.
case.facts: FBI agents suspected Charles Katz of transmitting gambling information by telephone across state lines. Without obtaining a warrant, agents attached an electronic listening and recording device to the outside of a public telephone booth Katz regularly used. By listening only when Katz used the booth, the agents recorded his end of conversations transmitting wagering information. Based on those recordings, Katz was convicted of transmitting wagering information by wire in violation of federal law. Katz challenged the conviction, arguing the eavesdropping was a search and seizure that violated his Fourth Amendment rights even though agents never physically entered the booth, and that the recordings should have been suppressed for lack of a warrant. The agents attached the listening device to the booth's exterior and monitored only Katz's calls; the government argued no trespass into a protected area had occurred at all. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Katz was convicted in the federal district court in Los Angeles of transmitting wagering information by telephone. The Ninth Circuit sustained the conviction, reasoning that no physical intrusion into a protected area had occurred under then-governing Fourth Amendment doctrine. The Supreme Court granted certiorari.
case.evidence: The contested evidence consisted of the FBI's recordings of Katz's telephone conversations from the tapped phone booth, introduced over his objection. It was undisputed that the agents had no warrant, that they used an electronic device attached to the booth's exterior, and that they monitored only Katz's calls — presenting the question whether the Fourth Amendment turned on physical trespass or on reasonable expectation of privacy.
case.plaintiffArguments: Katz argued that the Fourth Amendment protects a person's reasonable expectation of privacy, and that closing the door of a phone booth is an effort to keep a conversation private that the government may not defeat without a warrant. He contended the trespass doctrine of Olmstead was outdated in an age of electronic surveillance, that the booth was a constitutionally protected area for these purposes, and that the recordings were the fruit of a warrantless search and should have been suppressed.
case.defendantArguments: The United States argued that the agents never physically entered the booth, so under Olmstead v. United States no 'search' occurred within the Fourth Amendment's protection of places. It contended a phone booth open to public view was not a constitutionally protected area, that the surveillance was narrowly targeted and minimally intrusive, and that the recordings were properly admitted as evidence of interstate wagering.
case.applicableLaw: The Fourth Amendment; the federal wiretapping framework and the Communications Act of 1934 (Section 605); the physical-trespass conception of searches from Olmstead and Goldman v. United States.
case.precedents: Olmstead v. United States (1928); Goldman v. United States (1942); Berger v. New York (1967) (electronic surveillance); Silverman v. United States (1961).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Fourth Amendment / wiretapping. Decided 1967. The case arrived as electronic eavesdropping was displacing physical entry, pressing the Court to rethink what the Fourth Amendment protects.
case.tldr: Agents wiretapped a public phone booth without a warrant. The Court suppressed the recordings, holding the Fourth Amendment protects reasonable expectations of privacy, not just places.

case.title: Terry v. Ohio
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. A brief stop and protective frisk on reasonable suspicion is permissible; the conviction stood.
case.caseType: constitutional – Fourth Amendment / stop and frisk
case.questionPresented: Whether police may briefly stop and conduct a limited pat-down search of a person on the street, based on less than probable cause, consistent with the Fourth Amendment.
case.facts: A Cleveland plainclothes detective with nearly forty years' experience observed John Terry and another man walk repeatedly past a store window, conferring in a manner the officer concluded meant they were 'casing' the store for a robbery. Suspecting the men were armed, the officer approached, identified himself, and asked their names; when they mumbled a response, he spun Terry around and patted down the outside of his clothing, feeling a pistol in the coat pocket. He seized the gun, and Terry was charged with carrying a concealed weapon. Terry moved to suppress the gun as the fruit of an unlawful search, arguing the officer lacked probable cause for an arrest when he stopped and searched him. The case asked whether the Fourth Amendment permits a limited stop-and-frisk on articulable suspicion short of probable cause. The officer testified that the men's repeated passes and conferences suggested they were casing the store for a robbery and might be armed, justifying a pat-down for weapons.
case.proceduralHistory: Terry was tried and convicted of carrying a concealed weapon in the Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas after his suppression motion was denied; the trial court distinguished a 'stop and frisk' from a formal search. The Ohio Court of Appeals sustained the conviction, and the Ohio Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. The Supreme Court granted certiorari.
case.evidence: The key testimony was the officer's account of observing the men's repeated, suspicious circuit past the store window and his inference from experience that a robbery was being planned and that the men were armed. The gun itself was found in a pat-down of outer clothing; the dispute was whether such an on-the-street intrusion could be justified without probable cause to arrest.
case.plaintiffArguments: Terry argued that the stop and frisk was a seizure and search within the Fourth Amendment requiring probable cause, which the officer lacked — the men had done nothing overtly criminal. He contended that allowing searches on mere suspicion would expose citizens, especially in cities, to harassment, that the exclusionary rule should apply, and that the gun was the inadmissible product of an unconstitutional search.
case.defendantArguments: Ohio argued that a brief investigatory stop and a limited protective frisk are lesser intrusions justified by reasonable suspicion, distinct from an arrest requiring probable cause. The state contended officer safety demanded the ability to disarm persons reasonably believed armed and dangerous, that the officer's specific observations supported suspicion, and that suppressing the gun would leave police helpless to protect themselves during street encounters.
case.applicableLaw: The Fourth Amendment (unreasonable searches and seizures); the probable-cause standard for arrests and full searches; the government's proposed reasonable-suspicion standard for limited investigatory stops and protective frisks.
case.precedents: Weeks v. United States (1914); Mapp v. Ohio (1961); Beck v. Ohio (1964) (probable cause); no direct precedent on suspicion-based street stops.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Fourth Amendment / stop and frisk. Decided 1968. The case reached the Court as urban policing and street crime dominated national politics, and it created the framework for 'Terry stops.'
case.tldr: An officer patted down a man acting suspiciously and found a gun. The Court upheld the stop-and-frisk on reasonable suspicion short of probable cause.

case.title: Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Students retain free-speech rights absent substantial disruption; the armband suspension was unconstitutional.
case.questionPresented: Whether public school students' wearing of black armbands to protest the Vietnam War is symbolic speech protected by the First Amendment that school officials may not suppress absent a showing of substantial disruption.
case.facts: A group of Des Moines students, including teenagers Mary Beth and John Tinker and Christopher Eckhardt, decided to wear black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War. Learning of the plan, school principals adopted a policy forbidding armbands and warning that students who wore them would be suspended. The students wore armbands anyway; none caused any disruption, disturbance, or interference with school activities, but they were sent home and suspended until they agreed to return without armbands. Their parents sued the school district, arguing the suspension punished peaceful political expression. The district defended the ban as a reasonable measure to prevent disruption in schools, where officials claimed broad authority to maintain order and discipline. The district banned armbands after learning of the plan; the students wore them silently, caused no disruption, and were suspended while other political symbols were allowed without incident. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: The students' fathers sued in the Southern District of Iowa for nominal damages and an injunction. The district court dismissed the complaint, finding the ban reasonable to prevent disturbance. An evenly divided Eighth Circuit sustained the dismissal without opinion. The Supreme Court granted certiorari.
case.evidence: The record established that the armband wearing was silent, passive protest unaccompanied by disruption, demonstrations, or interference with classes. The school district offered no evidence of actual disturbance — only fear that protests might cause disorder — while the students showed that other political symbols, such as campaign buttons, were permitted without incident.
case.plaintiffArguments: The students argued that wearing an armband was pure symbolic speech indistinguishable from spoken dissent, fully protected by the First Amendment, which does not stop at the schoolhouse gate. They contended the school punished expression based solely on fear of possible disruption, that no actual disturbance occurred or was reasonably forecast, and that officials may not suppress speech merely because they disagree with its message or anticipate discomfort.
case.defendantArguments: The school district argued that school authorities must have latitude to maintain discipline and prevent disruption, and that the armband policy was a reasonable, content-neutral regulation of conduct in an educational setting. It contended that students are not adults with full expressive rights in a structured school environment, that the policy applied to all armbands equally, and that the potential for disturbance during a divisive war justified the precautionary ban.
case.applicableLaw: The First Amendment's speech clause, applied through the Fourteenth Amendment; the school district's anti-armband regulation; emerging doctrine on symbolic speech and on the constitutional rights of students.
case.precedents: West Virginia v. Barnette (1943); Thornhill v. Alabama (1940); Stromberg v. California (1931); Burnside v. Byars (5th Cir. 1966) (student speech in school).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Student speech. Decided 1969. The case grew out of antiwar protest in the Midwest at the height of the Vietnam War and became the foundational statement of students' First Amendment rights.
case.tldr: Students were suspended for wearing black armbands protesting the Vietnam War. The Court ruled the silent protest was protected speech absent substantial disruption.

case.title: Brandenburg v. Ohio
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Speech may be punished only if directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it.
case.questionPresented: Whether Ohio's criminal syndicalism statute, punishing advocacy of violence or unlawful methods of political change, violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments as applied to speech that is not directed to inciting imminent lawless action.
case.facts: Clarence Brandenburg, a leader of a Ku Klux Klan group in rural Ohio, invited a television reporter to film a Klan rally. The footage showed hooded figures, some armed, burning a cross and making speeches containing derogatory references to Black and Jewish people and vague statements about 'revengeance' and a possible march on Washington. No specific unlawful act was planned or imminent. Brandenburg was convicted under Ohio's Criminal Syndicalism Act, which punished advocating crime, sabotage, violence, or unlawful methods of terrorism as a means of accomplishing political reform, and assembling to teach such doctrines. He argued that the statute punished abstract advocacy of doctrine rather than incitement to imminent lawless action, criminalizing speech protected by the First Amendment. The filmed rally showed armed figures and a cross burning; Brandenburg's speech used vague threats and a possible march on Washington, with no concrete plan or imminent unlawful act. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Brandenburg was convicted in the Hamilton County Court of Common Pleas, fined, and sentenced to prison under the syndicalism statute. The Ohio courts sustained the conviction; the Ohio Supreme Court dismissed his appeal as raising no substantial constitutional question. The Supreme Court noted probable jurisdiction and heard the case.
case.evidence: The prosecution relied on the television film of the rally — the speeches, the cross burning, and the firearms — and on the invitation to the press as evidence of advocacy. The record contained no evidence of any planned or imminent unlawful act, audience incitement, or resulting violence; the criminality turned on whether advocacy of doctrine alone could be punished.
case.plaintiffArguments: Brandenburg argued that the statute unconstitutionally punished the mere advocacy and teaching of abstract doctrine — the desirability of violence as political theory — rather than incitement to imminent lawless action. He contended the film showed vague rhetoric and no concrete call to immediate unlawful acts, that the clear-and-present-danger principle as refined required more than advocacy of belief, and that the statute was indistinguishable from the criminal-anarchy and syndicalism laws the Court had questioned.
case.defendantArguments: Ohio argued that the statute punished advocacy of violence and unlawful action, not mere belief, and that the Klan rally — with arms, cross-burning, and threats — showed advocacy beyond abstract doctrine. The state contended the film established concerted organization to promote violence, that states retained power to forbid terrorism and violent political methods, and that its own courts had sustained the statute consistently with the First Amendment.
case.applicableLaw: The First and Fourteenth Amendments; Ohio's Criminal Syndicalism Act of 1919; the evolving clear-and-present-danger doctrine and the distinction between advocacy of doctrine and incitement to action.
case.precedents: Schenck v. United States (1919); Whitney v. California (1927) (and Brandeis's concurrence); Dennis v. United States (1951); Yates v. United States (1957) (doctrine vs. action).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Free speech / incitement. Decided 1969. The case involved a Klan rally filmed for television and produced the modern imminent-lawless-action test protecting even hateful advocacy.
case.tldr: A Klan leader was convicted under Ohio's syndicalism law after a filmed rally. The Court reversed, holding speech may be punished only if it incites imminent lawless action.

case.title: New York Times Co. v. United States (Pentagon Papers)
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Injunctions denied. The government did not meet the heavy burden required to justify a prior restraint on publishing the Pentagon Papers.
case.questionPresented: Whether the government may obtain a court injunction barring newspapers from publishing a classified history of the Vietnam War on grounds of national security, consistent with the First Amendment.
case.facts: In 1971 the New York Times and then the Washington Post began publishing excerpts of a classified Defense Department study of the Vietnam War — the 'Pentagon Papers' — leaked by Daniel Ellsberg. The Nixon administration sued in federal court to enjoin further publication, arguing that disclosure would gravely damage national security and ongoing diplomacy. The study was a historical narrative of decision-making through 1968, largely complete before the current administration took office; the government did not claim it revealed troop movements or current operational secrets, but invoked general harms to intelligence and foreign relations. The case came to the Court within days, on an extraordinary expedited schedule, pitting the government's claim that prior restraint was necessary to protect the nation against the press's claim that prior restraints are presumptively unconstitutional. The study traced decision-making through 1968, largely predating the incumbent administration, and the government's claim of harm rested on generalized national-security assertions rather than identified operational secrets.
case.proceduralHistory: The government sued the Times in the Southern District of New York and the Post in the District of Columbia. The Second Circuit enjoined the Times pending further review; the D.C. Circuit refused to enjoin the Post. Both sides sought immediate Supreme Court review; the Court granted certiorari within days and heard argument on a dramatically accelerated schedule, deciding the case roughly two weeks after publication began.
case.evidence: The government's case rested on affidavits and sealed submissions from officials asserting that publication would harm national security, intelligence gathering, and diplomatic negotiations, without identifying specific operational secrets in the historical study. The newspapers emphasized the classified-but-historical nature of the documents and the absence of any showing of direct, immediate, irreparable harm to the nation.
case.plaintiffArguments: The United States argued that publication of classified material during wartime posed a grave threat to national security, diplomatic relations, and the safety of military and intelligence personnel, justifying an exceptional prior restraint. It contended the executive's judgment about national-security harm deserved judicial deference, that the First Amendment did not absolutely bar all prior restraints, and that the sensitive nature of the documents outweighed the press's interest in publication.
case.defendantArguments: The newspapers argued that prior restraint is the most serious infringement of First Amendment rights and bears a heavy presumption of invalidity that the government had not met with vague, speculative claims of harm. They contended the study was historical rather than operational, that the public had a right to know how the war began, and that the executive could not suppress embarrassing revelations by labeling them secret; any harm alleged was not the direct, immediate, irreparable injury that might justify censorship.
case.applicableLaw: The First Amendment's press and speech clauses; the government's inherent and statutory authority over classified information; the Espionage Act (which the government notably did not invoke for an injunction); prior-restraint doctrine.
case.precedents: Near v. Minnesota (1931) (heavy presumption against prior restraints, with a narrow wartime exception); Schenck v. United States (1919); Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe (1971).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Prior restraint / national security. Decided 1971. The case arose when a defense analyst leaked a secret history of the Vietnam War to newspapers during the Nixon administration, prompting an unprecedented attempt to censor the press.
case.tldr: The Nixon administration sued to stop publication of the Pentagon Papers. The Court lifted the injunctions, holding the government had not met its heavy burden for prior restraint.
