case.title: Lemon v. Kurtzman
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. State salary supplements to parochial school teachers created excessive entanglement and violated the Establishment Clause (Lemon test).
case.caseType: constitutional – Establishment Clause / parochial school aid
case.questionPresented: Whether state statutes providing salary supplements and instructional materials to teachers in religiously affiliated schools violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.
case.facts: Pennsylvania's Nonpublic Elementary and Secondary Education Act authorized the state to reimburse church-related schools for the cost of teachers' salaries, textbooks, and instructional materials in secular subjects like mathematics, languages, and science. Teachers in parochial schools — the overwhelming majority Catholic — received supplements for teaching secular subjects, subject to statutory restrictions that the materials be secular and used only for secular instruction. Alton Lemon and other taxpayers sued state officials, arguing the program funneled public money to religious institutions and required constitutionally impermissible state involvement with church schools. A companion case challenged Rhode Island's similar salary-supplement statute. The states defended the programs as neutral aid to secular education that benefited children, not religion, and as a lawful way to support the secular functions of religiously affiliated schools. The supplemented subjects were secular — mathematics, languages, and the like — but the recipient schools were pervasively religious, requiring ongoing surveillance to keep the public aid confined to secular use.
case.proceduralHistory: Lemon sued in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania challenging the salary supplements. A three-judge district court dismissed the complaint, finding no establishment violation. In the companion case, a Rhode Island court reached the opposite result and enjoined that state's program. The Supreme Court consolidated the appeals and heard argument in 1971.
case.evidence: The record included the statutes' terms, the religious character and governance of the recipient schools, the subjects taught, and the mechanisms for monitoring whether funds and materials were used only secularly. Central facts concerned how pervasively religious the schools were and how much ongoing state surveillance would be needed to prevent the secular aid from advancing religion.
case.plaintiffArguments: The taxpayers argued that direct salary supplements to teachers in pervasively religious schools had the primary effect of advancing religion, since those teachers could inculcate faith even in secular subjects. They contended that policing the restriction would require constant government surveillance of religious classrooms — an excessive entanglement of church and state — and that using tax funds to support church schools violated the Establishment Clause's prohibition on compelled support of religion.
case.defendantArguments: Pennsylvania and the school interests argued the program served the secular purpose of educating children and provided aid only for secular subjects with adequate safeguards against religious use. They contended that aid went to secular instruction benefiting students rather than the church itself, that states could accommodate the secular functions of religious schools without establishing religion, and that the monitoring required was no more intrusive than oversight of other funded programs.
case.applicableLaw: The Establishment Clause of the First Amendment, applied to the states through the Fourteenth; Pennsylvania's Nonpublic Elementary and Secondary Education Act; Rhode Island's similar statute; the developing doctrine on public aid to religious schools.
case.precedents: Everson v. Board of Education (1947); Board of Education v. Allen (1968); Walz v. Tax Commission (1970); Abington School District v. Schempp (1963).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Establishment Clause. Decided 1971. The case tested state efforts to support financially struggling parochial schools and produced the three-part 'Lemon test' that governed establishment law for decades.
case.tldr: Pennsylvania reimbursed church-school teachers' salaries for secular subjects. The Court struck the program down, announcing a three-part test for laws touching religion.

case.title: Furman v. Georgia
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Death sentences imposed under standardless discretionary schemes were cruel and unusual; existing capital statutes invalidated.
case.questionPresented: Whether the imposition and execution of the death penalty under statutes giving juries unguided discretion constitutes cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments.
case.facts: William Furman was convicted of murder and sentenced to death in Georgia; his case was consolidated with two others (Jackson v. Georgia, for rape, and Branch v. Texas) in which juries imposed death sentences under statutes that gave the jury complete, unguided discretion whether to impose death or life imprisonment. The statutes contained no standards to channel the decision and no meaningful appellate review of the sentence. The petitioners argued that the death penalty as then administered was imposed so arbitrarily, infrequently, and discriminatorily — disproportionately on Black defendants, the poor, and those who killed white victims — that it amounted to cruel and unusual punishment. Georgia defended capital punishment as a constitutionally permissible penalty that juries had applied reasonably and that served retribution and deterrence. The three consolidated cases involved unguided jury discretion to choose death or life imprisonment, and the petitioners presented statistical studies on the rarity and racial disproportion of executions.
case.proceduralHistory: Furman was convicted and sentenced to death by a Georgia jury under a statute allowing the jury unlimited discretion in choosing death. The Georgia Supreme Court sustained the conviction and sentence, as did the courts in the companion cases. The Supreme Court granted certiorari limited to whether the death penalty's imposition in these cases violated the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments.
case.evidence: The record included the trial transcripts and sentencing verdicts, along with statistical studies submitted by the petitioners showing the infrequency and racial disproportion of capital sentencing. The constitutional challenge concerned the pattern and arbitrariness of death sentences nationwide rather than any claim of innocence; Furman's own trial record included questions about his mental capacity.
case.plaintiffArguments: Furman argued that the death penalty as administered was cruel and unusual because it was imposed so rarely and randomly — like being struck by lightning — and so discriminatorily against Black and poor defendants that it served no legitimate penal purpose. He contended that giving juries unguided discretion produced arbitrary results, that standards for the death penalty were impossible absent guidance, and that evolving standards of decency had rendered capital punishment unconstitutional.
case.defendantArguments: Georgia argued that the death penalty was expressly contemplated by the Constitution — the Fifth Amendment twice mentions capital cases — and had been continuously accepted by the states, so it could not be categorically cruel and unusual. The state contended sentencing disparities reflected legitimate jury mercy rather than arbitrary discrimination, that no manageable standards were constitutionally required, and that capital punishment served deterrence and retribution within the states' police power.
case.applicableLaw: The Eighth Amendment (cruel and unusual punishment), applied to the states through the Fourteenth; Georgia's capital-sentencing statute granting juries unguided discretion; the constitutional text's own references to capital punishment.
case.precedents: McGautha v. California (1971) (due process and unguided discretion); Trop v. Dulles (1958) (evolving standards of decency); Weems v. United States (1910); Powell v. Alabama (1932).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Eighth Amendment / death penalty. Decided 1972. The consolidated cases produced a fractured per curiam that effectively halted executions nationwide and forced states to rewrite capital statutes.
case.tldr: Furman challenged his death sentence under statutes giving juries unguided discretion. The Court invalidated existing capital schemes as arbitrary and cruel and unusual.

case.title: Roe v. Wade
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed in part. Texas's criminal abortion ban violated the right to privacy under the Due Process Clause; trimester framework adopted. Overruled by Dobbs (2022).
case.questionPresented: Whether a Texas statute criminalizing abortion except to save the mother's life violates a woman's constitutional right to privacy under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
case.facts: Norma McCorvey, using the pseudonym 'Jane Roe,' was a pregnant single woman in Texas who could not legally obtain an abortion there because Texas law prohibited all abortions except to save the life of the mother. Unable to afford travel to a state where abortion was legal and unable to establish that her life was endangered, she sued Dallas County District Attorney Henry Wade for a declaratory judgment that the statute was unconstitutional and an injunction against its enforcement. Roe argued that the decision whether to bear a child was a private one protected by the Constitution's recognition of liberty and privacy. Texas defended the statute as protecting potential human life, asserting the state's interest in the unborn and the legislative judgment that life begins at conception. The case reached the Court alongside a companion challenge to Georgia's reform abortion statute. The Texas statute dated to the nineteenth century and banned abortion except to save the mother's life; the challenge came amid a reform movement that had liberalized several states' laws.
case.proceduralHistory: Roe sued in the Northern District of Texas; a three-judge district court declared the statutes unconstitutional but declined to issue an injunction. Both sides appealed to the Supreme Court, which heard argument twice — first in December 1971 and again in October 1972 after the Court's membership changed — before deciding the case in 1973.
case.evidence: The record was primarily legal and legislative: the text of the Texas statutes, medical and historical materials on abortion practice and the origins of nineteenth-century abortion laws, and briefs and amicus submissions on the status of the fetus and the meaning of privacy. Roe's standing and mootness were contested because she was no longer pregnant by the time of decision.
case.plaintiffArguments: Roe argued that the right to privacy — recognized in Griswold and rooted in the Fourteenth Amendment's liberty or the Ninth Amendment — extends to a woman's decision whether to terminate a pregnancy, a decision of profound personal consequence. She contended the statute was not the least restrictive means of serving any compelling interest, that the fetus was not a person within the Fourteenth Amendment, and that the ban intruded on bodily autonomy, health, and equality far beyond any legitimate state concern.
case.defendantArguments: Texas argued that the state had a compelling interest in protecting unborn human life, which it asserted began at conception, and that this interest outweighed any privacy claim. It contended the Constitution did not recognize a right to abortion, that the statute was a valid exercise of the police power to protect life and health, and that the question of when life begins was for the legislature rather than the courts.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; the Ninth Amendment; Texas's abortion statutes criminalizing abortion except to save the mother's life; the developing constitutional right of privacy.
case.precedents: Griswold v. Connecticut (1965); Eisenstadt v. Baird (1972); Skinner v. Oklahoma (1942); Meyer v. Nebraska (1923) and Pierce v. Society of Sisters (1925).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Privacy / abortion. Decided 1973. The case arose amid a national reform movement that had liberalized abortion laws in several states while most retained nineteenth-century criminal bans.
case.tldr: Roe challenged Texas's near-total abortion ban. The Court struck it down, recognizing a constitutional right to abortion and adopting a trimester framework.

case.title: Miller v. California
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Vacated and remanded. The Court announced the three-part Miller test for obscenity and sent the case back for reconsideration under it; neither side won outright.
case.questionPresented: What constitutional standard governs whether material is obscene and therefore unprotected by the First Amendment, specifically whether the 'utterly without redeeming social value' test should be retained.
case.facts: Marvin Miller conducted a mass mailing campaign advertising sexually explicit books and films, sending unsolicited brochures containing pictures and drawings of explicit sexual activity to unwilling recipients, including a restaurant owner in Newport Beach, California, who complained to police. Miller was convicted under California law of knowingly distributing obscene matter. At the time, the governing obscenity test asked whether material was utterly without redeeming social value — a standard prosecutors found nearly impossible to satisfy. California urged the Court to abandon that test in favor of a community-standards approach that would let local juries judge obscenity by local norms. The case required the Court to formulate the controlling definition of unprotected obscenity. The brochures advertised sexually explicit books and films and reached unwilling recipients; the legal fight concerned which definition of obscenity the jury should have been instructed to apply. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Miller was convicted in the Orange County Superior Court of distributing obscene matter after a jury trial. The conviction was sustained through the state courts, and Miller appealed to the Supreme Court, which vacated and remanded a related earlier case and set Miller for full argument on the obscenity standard.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the mailed brochures with their explicit imagery, evidence of the unsolicited mass mailing to unwilling recipients, and the jury instructions under the existing obscenity standards. There was no dispute about the mailing or its contents; the fight was over which constitutional test the jury should have applied.
case.plaintiffArguments: Miller argued that the materials were protected expression under the First Amendment and that the 'utterly without redeeming social value' standard was the proper constitutional test, which the prosecution had not met. He contended that a variable local-standards approach would subject national distribution to the most restrictive community's judgment and chill protected speech, and that the materials were not obscene as a matter of law.
case.defendantArguments: California argued that the 'utterly without redeeming social value' test had proven unworkable and should be replaced by a standard asking whether the work, taken as a whole, appeals to prurient interest by local community standards, is patently offensive, and lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. The state contended that regulation of obscene material was within its police power and that juries should apply the standards of their own communities rather than a national standard.
case.applicableLaw: The First Amendment (obscenity as unprotected speech); California Penal Code obscenity provisions; the constitutional tests for obscenity from Roth v. United States and Memoirs v. Massachusetts.
case.precedents: Roth v. United States (1957); Memoirs v. Massachusetts (1966) (utterly-without-redeeming-social-value test); Jacobellis v. Ohio (1964); Stanley v. Georgia (1969).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Obscenity. Decided 1973. The case was one of several in which the Burger Court sought to recalibrate obscenity law after years of fractured and unworkable standards.
case.tldr: Miller was convicted for mass-mailing sexually explicit brochures. The Court vacated the conviction and set out a three-part community-standards test for obscenity.

case.title: United States v. Nixon
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Executive privilege is qualified; the subpoena for the tapes must be obeyed.
case.questionPresented: Whether the President's claim of absolute executive privilege permits him to withhold subpoenaed tape recordings and documents from a federal criminal prosecution, and whether the dispute is justiciable.
case.facts: A federal grand jury investigating the Watergate break-in and cover-up indicted seven of President Nixon's aides and named Nixon an unindicted co-conspirator. The Special Prosecutor obtained a subpoena directing the President to produce tape recordings and documents of White House conversations believed to contain evidence of the conspiracy. Nixon released edited transcripts but moved to quash the subpoena, claiming absolute executive privilege over confidential presidential communications and arguing the dispute was a nonjusticiable intra-branch matter within executive discretion. Jaworski responded that the fair administration of criminal justice required the evidence and that executive privilege, if it existed at all, was qualified and had to yield to a demonstrated, specific need in a pending criminal trial. The case placed the judiciary's authority over criminal evidence in direct conflict with presidential confidentiality. The subpoena sought particular recorded conversations the Special Prosecutor tied to the pending trial; Nixon released edited transcripts and claimed absolute privilege over confidential presidential communications.
case.proceduralHistory: The Special Prosecutor moved for the subpoena in the District Court for the District of Columbia, which ordered production, rejecting the privilege claim and the justiciability objection. The President sought review, and the Supreme Court granted certiorari before judgment in the court of appeals to resolve the urgent constitutional question on an expedited basis.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the subpoena's itemized demand for specific recorded conversations, the Special Prosecutor's showing that the tapes were relevant and admissible evidence in the pending criminal trial, and the President's generalized claim that confidentiality of presidential communications required absolute protection. No claim was made that the tapes involved military, diplomatic, or national-security secrets.
case.plaintiffArguments: The United States argued that a demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial outweighed a generalized claim of presidential confidentiality, and that any executive privilege is qualified, not absolute. It contended the judiciary, not the President, determines the existence and scope of privilege, that the subpoena sought evidence of crime rather than state secrets, and that separation of powers did not immunize evidence of possible official wrongdoing from the criminal process.
case.defendantArguments: President Nixon argued that confidential communications among the President and his advisers were protected by an absolute executive privilege grounded in the separation of powers and the need for candid counsel, and that the dispute between the President and a prosecutor he appointed was a nonjusticiable executive-branch matter. He contended that subjecting presidential conversations to judicial review would chill advice and impair executive functioning, and that the courts lacked power to order the President to produce records.
case.applicableLaw: The separation of powers and Article II executive power; the asserted doctrine of executive privilege; Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 17(c) subpoena standards; the judiciary's authority to determine privilege under Marbury v. Madison.
case.precedents: Marbury v. Madison (1803) (the province of the judiciary to say what the law is); United States v. Burr (1807) (subpoena duces tecum to Jefferson); Gravel v. United States (1972); Ex parte Milligan (1866).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Executive privilege. Decided 1974. The case was the constitutional climax of the Watergate investigation, with the President resisting a subpoena for recordings at the heart of the cover-up inquiry.
case.tldr: Nixon refused to surrender White House tapes subpoenaed for the Watergate trial. The Court unanimously ordered production, holding executive privilege qualified, not absolute.

case.title: Gregg v. Georgia
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. The death penalty is not per se unconstitutional; Georgia's guided-discretion statute satisfied the Eighth Amendment.
case.questionPresented: Whether the death penalty is invariably cruel and unusual punishment, and whether Georgia's revised capital statute — providing guided discretion, bifurcated trial, and appellate review — satisfies the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments.
case.facts: After Furman invalidated existing capital statutes as arbitrarily administered, Georgia enacted a revised scheme providing for a bifurcated trial separating guilt and sentencing, requiring the jury to find at least one statutory aggravating circumstance beyond a reasonable doubt before death could be imposed, allowing consideration of mitigating evidence, and mandating expedited review by the state supreme court. Troy Gregg was convicted by a Georgia jury of armed robbery and murder of two men who had picked him up hitchhiking. At the separate sentencing phase, the jury found statutory aggravating circumstances and imposed death. Gregg challenged the sentence, arguing that the death penalty was categorically cruel and unusual under evolving standards of decency, or that the new statute still permitted arbitrary and discriminatory application. Georgia's post-Furman statute required a bifurcated trial, a jury finding of at least one statutory aggravating circumstance, and mandatory appellate review; Gregg had been convicted of murdering two men who picked him up hitchhiking.
case.proceduralHistory: Gregg was convicted and sentenced to death in the Superior Court of Georgia after a bifurcated trial. The Georgia Supreme Court sustained the conviction and, as required by the statute, reviewed and sustained the death sentence. Gregg appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States, which consolidated the case with companion challenges to the revised statutes of Florida, Texas, North Carolina, and Louisiana.
case.evidence: The record included the trial and sentencing proceedings, the jury's written findings of statutory aggravating circumstances, and the statute's procedural safeguards — the bifurcated structure, the enumerated aggravating factors, and the mandatory proportionality review. Statistical and comparative evidence about post-Furman sentencing patterns was presented on whether the guided-discretion scheme reduced arbitrariness.
case.plaintiffArguments: Gregg argued that the death penalty was cruel and unusual per se under contemporary standards of decency, that it served no valid deterrent or retributive function beyond life imprisonment, and that it remained inevitably arbitrary and discriminatory even under the revised statute. He contended the guided-discretion procedures still left juries with unreviewable moral choices, and that the penalty was excessive and degrading regardless of procedural refinements.
case.defendantArguments: Georgia argued that the Constitution expressly contemplated capital punishment, that it was not per se cruel and unusual, and that the revised statute's guided discretion, bifurcated trial, aggravating-circumstance requirement, and mandatory appellate review cured the arbitrariness condemned in Furman. The state contended capital punishment served legitimate retributive and deterrent purposes and that the legislature's judgment in favor of it deserved deference.
case.applicableLaw: The Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments; Georgia's revised capital-sentencing statute providing guided discretion, bifurcated proceedings, statutory aggravating circumstances, and mandatory appellate review; the Furman framework on arbitrary sentencing.
case.precedents: Furman v. Georgia (1972); McGautha v. California (1971); Trop v. Dulles (1958); Woodson v. North Carolina (decided the same day, striking mandatory death).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Eighth Amendment / death penalty. Decided 1976. The case tested whether the procedural reforms enacted after Furman could make the death penalty constitutionally permissible, and it restarted executions after a decade-long moratorium.
case.tldr: After Furman, Georgia enacted a guided-discretion death penalty scheme. The Court upheld it, ruling capital punishment is not per se unconstitutional.

case.title: Buckley v. Valeo
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed in part, reversed in part. Contribution limits and disclosure upheld; limits on independent expenditures and candidate spending struck down.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Federal Election Campaign Act's limits on contributions, expenditures, and candidate spending, and its disclosure and appointment provisions, violate the First Amendment and separation of powers.
case.facts: The Federal Election Campaign Act Amendments of 1974, enacted after Watergate, imposed limits on contributions to candidates, limits on expenditures by candidates and independent groups, public financing of presidential campaigns, and disclosure requirements, administered by a new Federal Election Commission appointed partly by Congress. Senator James Buckley, former Senator Eugene McCarthy, and others sued, arguing that limiting contributions and expenditures suppressed political speech and association — treating money spent on politics as speech — and that the appointment of FEC members by congressional officials violated the Appointments Clause. The government defended the law as necessary to prevent corruption and its appearance in elections. The case required the Court to sort which restrictions survived First Amendment scrutiny. The post-Watergate amendments combined contribution caps, expenditure ceilings, disclosure rules, public financing, and a congressionally appointed commission; the challengers attacked the whole scheme as a restraint on political speech. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: The challengers sued in the District of Columbia under the Act's expedited review provision. The district court sustained the Act, and the D.C. Circuit largely upheld it. The Supreme Court granted review and issued a per curiam opinion upholding some provisions and striking others.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the statute's detailed provisions, congressional findings about corruption and the appearance of corruption from large contributions, and submissions on the effect of expenditure limits on political communication. The constitutional analysis treated contribution limits, expenditure ceilings, disclosure rules, and the FEC's appointment mechanism as distinct legal questions.
case.plaintiffArguments: The challengers argued that spending money to communicate political messages is speech protected by the First Amendment, so limits on expenditures and candidate spending were direct restraints on political expression that could not survive strict scrutiny. They contended that preventing corruption did not justify suppressing speech and association, that contribution and expenditure limits were indistinguishable for First Amendment purposes, and that the FEC's congressional appointments violated the Appointments Clause.
case.defendantArguments: The government argued that contribution limits were a minimal restriction justified by the compelling interest in preventing corruption and its appearance, and that expenditure limits and disclosure were constitutionally permissible means of safeguarding electoral integrity. It contended that money is conduct, not pure speech, that unlimited spending allowed the wealthy to dominate politics, and that Congress could rationally regulate campaign finance to prevent quid pro quo corruption.
case.applicableLaw: The First Amendment; the Federal Election Campaign Act Amendments of 1974; the Appointments Clause; the congressional power to regulate federal elections.
case.precedents: United States v. O'Brien (1968) (symbolic conduct); NAACP v. Alabama (1958) (disclosure and association); United States v. Rumely (1953); no prior case squarely governed contribution versus expenditure limits.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Campaign finance. Decided 1976. The case was the foundational modern campaign-finance decision, distinguishing permissible contribution limits from impermissible expenditure limits in the post-Watergate reforms.
case.tldr: Challengers attacked the post-Watergate campaign-finance law. The Court upheld contribution limits and disclosure but struck down expenditure and candidate-spending caps.

ruling.ruling: Relief granted in part and denied in part. Decision below: affirmed in part reversed in part.

case.title: Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California
case.court: Supreme Court of California
case.actualOutcome: Reversed; complaint stated a cause of action. A therapist who determines a patient poses a serious danger to an identifiable victim has a duty to use reasonable care to protect that victim.
case.caseType: tort – duty to warn / third parties
case.questionPresented: Whether a psychotherapist who determines that a patient presents a serious danger of violence to an identifiable victim owes a duty to exercise reasonable care to protect that victim.
case.facts: Prosenjit Poddar, a student at the University of California, told his therapist, a psychologist employed by the university, that he intended to kill Tatiana Tarasoff when she returned from abroad. The therapist notified campus police, who briefly detained Poddar but released him after he appeared rational and promised to stay away from Tarasoff. No one warned Tarasoff or her family. When Tarasoff returned, Poddar killed her. Her parents sued the university's therapists, campus police, and regents, alleging negligent failure to warn and failure to confine. The defendants argued therapists owed no duty to a third party who was not their patient and that predicting violence was inherently uncertain. The case required the court to decide whether the special therapist-patient relationship created a duty to an identifiable third-party victim. The therapist notified campus police, who briefly detained and released Poddar after he appeared rational; no one warned Tarasoff, and she was killed upon her return from abroad.
case.proceduralHistory: The Tarasoffs' wrongful-death complaint was dismissed by the trial court for failure to state a cause of action, on the ground that no duty ran to the victim. The plaintiffs appealed to the Supreme Court of California, which considered whether the complaint stated a claim on which relief could be granted.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the pleadings alleging that the therapist knew of Poddar's specific intention to kill Tarasoff, that he notified police but not the victim or her family, and that the failure to warn or confine led to her death. The dispute was over the existence of a duty — whether the therapist-patient relationship extended protective obligations to identifiable third parties in danger.
case.plaintiffArguments: The Tarasoffs argued that the therapist, having determined that his patient posed a serious and identifiable threat to their daughter, owed her a duty of reasonable care, including the duty to warn. They contended the special relationship between therapist and patient carried an obligation to protect foreseeable victims, that the danger was specific and identifiable, and that the failure to warn or confine was the proximate cause of her death.
case.defendantArguments: The university and therapists argued that therapists owe duties to their patients, not to third parties, and that imposing a duty to warn would undermine therapist-patient confidentiality essential to treatment. They contended predicting violence is unreliable, that imposing liability for failing to protect strangers would make therapists liable for patients' unforeseeable acts, and that no duty existed toward an identifiable victim as a matter of law.
case.applicableLaw: California tort law on the duty of care; the special-relationship doctrine; therapist-patient confidentiality and its limits; the question whether a duty to protect an identifiable third party arises from a professional relationship.
case.precedents: Rowland v. Christian (1968) (general duty of care); the special-relationship cases imposing duties to protect; the Restatement (Second) of Torts provisions on undertakings and special relationships.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Torts / duty to warn. Decided 1976. The decision established the psychotherapist's duty to protect identifiable victims and reshaped mental-health practice and professional ethics nationwide.
case.tldr: A patient told his therapist he would kill Tarasoff, and no one warned her. The court allowed the suit, holding therapists must use reasonable care to protect identifiable victims.

case.title: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed in part, reversed in part. The rigid racial quota was unlawful and Bakke was ordered admitted, but race may be considered as one factor in admissions.
case.questionPresented: Whether a state medical school's special admissions program reserving a fixed number of seats for minority applicants violates Title VI of the Civil Rights Act or the Equal Protection Clause, and whether race may ever be considered in admissions.
case.facts: The University of California, Davis, medical school operated a special admissions program reserving sixteen of one hundred seats for disadvantaged minority applicants, who were evaluated separately and not compared with general applicants. Allan Bakke, a white applicant twice rejected, had higher undergraduate grades and test scores than most admitted special-program applicants. He sued, alleging the quota discriminated against him on the basis of race in violation of the Equal Protection Clause and Title VI, which bars racial discrimination in federally funded programs. The university defended the program as necessary to increase minority physicians and remedy societal discrimination. The case presented whether racial classifications designed to benefit minorities were permissible, what scrutiny applied, and whether a rigid quota differed from flexible consideration of race. Davis reserved sixteen of one hundred seats for a separate minority track; Bakke's grades and scores exceeded those of most special-program admits, and he had been rejected twice.
case.proceduralHistory: Bakke sued in the California state courts. The trial court found the program unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment but declined to order Bakke's admission. The California Supreme Court sustained that ruling, found the program unlawful, and ordered Bakke admitted after concluding the university had not shown he would have been rejected anyway. The university petitioned the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The record included the medical school's admissions procedures, Bakke's comparative qualifications, the number of seats reserved and the separate evaluation track for minority applicants, and submissions about the underrepresentation of minorities in medicine and the history of discrimination in medical education. No claim was made that any specific admittee's race was the product of intentional individual discrimination against Bakke apart from the quota structure.
case.plaintiffArguments: The university argued that remedying the effects of societal discrimination and achieving a diverse student body were compelling interests justifying the special-admissions quota, and that benign racial classifications serving disadvantaged minorities should not receive the same strict scrutiny as invidious discrimination. It contended Bakke was not qualified for admission in any event and that the program was a constitutionally permissible effort to increase minority representation in medicine.
case.defendantArguments: Bakke argued that the quota reserved seats solely by race, an explicit racial classification subject to strict scrutiny, and that the university's remedial purpose could not justify a rigid numerical set-aside that disadvantaged applicants who bore no responsibility for past discrimination. He contended Title VI flatly barred racial exclusions in federally funded programs regardless of motive, and that his superior credentials entitled him to admission if the program were invalid.
case.applicableLaw: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (racial discrimination in federally funded programs); strict scrutiny of racial classifications; the emerging doctrine on affirmative action.
case.precedents: Korematsu v. United States (1944) (strict scrutiny); Sweatt v. Painter (1950); Brown v. Board of Education (1954); Green v. County School Board (1968); San Antonio v. Rodriguez (1973).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Affirmative action. Decided 1978. The case produced no majority rationale but a pivotal Powell opinion permitting race as one admissions factor while invalidating quotas, shaping affirmative action for decades.
case.tldr: Bakke, a white applicant, was rejected by a medical school reserving seats for minorities. The Court struck the quota but allowed race as one admissions factor.

result.title: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke

ruling.ruling: Relief granted in part and denied in part. Decision below: affirmed in part reversed in part. Remedy: specific performance or injunction.

case.title: Diamond v. Chakrabarty
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. A live, human-made microorganism is patentable subject matter as a 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter.'
case.questionPresented: Whether a live, human-made microorganism is patentable subject matter as a 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter' under the Patent Act.
case.facts: Ananda Chakrabarty, a researcher at General Electric, genetically engineered a bacterium by inserting plasmids that enabled it to break down components of crude oil, making it useful for oil-spill cleanup. He applied for a patent on the bacterium itself. The Patent Office rejected the claim on the ground that living things are not patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Sidney Diamond, Commissioner of Patents, sought review, arguing that Congress did not intend 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter' to include living organisms, that cell patents raised distinct policy concerns for Congress, and that the Plant Patent Acts showed Congress legislated separately for living things. Chakrabarty argued the bacterium was a human-made invention — a product of human ingenuity unlike anything found in nature — squarely within the statute's broad terms. The engineered bacterium degraded components of crude oil useful for cleaning spills; the Patent Office allowed the process claims but rejected the claim to the living organism itself.
case.proceduralHistory: The Patent Office Board of Appeals allowed the process claims but rejected the claim to the bacterium itself. The Court of Customs and Patent Appeals disagreed, holding the microorganism patentable. The Commissioner petitioned the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the patent application, the scientific description of the engineered bacterium and its novel oil-degrading capability, and the statute's text. The legal dispute was whether a living, genetically engineered organism fell within § 101's 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter,' or was categorically excluded as a product of nature or a living thing.
case.plaintiffArguments: The Patent Office argued that living organisms were not patentable subject matter under § 101, that Congress had legislated separately for plants in the Plant Patent Acts, showing an intent to treat living things differently, and that extending patents to life forms raised policy questions for the legislature. It contended 'manufacture' and 'composition of matter' were not intended to encompass living organisms and that the bacterium was a product of nature at its core.
case.defendantArguments: Chakrabarty argued that the bacterium was a human-made manufacture or composition of matter — a product of human ingenuity with markedly different characteristics from anything found in nature — falling within § 101's broad language. He contended Congress intended the statute to be construed expansively to include 'anything under the sun made by man,' that the distinction was between products of nature and human-made inventions, and that the plant statutes did not exclude all living things.
case.applicableLaw: 35 U.S.C. § 101 patentable subject matter ('manufacture' and 'composition of matter'); the product-of-nature doctrine; the Plant Patent Act and its relationship to utility patents; the broad congressional intent behind the patent statute.
case.precedents: The product-of-nature cases excluding natural discoveries; the Plant Patent Act of 1930; Funk Brothers Seed Co. v. Kalo Inoculant (1948); the § 101 cases on process versus product claims.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Patent law / living organisms. Decided 1980. The ruling opened the door to biotechnology patents, holding that human-made living organisms are patentable subject matter.
case.tldr: The Patent Office refused a patent on a genetically engineered bacterium. The Court allowed it, ruling human-made living organisms are patentable subject matter.

case.title: Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Courts defer to an agency's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute; EPA's bubble rule upheld. Chevron deference overruled by Loper Bright (2024).
case.questionPresented: Whether a court must defer to the Environmental Protection Agency's reasonable interpretation of the Clean Air Act's term 'stationary source' when the statute is ambiguous, or instead exercise independent judgment.
case.facts: The Clean Air Act required states to regulate new or modified 'stationary sources' of air pollution, but did not clearly define the term. The EPA adopted the 'bubble' concept, treating an entire industrial plant — rather than each individual smokestack or emission point — as a single source, so a plant could increase emissions at one point if offset elsewhere. The Natural Resources Defense Council challenged the rule as permitting net increases in pollution contrary to the statute. The D.C. Circuit set aside the rule, and Chevron, which intervened to defend the more flexible interpretation, appealed. The case asked the Court to determine the proper standard of judicial review when an agency interprets an ambiguous statute it administers — whether courts should defer to reasonable agency constructions or decide statutory meaning independently. The 'bubble' rule let a plant treat all its emission points as one source, offsetting increases at one stack with decreases elsewhere; the statute did not define the term 'stationary source.'
case.proceduralHistory: The NRDC petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review of the EPA's bubble rule. The court of appeals set aside the rule, applying what it understood as governing precedent requiring a per-source definition. Chevron and the EPA petitioned the Supreme Court, which granted certiorari to resolve the proper framework for reviewing agency statutory interpretation.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the Clean Air Act's text and legislative history, the EPA's rulemaking record and stated rationale for the bubble concept, and the competing constructions of 'stationary source.' The central question was not factual but legal: whether the statute unambiguously foreclosed the agency's interpretation and, if not, whether the court should defer.
case.plaintiffArguments: Chevron argued that the Clean Air Act did not unambiguously define 'stationary source,' and that courts should defer to an agency's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute it administers, because agencies possess expertise and political accountability for policy choices Congress left open. It contended the D.C. Circuit had substituted its own construction for the agency's permissible one, contrary to the principle that reasonable agency interpretations fill statutory gaps.
case.defendantArguments: The NRDC argued that the statute's text, structure, and purpose unambiguously required a per-source definition aimed at reducing emissions, so no deference was owed because the agency had no gap to fill. It contended the bubble concept permitted net pollution increases contrary to the Act's air-quality goals, that courts have the independent duty to say what the law is, and that deference would allow agencies to rewrite statutes.
case.applicableLaw: The Clean Air Act's new-source review provisions; the Administrative Procedure Act's arbitrary-and-capricious and statutory-construction standards; the emerging doctrine of judicial deference to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes.
case.precedents: NLRB v. Hearst Publications (1944); Skidmore v. Swift (1944); SEC v. Chenery; the Court's pre-1984 deference cases turning on statutory ambiguity.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Administrative law / agency deference. Decided 1984. The case established the two-step framework that made Chevron the most-cited administrative-law decision of the modern era.
case.tldr: The NRDC challenged EPA's 'bubble' reading of the Clean Air Act. The Court upheld it, ruling courts must defer to reasonable agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes.

case.title: Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, Inc. (Betamax)
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed in favor of Sony. Home time-shifting is fair use, and a device capable of substantial non-infringing uses does not make its maker a contributory infringer.
case.questionPresented: Whether a manufacturer of videocassette recorders is liable for contributory copyright infringement because consumers use the device to record television programs, and whether home time-shifting is fair use.
case.facts: Sony manufactured the Betamax videocassette recorder, which allowed consumers to record television broadcasts for later viewing — 'time-shifting.' Universal City Studios and Walt Disney Productions sued Sony, arguing that home taping infringed their copyrights and that Sony, by selling the VCR, was a contributory infringer. Sony argued the VCR was capable of substantial non-infringing uses, that home time-shifting of free broadcast television was fair use, and that the device could not be banned merely because it could also be used to infringe. The studios contended that unauthorized reproduction of their programs was infringement, that most taping was not authorized, and that Sony profited from and facilitated infringement. The case required the Court to decide whether a device's manufacturer is liable for users' infringement and whether time-shifting is fair use. Consumers used the VCR overwhelmingly to record free broadcasts for later viewing; the studios argued unauthorized reproduction, while Sony pointed to the device's substantial non-infringing uses.
case.proceduralHistory: The studios sued in the Central District of California, which found for Sony, concluding that home time-shifting was fair use and that Sony was not a contributory infringer. The Ninth Circuit disagreed, holding Sony liable for the infringing capability of the VCR. Sony petitioned the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The record included the VCR's capabilities and uses, evidence about how consumers used the device — overwhelmingly for time-shifting programs to watch once — and survey and expert evidence on the effect on the studios' markets. The legal dispute concerned the standard for contributory infringement by a manufacturer and whether home time-shifting of free broadcasts qualified as fair use.
case.plaintiffArguments: The studios argued that home taping of copyrighted broadcasts was unauthorized reproduction, not fair use, and that Sony was a contributory infringer because it sold a device whose primary purpose was recording copyrighted works. They contended Sony knew and profited from the infringement, that the fair-use defense did not cover wholesale copying of entire programs, and that the device's sale facilitated mass infringement.
case.defendantArguments: Sony argued that the VCR was capable of substantial non-infringing uses — including time-shifting, which it contended was fair use — and that a manufacturer cannot be held a contributory infringer merely because a product might be used to infringe. It contended home time-shifting of free broadcast television caused no demonstrable harm, that the studios had authorized or acquiesced in much broadcast use, and that imposing liability would stifle innovation.
case.applicableLaw: The Copyright Act; the fair-use doctrine (17 U.S.C. § 107); contributory-infringement liability for manufacturers of devices capable of both infringing and non-infringing uses; the staple-article doctrine from patent law invoked by analogy.
case.precedents: The fair-use framework of § 107 and its codified predecessors; the patent-law staple-article doctrine (Henry v. A.B. Dick, adapted); Williams & Wilkins v. United States (1975) (photocopying).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Copyright / fair use. Decided 1984. The 'Betamax' decision protected home video recording and established the substantial-non-infringing-use rule for technology manufacturers.
case.tldr: Studios sued the VCR maker for enabling home taping. The Court found for Sony, ruling home time-shifting is fair use and the device has substantial non-infringing uses.

case.title: New Jersey v. T.L.O.
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. School officials need only reasonable suspicion, not probable cause or a warrant; the purse search was reasonable.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Fourth Amendment applies to searches of students by public school officials and, if so, what standard — probable cause or reasonable suspicion — governs a search of a student's purse.
case.facts: A teacher at a New Jersey high school caught T.L.O., a freshman, smoking in a lavatory and took her to the assistant vice principal's office. When T.L.O. denied smoking, the vice principal opened her purse and found cigarettes; reaching for them, he noticed rolling papers, prompting a further search that revealed marijuana, a pipe, a list of students who owed her money, and cash. The state brought delinquency proceedings based on the marijuana. T.L.O. moved to suppress the evidence as the fruit of an unlawful warrantless search, arguing that the Fourth Amendment required school officials to have probable cause and a warrant like any other government search. The state contended school searches were governed by a lesser standard suited to the educational environment. The purse search began when the vice principal saw cigarettes and escalated when rolling papers suggested dealing; the marijuana, cash, and debtor list were found in the deeper search.
case.proceduralHistory: T.L.O. moved to suppress in the juvenile court, which denied the motion and adjudged her delinquent. The New Jersey Supreme Court disagreed, holding the purse search unreasonable, and suppressed the evidence. The State of New Jersey petitioned the Supreme Court of the United States to restore the delinquency finding.
case.evidence: The record established the sequence of the search — cigarettes discovered first, then rolling papers, then the marijuana and cash found during a further search prompted by the rolling papers. The legal contest was over the applicable standard: whether a school official's reasonable suspicion, rather than a warrant supported by probable cause, could justify the search of a student's belongings.
case.plaintiffArguments: New Jersey argued that the Fourth Amendment applies to school officials but that the school setting requires a flexible reasonable-suspicion standard rather than warrant and probable cause, because educators must act quickly to maintain discipline and safety. It contended the vice principal had reasonable grounds to suspect the purse contained evidence of smoking, that the search was justified at its inception and reasonable in scope, and that the exclusionary rule's application should not cripple school discipline.
case.defendantArguments: T.L.O. argued that school officials are government agents bound by the Fourth Amendment's warrant and probable-cause requirements, and that students do not shed constitutional rights at school. She contended the search exceeded its justification — the further search of the purse for evidence of dealing was unsupported — and that applying a diluted standard to minors would invite intrusive searches without adequate justification.
case.applicableLaw: The Fourth Amendment (unreasonable searches and seizures), applied through the Fourteenth; the balance between school disciplinary needs and student privacy; the evolving reasonable-suspicion standard for lesser intrusions.
case.precedents: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969); Terry v. Ohio (1968) (reasonable suspicion); Camara v. Municipal Court (1967); Wyman v. James (1971).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Fourth Amendment / school searches. Decided 1985. The case set the constitutional baseline for student searches that courts have applied to lockers, backpacks, and drug testing ever since.
case.tldr: A school official searched a student's purse after catching her smoking. The Court upheld the search, ruling school searches need only reasonable suspicion, not probable cause.

case.title: Batson v. Kentucky
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed and remanded. Peremptory strikes based on race violate the Equal Protection Clause; defendant may make a prima facie showing from his own trial.
case.questionPresented: Whether a prosecutor's use of peremptory challenges to exclude jurors solely on account of their race violates the Equal Protection Clause, and what showing a defendant must make to establish such discrimination.
case.facts: James Batson, a Black man, was tried in Kentucky on burglary and receipt-of-stolen-goods charges. During jury selection, the prosecutor used peremptory challenges to strike all four Black members of the venire, producing an all-white jury that convicted Batson. Batson moved to discharge the jury, arguing the strikes were racially motivated and violated equal protection; the trial court denied the motion without requiring the prosecutor to explain the strikes. Under the prevailing rule of Swain v. Alabama, a defendant had to show a systematic pattern of discriminatory strikes across multiple cases — a burden nearly impossible to meet — to prove racially motivated peremptory challenges. Batson argued that the strikes in his own trial alone should suffice to raise an inference of discrimination. The governing rule required proof of a pattern of strikes across multiple cases, a burden almost never met; Batson's own trial alone showed all four Black venire members struck by the prosecutor.
case.proceduralHistory: Batson was convicted in the Kentucky trial court after his motion to discharge the jury was denied. The Kentucky Supreme Court sustained the conviction, applying Swain's requirement of a pattern of strikes across cases. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to reconsider the evidentiary burden for proving racially discriminatory peremptory challenges.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the voir dire, showing the prosecutor struck all four Black venire members and produced an all-white jury. No evidentiary hearing was held on the prosecutor's reasons; the constitutional question was whether the facts of the single trial — the defendant's race, the excluded jurors' race, and the prosecutor's use of peremptories — sufficed to make a prima facie case of discrimination.
case.plaintiffArguments: Batson argued that the Swain rule made discrimination in jury selection effectively unreviewable, because a defendant could almost never prove a pattern across separate cases. He contended that striking all Black jurors in the defendant's own trial raised an inference of discrimination sufficient to require the prosecutor to offer race-neutral reasons, that equal protection forbids race-based jury selection as it does other racial classifications, and that the defendant and excluded jurors were injured by the practice.
case.defendantArguments: Kentucky argued that peremptory challenges are traditionally exercised without stated reasons, that Swain correctly required proof of a systematic pattern rather than a single trial's strikes, and that the prosecutor's peremptories were a legitimate exercise of discretionary challenge. The state contended that requiring explanations would undermine the peremptory system and that the defendant was tried by a fairly selected jury regardless of the venire members struck.
case.applicableLaw: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; the jury-trial right; the peremptory-challenge doctrine and the Swain v. Alabama evidentiary standard it displaced.
case.precedents: Swain v. Alabama (1965); Strauder v. West Virginia (1880); Norris v. Alabama (1935); Castaneda v. Partida (1977) (prima facie discrimination).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Jury selection / equal protection. Decided 1986. The case produced the three-step 'Batson challenge' framework used to police racial discrimination in jury selection, later extended to gender and to defense peremptories.
case.tldr: A prosecutor struck all Black jurors at Batson's trial. The Court reversed, holding race-based peremptory strikes violate equal protection and can be challenged on the trial record.

case.title: Bowers v. Hardwick
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed in favor of Georgia. No fundamental right to engage in homosexual sodomy; statute upheld. Overruled by Lawrence v. Texas (2003).
case.questionPresented: Whether the Constitution confers a fundamental right to engage in private consensual homosexual sodomy, such that Georgia's sodomy statute violates the Due Process Clause.
case.facts: Michael Hardwick was arrested in his own bedroom in Atlanta after a police officer, admitted by a houseguest, discovered him engaged in consensual oral sex with another adult man. Georgia's sodomy statute criminalized oral and anal sex between consenting adults, whether heterosexual or homosexual, though Hardwick was charged and the case litigated as to homosexual sodomy. The district attorney declined to prosecute, but Hardwick sued the Georgia attorney general for a declaratory judgment that the statute was unconstitutional as applied to private consensual conduct. He argued that the constitutional right of privacy, recognized in decisions protecting marriage, procreation, and contraception, extended to intimate sexual conduct between consenting adults in the home, and that no state interest justified criminalizing it. The arrest occurred in Hardwick's own bedroom after an officer was admitted by a houseguest; the district attorney declined to prosecute, but Hardwick sued to have the statute declared invalid. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Hardwick sued in the Northern District of Georgia; the district court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim. The Eleventh Circuit set aside that dismissal, holding that the statute implicated the right of privacy and required a compelling justification under heightened scrutiny. Georgia petitioned the Supreme Court, which granted certiorari.
case.evidence: The record was minimal: the circumstances of the arrest in Hardwick's bedroom and the statutory text. The dispute was purely legal — whether the privacy line of cases extended to consensual homosexual conduct — and the arguments concerned the framing of the right (private intimacy generally versus homosexual sodomy specifically) and the history of sodomy prohibitions.
case.plaintiffArguments: Hardwick argued that the right of privacy protected intimate consensual conduct in the home as part of the liberty the Due Process Clause guarantees, drawing on the marital, procreative, and contraception cases. He contended the state had no legitimate interest in regulating private adult conduct, that morality alone could not justify criminalization, and that the statute's intrusion into the bedroom was precisely the kind of government overreach the privacy cases forbade.
case.defendantArguments: Georgia argued that no fundamental right to homosexual sodomy existed, that the privacy cases protected family, marriage, and procreation — not sexual conduct — and that the Constitution did not bar states from criminalizing conduct long condemned by law and morality. It contended morality was a rational and legitimate basis for legislation, that the statute applied to all sodomy regardless of orientation, and that creating a new fundamental right was for legislatures, not courts.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; Georgia's sodomy statute; the right-of-privacy doctrine and its boundary at intimate conduct; the historical treatment of sodomy in Anglo-American law invoked by the state.
case.precedents: Griswold v. Connecticut (1965); Eisenstadt v. Baird (1972); Roe v. Wade (1973); Carey v. Population Services (1977); Stanley v. Georgia (1969).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Privacy / sodomy laws. Decided 1986. The case arose from a bedroom arrest and became the landmark later repudiated when the Court recognized a liberty interest in private intimate conduct.
case.tldr: Hardwick was arrested in his bedroom for consensual sodomy. The Court upheld Georgia's law, finding no fundamental right to homosexual intimacy.

case.title: People v. Goetz
case.court: New York Court of Appeals
case.actualOutcome: Reversed; indictment reinstated. Justification requires that the defendant's belief in the need for deadly force be objectively reasonable, not merely sincere.
case.questionPresented: Whether a claim of justification in the use of deadly force requires that the defendant's belief in the need for such force be objectively reasonable, or whether a subjective sincere belief suffices.
case.facts: Bernhard Goetz was approached on a New York City subway train by four youths, one of whom asked him for five dollars. Goetz drew a concealed revolver and fired at all four, injuring them; he fired again at one youth who appeared unhurt. Goetz fled and later surrendered, telling police he had been mugged before and fired in self-defense. A grand jury indicted him only for weapons offenses, but a second grand jury added attempted murder charges. Goetz moved to dismiss the indictment, arguing that the grand jury had been instructed that his belief in the need for deadly force must be objectively reasonable, whereas he contended his subjective, honest belief — given his fear and prior victimization — should govern. The case asked the Court of Appeals to determine the proper mens rea standard for justification. The youths approached Goetz on the subway and one asked for money; he fired at all four and fired again at one who appeared unhurt; the grand-jury instruction on reasonableness drove the appeal.
case.proceduralHistory: The trial court dismissed the attempted-murder counts of the second indictment, holding that justification required only the defendant's subjective belief. The Appellate Division sustained the dismissal. The People appealed to the New York Court of Appeals on whether the justification defense required an objectively reasonable belief in the need for deadly force.
case.evidence: The record included Goetz's own statements about the incident, the circumstances of the subway encounter, his prior experience of being mugged, and the evidence presented to the second grand jury. The legal dispute was whether the justification statute's 'reasonably believes' standard imported an objective reasonableness requirement rather than the defendant's subjective perception.
case.plaintiffArguments: The People argued that the justification statute requires that the defendant 'reasonably believe' deadly force is necessary — an objective standard under which the trier of fact assesses the reasonableness of the belief, not merely its sincerity. It contended the grand jury had been properly instructed, that a purely subjective test would immunize reckless or mistaken shootings, and that the statute's language embodied the community's judgment about when deadly force is justified.
case.defendantArguments: Goetz argued that his justification should be judged by his own subjective belief in the need for deadly force, informed by his fear and prior experience as a crime victim, rather than by an external reasonableness standard. He contended a frightened person may sincerely believe deadly force necessary even if an objective observer would not, that the statute protected the actor's perspective, and that the indictment should not stand on the objective instruction.
case.applicableLaw: New York Penal Law's justification (self-defense) statute — the 'reasonably believes' standard for the use of deadly force; the distinction between objective reasonableness and subjective sincerity in self-defense.
case.precedents: The New York self-defense cases interpreting 'reasonably believes'; the statutory codification of justification; earlier decisions on the actor's perspective versus objective standards.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Criminal law / self-defense standard. Decided 1986. The subway shooting drew intense public attention and produced the rule that justification requires an objectively reasonable belief in the need for deadly force.
case.tldr: Goetz shot four youths who approached him on the subway. The court reinstated the indictment, holding self-defense requires an objectively reasonable belief in the need for deadly force.

case.title: Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Educators may exercise editorial control over school-sponsored publications for legitimate pedagogical reasons.
case.questionPresented: Whether school officials may exercise editorial control over the content of a school-sponsored student newspaper without violating the First Amendment rights of student journalists.
case.facts: The Spectrum was the student newspaper of Hazelwood East High School in Missouri, produced as part of the journalism curriculum and funded partly by the school. The principal removed two pages of an issue containing articles about students' experiences with teen pregnancy and the impact of divorce, objecting to their anonymity sufficiency and the discussion of sexual topics and birth control for younger students. Student journalists, including editor Cathy Kuhlmeier, sued, arguing the censorship violated their First Amendment rights and that the paper was a public forum for student expression protected under Tinker. The school district argued the newspaper was a school-sponsored, curricular publication — not a public forum — over which educators retained legitimate pedagogical authority to set and enforce standards. The Spectrum was a credit-bearing, school-funded class project subject to the principal's review; the excised pages carried articles on teen pregnancy and the effects of divorce on students.
case.proceduralHistory: The students sued in the Eastern District of Missouri, which ruled for the school district, finding no First Amendment violation. The Eighth Circuit ruled for the students, concluding the newspaper was a public forum and the censorship unjustified under Tinker. The school district petitioned the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The record included the newspaper's status as a credit-bearing curricular activity, the school's funding and oversight, the principal's regular practice of reviewing proofs, and the two excised articles on pregnancy and divorce. The legal dispute turned on whether the Spectrum was a public forum for student speech or a supervised school activity subject to pedagogical control.
case.plaintiffArguments: The school district argued that the Spectrum was a school-sponsored curricular publication, not a public forum, and that educators may exercise editorial control over school activities to ensure quality, appropriateness, and legitimate pedagogical goals. It contended the principal acted reasonably to protect student privacy and younger readers, that Tinker's tolerance for student expression did not extend to school-sponsored curricular publications, and that curricular decisions are within educators' discretion.
case.defendantArguments: The student journalists argued that the Spectrum operated as a forum for student expression and that the censorship was content-based suppression inconsistent with Tinker, which protects student speech absent substantial disruption. They contended the principal's objections were not pedagogically reasonable but moral and topical censorship, that the paper functioned as a student voice rather than the school's speech, and that suppression chilled press freedom in schools.
case.applicableLaw: The First Amendment, applied through the Fourteenth; the public-forum doctrine; Tinker's substantial-disruption standard and the different standard for school-sponsored curricular expression.
case.precedents: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969); Bethel School District v. Fraser (1986) (school speech); Papish v. Board of Curators (1973); Pickering v. Board of Education (1968).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Student press. Decided 1988. The decision distinguished school-sponsored expression from independent student speech and remains the governing standard for school newspapers.
case.tldr: A principal removed articles from the school newspaper. The Court upheld the censorship, ruling educators may control school-sponsored publications for pedagogical reasons.

case.title: Texas v. Johnson
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Burning the flag as political protest is protected expressive conduct; the conviction could not stand.
case.questionPresented: Whether burning the American flag as political protest is expressive conduct protected by the First Amendment, such that a state may not criminalize it as flag desecration.
case.facts: During the 1984 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Gregory Lee Johnson participated in a political demonstration protesting the Reagan administration's policies. He burned an American flag while the crowd chanted, in front of Dallas City Hall. No one was injured and no riot ensued, though witnesses were offended. Johnson was convicted under a Texas statute criminalizing flag desecration — conduct that 'seriously offends' observers — and sentenced to a year in prison and a fine. Texas defended the statute as preserving the flag as a symbol of national unity and preventing breaches of the peace. Johnson argued his act was political expression at the core of the First Amendment and that the state could not punish him because his message offended others. The burning occurred at a convention protest amid chanting but no riot; the statute punished desecration that 'seriously offends' observers, making audience offense the trigger for liability. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Johnson was convicted of flag desecration in a Dallas County court and sentenced to a year in prison and a $2,000 fine. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals set aside the conviction, finding the conduct protected symbolic speech. Texas petitioned the Supreme Court of the United States.
case.evidence: The record established that Johnson burned the flag as part of a demonstration to convey a political message, that the act was expressive and intentional, and that no breach of the peace actually occurred. The dispute centered on whether the state's interests — preserving the flag as a symbol and preventing offense or disorder — justified punishing this particular mode of expression.
case.plaintiffArguments: Texas argued that flag desecration is conduct, not pure speech, and that the state had legitimate interests in preserving the flag as a symbol of nationhood and preventing breaches of the peace that justified the prohibition. It contended that burning the flag in public was inherently inflammatory, that the law punished the manner of expression rather than its content, and that other means of expressing the same political message remained open to Johnson.
case.defendantArguments: Johnson argued that flag burning in a political demonstration was expressive conduct communicating a message of dissent, entitled to First Amendment protection, and that Texas's asserted interests were based on the offense the message caused. He contended the statute was content-based because it punished only desecration that 'seriously offends' observers, that no breach of the peace resulted, and that government may not preserve a symbol by punishing those who use it to express protest.
case.applicableLaw: The First Amendment, applied through the Fourteenth; Texas's flag-desecration statute; the doctrine governing expressive conduct and the O'Brien test for regulations of conduct with expressive elements.
case.precedents: United States v. O'Brien (1968); Spence v. Washington (1974); Tinker v. Des Moines (1969); Street v. New York (1969) (flag words); Smith v. Goguen (1974).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Symbolic speech / flag burning. Decided 1989. The ruling prompted Congress to enact a federal flag-protection statute and a sustained, unsuccessful campaign for a constitutional amendment to ban flag desecration.
case.tldr: Johnson burned the flag at a political protest. The Court overturned his conviction, holding flag burning is protected expressive conduct.
