case.title: Cruzan v. Director, Missouri Department of Health
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. A competent person has a liberty interest in refusing treatment, but Missouri may require clear and convincing evidence of an incompetent patient's wishes.
case.questionPresented: Whether a state may require clear and convincing evidence of an incompetent patient's wish to refuse life-sustaining treatment before permitting withdrawal of artificial hydration and nutrition.
case.facts: Nancy Cruzan suffered catastrophic brain injuries in a 1983 automobile accident and lapsed into a persistent vegetative state, kept alive by surgically implanted feeding and hydration tubes with no hope of recovery. Several years later, her parents and court-appointed guardians asked to have the tubes removed, believing she would not have wanted to exist in such a condition. Missouri authorities refused absent a court order, and the state required clear and convincing evidence of the patient's own wishes. There was no advance directive; the only evidence of Cruzan's wishes was a housemate's recollection of a somewhat general statement that she would not want to live as a 'vegetable.' The Missouri courts found that evidence insufficient under the clear-and-convincing standard. Her parents argued the standard unconstitutionally burdened a competent person's right to refuse treatment, asserted on her behalf. The only evidence of Nancy's wishes was a housemate's recollection of a general remark about not wanting to live as a 'vegetable'; she had left no written directive of any kind.
case.proceduralHistory: The trial court authorized withdrawal of the feeding tube, finding a constitutional right to refuse treatment and sufficient evidence of intent. The Missouri Supreme Court set aside that order, holding that no right permitted withdrawal absent clear and convincing evidence of the patient's wishes, which it found lacking. The parents petitioned the Supreme Court of the United States.
case.evidence: The record contained medical evidence of Cruzan's persistent vegetative state and the trial testimony of a former housemate recalling a conversation in which Cruzan said she would not wish to continue life if she could not live 'halfway normally.' There was no living will or formal directive. The dispute concerned the evidentiary standard a state could constitutionally demand before terminating life support for an incompetent patient.
case.plaintiffArguments: Cruzan's parents argued that a competent person has a constitutionally protected liberty interest in refusing unwanted medical treatment, which survives incompetence and may be exercised by a surrogate on reliable evidence of the patient's wishes. They contended Missouri's heightened clear-and-convincing standard erected an unconstitutional barrier, that the state's interests in life did not outweigh the patient's interest in avoiding a prolonged vegetative existence, and that the evidence of Nancy's wishes sufficed.
case.defendantArguments: Missouri argued that the state had a strong interest in preserving life and that where the patient is incompetent and the decision irrevocable, a clear-and-convincing-evidence standard was a constitutionally permissible safeguard against erroneous or surrogate-driven termination of life. It contended that an incompetent patient's autonomy could not be exercised personally, that the informal statement of wishes was insufficiently specific, and that protecting life justified erring on the side of continued treatment.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment (liberty in bodily integrity and refusal of treatment); Missouri's living-will and guardianship standards requiring clear and convincing evidence of intent; common-law right to refuse treatment.
case.precedents: Griswold v. Connecticut (1965); In re Quinlan (N.J. 1976) (state right-to-die case); the line of state decisions on substituted judgment; Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Right to refuse treatment. Decided 1990. The case was the Court's first major 'right to die' decision and spurred national adoption of living wills and advance directives.
case.tldr: Cruzan's parents sought to remove her feeding tube after years in a vegetative state. The Court upheld Missouri's requirement of clear and convincing evidence of the patient's wishes.

case.title: Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed in part, reversed in part. Roe's core holding reaffirmed under an undue-burden standard; spousal notification struck down, other provisions (waiting period, informed consent, parental consent) upheld.
case.questionPresented: Whether Pennsylvania's Abortion Control Act provisions — informed consent, a 24-hour waiting period, parental consent, spousal notification, and reporting requirements — impose an unconstitutional burden on the right to abortion.
case.facts: Pennsylvania's Abortion Control Act required a woman seeking an abortion to receive specified information and wait twenty-four hours, required a minor to obtain parental consent, required a married woman to notify her husband, and imposed reporting requirements on providers, with exemptions for medical emergencies. Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania sued for a declaratory judgment that the provisions were facially unconstitutional, arguing they burdened the abortion right recognized in Roe. The state defended the provisions as permissible regulations that did not prohibit abortion. The case required the Court to revisit the constitutional status of abortion and articulate the governing standard — whether strict scrutiny, trimester framework, or a new undue-burden test — for evaluating such regulations. The Act combined informed consent, a waiting period, parental and spousal provisions, and reporting rules; the dispute concerned which of them unduly burdened the right recognized in Roe. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Planned Parenthood sued in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, which invalidated all challenged provisions. The Third Circuit disagreed in part, sustaining most of the Act but invalidating spousal notification under an undue-burden framework. Both sides petitioned the Supreme Court, which granted certiorari amid widespread expectation that the Court might reconsider Roe.
case.evidence: The record included the statute's provisions, legislative findings, and submissions about the practical effects of waiting periods, notification, and consent requirements on women seeking abortions — particularly poor, rural, and abused women. There was no dispute about the provisions' content; the contest was over the constitutional standard and whether each provision unduly burdened the right.
case.plaintiffArguments: Planned Parenthood argued that the essential holding of Roe — that the Constitution protects a woman's right to choose abortion before viability — must be retained under stare decisis and evolving reliance, and that Pennsylvania's provisions imposed undue burdens by creating substantial obstacles to abortion. It contended spousal notification endangered battered women, that waiting periods and consent requirements burdened poor and young women, and that the provisions were designed to deter rather than inform.
case.defendantArguments: Pennsylvania argued that Roe was wrongly decided and should be reconsidered, and that the state had legitimate interests in maternal health and potential life permitting reasonable regulation. It contended informed consent, waiting periods, and parental and spousal involvement promoted informed decision-making without banning abortion, that only regulations creating an undue burden should fail, and that most provisions fell within the state's power to regulate medical practice.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; Pennsylvania's Abortion Control Act; the undue-burden standard articulated to replace the trimester framework; stare decisis principles on reaffirming a constitutional right.
case.precedents: Roe v. Wade (1973); Akron v. Akron Center (1983); Thornburgh v. American College (1986); Webster v. Reproductive Health Services (1989); Bellotti v. Baird (1979).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Abortion regulation. Decided 1992. The case was decided amid intense national debate over whether the Court would overturn Roe, and its 'undue burden' standard governed abortion law until 2022.
case.tldr: Planned Parenthood challenged Pennsylvania's abortion restrictions. The Court reaffirmed Roe's core under an 'undue burden' test, upholding most provisions but striking spousal notice.

case.title: Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed and remanded. A regulation depriving land of all economically beneficial use is a per se taking requiring compensation unless background principles of property law would bar the use.
case.questionPresented: Whether a land-use regulation that deprives beachfront property of all economically beneficial use effects a taking requiring compensation under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, absent a showing that the prohibited use was already barred by state property or nuisance law.
case.facts: In 1986 David Lucas purchased two residential beachfront lots on the Isle of Palms, South Carolina, for $975,000, intending to build homes; neighboring lots were already developed. Two years later, the state enacted the Beachfront Management Act, which barred construction seaward of a setback line to protect the barrier-island coast from erosion and storms. The Act rendered Lucas's lots valueless for residential building. Lucas sued the South Carolina Coastal Council, arguing the regulation effected a taking of his property without just compensation. The trial court found the lots had been rendered valueless. The state defended the Act as an exercise of the police power to prevent serious public harm — coastal erosion and storm damage — traditionally not compensable under takings law. Lucas paid $975,000 for two buildable lots flanked by developed homes; the Act's setback line rendered them unbuildable, and the trial court found they had been left without economically viable use.
case.proceduralHistory: Lucas sued in the South Carolina Court of Common Pleas, which found that the Act had deprived the lots of all reasonable use and awarded compensation. The South Carolina Supreme Court set aside that judgment, holding the regulation a valid exercise of police power to prevent public harm that required no compensation regardless of the deprivation's extent. Lucas petitioned the Supreme Court of the United States.
case.evidence: The trial record included valuation evidence that the lots had no residual economically beneficial use after the Act, along with evidence of the lots' history and the developed neighboring parcels. The legal dispute concerned whether a regulation extinguishing all economic value was compensable regardless of the public-harm rationale, and whether the prohibited construction was already barred by background principles of nuisance law.
case.plaintiffArguments: Lucas argued that a regulation that deprives land of all economically viable use is a taking requiring compensation, without regard to the public interest served, because such total deprivation is the practical equivalent of physical appropriation. He contended the state's 'harm prevention' rationale was too broad — any regulation could be framed that way — and that unless the proposed use was already unlawful under nuisance or property law, the state had to pay for eliminating all value.
case.defendantArguments: The Coastal Council argued that regulations preventing serious public harm — like nuisance abatement — had never required compensation, and that the Act protected against coastal erosion and storm damage. It contended the trial court's 'valueless' finding was legally insufficient to establish a taking, that the lots retained some value and beach access, and that takings analysis traditionally weighed the regulation's character and purpose, not merely its economic effect.
case.applicableLaw: The Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment, applied through the Fourteenth; South Carolina's Beachfront Management Act; regulatory-takings doctrine and the nuisance/public-harm exception.
case.precedents: Pennsylvania Coal v. Mahon (1922); Agins v. Tiburon (1980); Keystone Bituminous v. DeBenedictis (1987); Mugler v. Kansas (1887) (nuisance exception).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Takings / regulatory taking. Decided 1992. The case became the leading statement of the 'total takings' rule for regulations extinguishing all economically beneficial use of land.
case.tldr: A coastal law barred Lucas from building on his beachfront lots. The Court ruled that a regulation wiping out all economic use is a taking requiring compensation.

case.title: Liebeck v. McDonald's Restaurants
case.court: New Mexico Second Judicial District Court
case.actualOutcome: Jury verdict for Liebeck: $200,000 compensatory (reduced 20% for her fault) and $2.7 million punitive damages, later reduced by the judge to $480,000; the parties then settled.
case.questionPresented: Whether McDonald's was liable for severe burns caused by coffee served at approximately 180–190°F, and whether punitive damages were warranted for knowingly serving dangerously hot coffee.
case.facts: Stella Liebeck, 79, bought coffee at a McDonald's drive-through in Albuquerque. Sitting in a parked car, she placed the cup between her knees and removed the lid to add cream and sugar; the cup tipped and spilled coffee onto her lap, causing third-degree burns requiring skin grafts and weeks of hospitalization. Liebeck offered to settle for her medical costs, about $20,000, and McDonald's offered only $800. At trial, the evidence showed McDonald's served coffee at 180–190°F, a temperature capable of causing third-degree burns in seconds, and that the company had received more than seven hundred prior burn complaints. McDonald's argued the coffee was hot because customers preferred it that way, that Liebeck was contributorily negligent in spilling it on herself, and that the company was not liable for a self-inflicted spill. Liebeck suffered third-degree burns requiring skin grafts; evidence showed McDonald's served coffee at 180–190°F and had logged hundreds of earlier burn complaints, and she initially offered to settle for her medical costs.
case.proceduralHistory: Liebeck sued McDonald's in the New Mexico Second Judicial District Court for compensatory and punitive damages. A jury trial proceeded to verdict; the jury found for Liebeck and awarded compensatory damages, reduced for her own comparative fault, and punitive damages. The judge later reduced the punitive award, and the parties settled for an undisclosed amount before appeal.
case.evidence: The record included evidence of the coffee's serving temperature (180–190°F), the severity and speed of the burns it could cause, McDonald's knowledge of more than seven hundred prior burn reports, and expert testimony on safe serving temperatures. Liebeck's damages evidence included medical records of the third-degree burns, skin grafts, and recovery; McDonald's emphasized her role in the spill.
case.plaintiffArguments: Liebeck argued that serving coffee at a temperature capable of causing third-degree burns in seconds was unreasonably dangerous and constituted a defective product or negligent practice, that McDonald's knew of hundreds of prior burns yet continued the practice, and that the coffee was far hotter than home-brewed or competitors' coffee. She contended the company's conscious disregard for safety warranted punitive damages and that her injuries were severe and foreseeable.
case.defendantArguments: McDonald's argued that coffee is a hot beverage customers expect to be served hot, that Liebeck caused her own injuries by spilling the cup in her lap, and that the company was not liable for an accident resulting from her handling. It contended the coffee temperature reflected customer preference and industry practice, that warning labels sufficed, and that the spill — not any defect — was the proximate cause of the burns.
case.applicableLaw: New Mexico tort law on negligence and products liability; comparative fault; punitive-damages standards for conscious disregard of safety; the duty to avoid serving a product at unreasonably dangerous temperatures.
case.precedents: The common-law products-liability and negligence framework; comparative-fault doctrine; New Mexico's punitive-damages standards for reckless conduct.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Torts / products liability (hot coffee). Decided 1994. The verdict became a celebrated and contested example in the debate over tort reform and jury awards.
case.tldr: Liebeck was badly burned by coffee served near boiling. A jury awarded her compensatory and large punitive damages, later reduced, before the case settled.

case.title: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc.
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed and remanded. Commercial parody can be fair use; the appeals court erred in presuming unfairness from commercial character.
case.questionPresented: Whether a commercial rap group's parody of a copyrighted song may qualify as fair use, and whether the commercial character of the parody creates a presumption against fair use.
case.facts: Luther Campbell and the rap group 2 Live Crew recorded 'Pretty Woman,' a song that parodied Roy Orbison's copyrighted 'Oh, Pretty Woman,' using its opening bass riff and first line while altering the lyrics and style to mock the original's idealized romanticism. Acuff-Rose Music, the copyright holder, refused to license the parody and sued for infringement. 2 Live Crew argued the parody was fair use: it copied only what was necessary to conjure up the original, commented on and criticized it, and could not substitute for it in the market. The copyright holder argued a commercial parody that took the song's heart was not fair use. The district court granted the group summary judgment; the court of appeals ruled for the copyright holder, reasoning the commercial nature of the parody weighed heavily against fair use. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Acuff-Rose sued in the Middle District of Tennessee; the district court granted the defendants summary judgment on fair use. The Sixth Circuit disagreed, holding that the commercial character of the parody weighed against fair use and that the taking of the 'heart' of the work was excessive. The defendants petitioned the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the two songs, the extent of the copying (the bass riff, the first line, and the structure used to parody the original), and submissions on whether the parody was transformative, how much of the original it took, and its effect on the market for the original and for licensed derivatives. The dispute centered on the four fair-use factors.
case.plaintiffArguments: 2 Live Crew argued that its parody was transformative — it used the original to create new expression criticizing the original's bland romanticism — and that commercial parody is not presumptively unfair. It contended the copying was limited to what was needed to conjure up the original, that parodies by their nature must take the recognizable heart, that the parody could not substitute for the original in the market, and that the fair-use factors must be weighed flexibly rather than mechanically.
case.defendantArguments: Acuff-Rose argued that the rap song was a commercial exploitation that took the most recognizable element of the original and that its commercial character presumptively disfavored fair use. It contended the defendants copied the heart of the work for profit, that the parody could harm the market for the original and for licensed parodies, and that the fair-use defense should not immunize commercial copying.
case.applicableLaw: The Copyright Act's fair-use provision (17 U.S.C. § 107) and its four factors: purpose and character (including transformative use), nature of the work, amount taken, and market effect; the treatment of parody within fair use.
case.precedents: Sony v. Universal (1984) (commercial-use presumption); Harper & Row v. Nation Enterprises (1985); the § 107 factors and earlier parody cases like Berlin v. E.C. Publications (1964).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Copyright / parody fair use. Decided 1994. The decision clarified that commercial parody can be fair use and rejected a presumption against commercial transformative works.
case.tldr: A rap group parodied 'Oh, Pretty Woman' commercially without a license. The Court held commercial parody can be fair use and sent the case back.

case.title: United States v. Lopez
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Possessing a gun in a school zone is not economic activity substantially affecting interstate commerce; the Act exceeded Congress's commerce power.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990, criminalizing possession of a firearm in a school zone, exceeds Congress's power under the Commerce Clause.
case.facts: Alfonso Lopez, a twelfth-grade student at a San Antonio high school, arrived at school carrying a concealed .38 caliber handgun and five bullets. Charged under the federal Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990, which made it a federal offense to possess a firearm in a school zone, Lopez moved to dismiss on the ground that the Act exceeded Congress's commerce power — possessing a gun at school was not economic activity in or affecting interstate commerce, and the statute contained no jurisdictional element tying the firearm to commerce. The government defended the statute under the commerce power, arguing that guns in schools threaten the educational environment, which in turn affects national productivity and commerce. The case required the Court to identify limits on what 'substantially affects' interstate commerce could reach. The Act contained no jurisdictional element tying the firearm to commerce and no congressional findings; the government defended it on the aggregate effects of school violence on the national economy.
case.proceduralHistory: Lopez was convicted in the federal district court and sentenced to six months' imprisonment after the trial court rejected his commerce-power challenge. The Fifth Circuit set aside the conviction, holding the Act exceeded Congress's Commerce Clause authority because gun possession in a school zone was not commerce or substantially connected to it. The United States petitioned the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The record was thin: Lopez's possession of a gun on school premises was undisputed, and the statute contained no findings or jurisdictional requirement connecting the firearm to interstate commerce. The legal question concerned the categories of activity reachable under the commerce power and whether gun possession near schools bore a substantial relation to interstate commerce.
case.plaintiffArguments: The United States argued that gun possession in school zones substantially affects interstate commerce because violence disrupts education, reduces the quality of the workforce, increases insurance and law-enforcement costs, and deters travel and business — effects that in the aggregate support federal regulation. It contended Congress had broad power under Wickard and Darby to reach local activities with substantial aggregate effects, and that the absence of findings did not defeat an otherwise rational basis.
case.defendantArguments: Lopez argued that possessing a firearm at school is a non-economic, intrastate activity traditionally regulated by states, with no substantial effect on interstate commerce sufficient to sustain federal criminalization. He contended the government's chain of effects — from school violence to workforce quality to commerce — had no limiting principle, that the statute lacked a jurisdictional element or findings connecting the conduct to commerce, and that upholding it would collapse the distinction between national and local authority.
case.applicableLaw: The Commerce Clause; the Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990; the 'substantially affects' doctrine and the distinction between economic and non-economic intrastate activity; federalism limits on congressional power.
case.precedents: Wickard v. Filburn (1942); United States v. Darby (1941); NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin (1937); Perez v. United States (1971) (jurisdictional element).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Commerce Clause limits. Decided 1995. The case marked the first time in nearly sixty years that the Court invalidated a statute as exceeding the commerce power, signaling a renewed federalism.
case.tldr: Lopez was convicted under the federal Gun-Free School Zones Act. The Court struck it down, holding gun possession near schools is not commerce Congress can reach.

case.title: People v. O.J. Simpson
case.court: Los Angeles County Superior Court
case.actualOutcome: Jury acquitted Simpson on both counts of murder after a nine-month trial; the defense argued reasonable doubt from evidence-handling and police credibility problems.
case.questionPresented: Whether the state could prove beyond a reasonable doubt that O.J. Simpson murdered Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, in light of challenges to the physical evidence and police credibility.
case.facts: Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman were stabbed to death outside her Los Angeles condominium. O.J. Simpson, Nicole's ex-husband, was charged with both murders. The prosecution presented DNA evidence linking blood at the scene to Simpson, a bloody glove found at his estate matching one at the scene, and evidence of a history of domestic violence. The defense argued the evidence was contaminated, that police procedures were sloppy, that a glove found at Simpson's home was planted, and that detective Mark Fuhrman — a key witness — was a racist who could not be trusted after denying and then being heard on tape using racial slurs. The defense urged the jury to find reasonable doubt from evidence-handling failures and police misconduct; the prosecution urged that the physical evidence overwhelmingly proved guilt. The prosecution's DNA, blood, and glove evidence met a defense attack on chain of custody, contamination, and a detective whose taped racial slurs contradicted his earlier testimony.
case.proceduralHistory: The case proceeded to a nine-month televised jury trial in Los Angeles County Superior Court. The jury heard months of testimony on DNA, blood evidence, the gloves, the timeline, and police conduct. After deliberating briefly, the jury returned verdicts of not guilty on both murder counts.
case.evidence: The record was extensive: DNA and blood evidence, the two gloves, the Bronco and crime-scene evidence, the domestic-violence history, the demonstration that the glove appeared not to fit, and the Fuhrman tapes revealing racist statements after he had denied using them. The defense's attack on the chain of custody and police credibility was central.
case.plaintiffArguments: The prosecution argued that the DNA and blood evidence, the matching gloves, and the evidence of Simpson's motive and history of domestic violence proved his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. It contended the physical evidence was reliable despite defense attacks, that Simpson had the motive, means, and opportunity, and that the timeline and forensic evidence pointed overwhelmingly to him.
case.defendantArguments: The defense argued that the evidence was contaminated and mishandled, that police procedures were sloppy and the chain of custody suspect, that the glove found at Simpson's home may have been planted, and that Fuhrman's demonstrated racism destroyed the credibility of the investigation. It contended the cumulative doubt from tainted evidence, police misconduct, and an unreliable timeline prevented proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
case.applicableLaw: California criminal law on murder; the reasonable-doubt standard; rules on the admissibility and reliability of forensic and DNA evidence and on witness credibility and impeachment.
case.precedents: The general criminal-trial and evidence rules rather than controlling precedent; the case turned on credibility, forensic reliability, and the burden of proof.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Criminal law / murder trial. Decided 1995. The televised 'trial of the century' became a landmark in American public perceptions of race, policing, and the criminal justice system.
case.tldr: Simpson was tried for the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. The jury acquitted him after the defense attacked the evidence handling and police credibility.

case.title: Romer v. Evans
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Amendment 2, barring anti-discrimination protections for gay people, lacked a rational relationship to a legitimate purpose and violated equal protection.
case.questionPresented: Whether a state constitutional amendment barring all governmental action designed to protect persons based on sexual orientation denies gay and lesbian citizens the equal protection of the laws.
case.facts: Colorado voters adopted Amendment 2 by statewide referendum, repealing and forbidding all state and local laws, policies, and ordinances that protected persons from discrimination on the basis of homosexual, lesbian, or bisexual orientation. The amendment responded to municipal anti-discrimination ordinances in Aspen, Boulder, and Denver and barred gay people from seeking specific legal protection at any level of state government. Richard Evans and other gay citizens, along with municipalities, sued to enjoin the amendment, arguing it singled out a class of citizens and disabled them from seeking legal protection available to everyone else. Colorado defended the measure as preserving associational freedom for religious objectors and landlords and as a permissible expression of majority disapproval of homosexual conduct. Amendment 2 swept away existing local ordinances and barred any future protection for gay citizens at any level of state or local government, an unprecedented categorical disability on one class. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: The challengers sued in Colorado state court, which enjoined the amendment's enforcement. The Colorado Supreme Court sustained the injunction, applying strict scrutiny and finding the amendment denied a fundamental right to participate in the political process. The state petitioned the Supreme Court of the United States, which granted certiorari.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the amendment's text, the municipal ordinances it nullified, and submissions about its breadth — stripping gay people of specific legal protections across all domains while leaving others free to seek such protections. The dispute was legal: whether such a targeted disability bore a rational relation to any legitimate state interest, or was instead born of animus.
case.plaintiffArguments: The challengers argued that Amendment 2 inflicted a broad, targeted disability on a single class — making gay people ineligible for legal protections others could seek — and so violated equal protection under even rational-basis review. They contended the amendment was motivated by animus rather than any legitimate purpose, that denying a class the ability to seek protection from discrimination was unprecedented and indefensible, and that mere moral disapproval was not a legitimate state interest.
case.defendantArguments: Colorado argued that the amendment was a permissible democratic judgment declining to extend special protections based on sexual orientation, which put gay people on the same footing as everyone else rather than disadvantaging them. It contended the amendment protected associational freedoms, religious liberty, and landlords' and employers' rights, and that democratic repeal of anti-discrimination ordinances was a rational choice within the state's authority over municipal law.
case.applicableLaw: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; Colorado's Amendment 2; rational-basis review and the principle that animus toward a class is not a legitimate state interest.
case.precedents: Hunter v. Erickson (1969) and Reitman v. Mulkey (1967) (targeted disabilities on racial protections); Department of Agriculture v. Moreno (1973); Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center (1985).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Equal protection / sexual orientation. Decided 1996. The case was the Court's first major decision addressing discrimination based on sexual orientation, and it presaged later gay-rights rulings.
case.tldr: Colorado's Amendment 2 barred anti-discrimination protections for gay people. The Court struck it down as lacking any rational, legitimate purpose.

case.title: United States v. Virginia (VMI)
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. VMI's exclusion of women violated equal protection; Virginia lacked an exceedingly persuasive justification, and the parallel women's program was no remedy.
case.questionPresented: Whether Virginia Military Institute's exclusion of women from admission violates the Equal Protection Clause, and whether a separate program for women at another college provides an adequate remedy.
case.facts: Virginia Military Institute, a public military college founded in 1839, admitted only men and employed an 'adversative' method of training designed to instill discipline through physical rigor and absence of privacy. After a female high-school student's complaint, the United States sued Virginia, arguing that VMI's male-only policy denied equal protection. In response to litigation, Virginia established the Virginia Women's Institute for Leadership at Mary Baldwin College — a parallel program that did not replicate VMI's adversative method, facilities, or alumni network — as a purported remedy. The United States argued that excluding women from a unique public educational institution could not survive scrutiny and that the parallel program was not comparable. Virginia defended single-sex education as pedagogically valuable and contended the alternative program provided adequate opportunity. VMI offered a distinctive adversative method, a storied alumni network, and a male-only tradition of more than 150 years; the parallel VWIL program did not replicate its methods, facilities, or prestige.
case.proceduralHistory: The United States sued in the Western District of Virginia, which ruled for the state, finding single-sex education added diversity and the parallel program adequate. The Fourth Circuit sustained the exclusion of women but required a remedy; it later accepted the VWIL program as sufficient. The United States petitioned the Supreme Court, which granted review.
case.evidence: The record included detailed comparisons of VMI and VWIL — curriculum, methods, facilities, endowment, faculty, and alumni prestige — and expert testimony on the benefits and diversity value of single-sex education versus the interest in admitting women to VMI's distinctive program. The core question was whether Virginia's justification was 'exceedingly persuasive' and whether VWIL was a genuinely comparable remedy.
case.plaintiffArguments: The United States argued that classifications based on sex require an exceedingly persuasive justification, which Virginia lacked because its asserted benefits of single-sex education were post hoc rationales and VMI's male-only policy rested on overbroad generalizations about women's abilities. It contended VWIL was not comparable to VMI in method, resources, or prestige and so was no remedy, and that some women capable of meeting VMI's standards were categorically denied the opportunity.
case.defendantArguments: Virginia argued that single-sex education provided genuine pedagogical benefits and educational diversity, and that admitting women would require VMI to abandon its distinctive adversative method. It contended the question was not whether women could benefit from VMI but whether single-sex public education was constitutionally permissible, and that the parallel women's program provided women an equivalent opportunity adequate to satisfy equal protection.
case.applicableLaw: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; the intermediate-scrutiny/'exceedingly persuasive justification' standard for sex classifications; the availability of single-sex education under equal protection.
case.precedents: Mississippi University for Women v. Hogan (1982); Frontiero v. Richardson (1973); Craig v. Boren (1976); Sweatt v. Painter (1950) (comparability of separate institutions).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Equal protection / sex discrimination. Decided 1996. The case applied heightened scrutiny to one of the last all-male public institutions of higher learning and clarified the standard for sex-based classifications.
case.tldr: The federal government challenged VMI's male-only admissions. The Court ruled the exclusion unconstitutional and rejected a separate women's program as no substitute.

case.title: Clinton v. Jones
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. A sitting President has no temporary immunity from civil litigation for unofficial conduct; the suit could proceed.
case.questionPresented: Whether a sitting President is entitled to temporary immunity from civil litigation, or a stay of proceedings, for unofficial conduct occurring before taking office.
case.facts: Paula Jones sued President Bill Clinton in federal court, alleging that while Governor of Arkansas he had made unwanted sexual advances toward her in a hotel room and that, after his election, associates defamed her when she described the incident. The alleged misconduct occurred before Clinton became President. Clinton moved to dismiss or stay the suit until after his presidency, arguing that the separation of powers and the demands of the office entitled a sitting President to temporary immunity from private civil damages actions for unofficial acts, so that defending such litigation would not impair the discharge of constitutional duties. Jones argued that no immunity shielded the President from suits for pre-office private conduct and that the district court could manage any burden through scheduling and deference to the President's duties. The alleged misconduct predated the presidency, and Jones argued that litigation over unofficial conduct could be managed through scheduling accommodations without disabling the executive's functions.
case.proceduralHistory: Jones filed suit in the Eastern District of Arkansas; the district court denied the immunity-based dismissal but stayed the trial until the end of the presidency. The Eighth Circuit lifted the stay, holding the President had no immunity from suit for unofficial conduct and that the litigation could proceed with accommodations. Clinton petitioned the Supreme Court.
case.evidence: The dispute was legal and structural rather than factual: the record concerned the allegations themselves and the question whether the Constitution or history afforded a sitting President temporary immunity from defending a private civil action. Submissions addressed the likely burden of litigation on presidential duties and historical practice regarding sitting presidents as parties.
case.plaintiffArguments: Jones argued that presidential immunity under Nixon v. Fitzgerald covered official acts, not unofficial conduct predating the presidency, and that the suit's continued adjudication did not threaten the executive's functioning. She contended the district court could manage scheduling to respect the President's duties, that delaying justice for years would prejudice her claim, and that the President, like any citizen, was subject to the rule of law for private conduct.
case.defendantArguments: President Clinton argued that the separation of powers and the unique burdens of the office entitled a sitting President to temporary immunity from civil damages litigation, even for unofficial acts, so that defending suits would not distract from constitutional duties. He contended the risk of judicial interference with the executive justified a categorical deferral, that Nixon v. Fitzgerald's immunity rationale extended to the burdens of litigation itself, and that the suit could proceed after he left office.
case.applicableLaw: Article II and the separation of powers; the doctrine of presidential immunity from civil damages for official acts (Nixon v. Fitzgerald) and its asserted extension to unofficial conduct; the judiciary's power to adjudicate claims against a sitting President.
case.precedents: Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982) (official-act immunity); United States v. Nixon (1974); Mississippi v. Johnson (1867); the historical practice of suits involving presidents.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Presidential immunity. Decided 1997. The suit's continuation ultimately led to the President's deposition testimony, which precipitated the independent-counsel investigation and impeachment proceedings.
case.tldr: Paula Jones sued the sitting President over pre-office conduct. The Court let the suit proceed, holding presidents have no temporary immunity for unofficial acts.

case.title: Bush v. Gore
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Florida's standardless manual recount violated equal protection and no constitutional recount could be completed by the safe-harbor deadline; recount ended.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Florida Supreme Court's order for a manual recount of undervoted ballots, under standards that varied by county, violated equal protection and due process, and whether any recount could be completed consistently with the federal safe-harbor deadline.
case.facts: The 2000 presidential election turned on Florida's electoral votes, where George W. Bush led Al Gore by a few hundred votes after a machine recount. Florida courts ordered manual recounts of 'undervote' ballots — those on which machines registered no vote — but counties applied varying standards for divining voter intent from punch-card ballots, such as whether dimpled chads counted. The Florida Supreme Court ordered a statewide manual recount of undervotes without a uniform standard for evaluating ballots and without completing it by the December 12 federal safe-harbor deadline protecting electors. Bush sought Supreme Court review, arguing the inconsistent, standardless recount treated ballots differently in violation of equal protection and that no constitutional recount could be completed in time. The case reached the Court amid an extraordinarily compressed and contested presidential transition. Counties applied varying standards to dimpled and hanging chads, and the statewide recount ordered late in the contest lacked a uniform rule for divining the intent of the voter.
case.proceduralHistory: After the Florida canvassing and contest proceedings, the Florida Supreme Court ordered a statewide manual recount of undervotes on December 8, 2000. The United States Supreme Court stayed the recount on December 9, granted certiorari, heard argument on December 11, and issued a per curiam decision the next day addressing the equal-protection defects and the impossibility of completing a constitutionally valid recount before the safe-harbor deadline.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the Florida Supreme Court's order, the varying county canvassing practices and counting standards, and the fact that the recount lacked uniform rules for assessing voter intent on undervoted ballots. There was no dispute that different counties used different standards or that the safe-harbor deadline was imminent; the constitutional defect lay in the absence of a uniform, sufficient standard.
case.plaintiffArguments: Bush argued that a manual recount conducted under standards that varied from county to county and judge to judge treated identical ballots differently, denying equal protection and due process in the counting of votes. He contended that the Florida court had altered the legislature's statutory scheme contrary to Article II, and that no constitutionally adequate recount could be completed before the December 12 safe-harbor deadline without running afoul of federal law.
case.defendantArguments: Gore argued that manual recounts to ascertain voter intent were a lawful and traditional remedy, that a uniform statewide 'intent of the voter' standard governed the recount, and that equal protection did not forbid reasonable local variation in administration. He contended the Florida court had merely interpreted state law, that the recount should proceed to count every vote, and that any constitutional concerns could be addressed by clearer standards rather than by halting the count.
case.applicableLaw: The Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses; Article II's delegation of elector selection to state legislatures; 3 U.S.C. § 5's safe-harbor deadline; Florida's election-contest statutes and the 'intent of the voter' standard.
case.precedents: Harper v. Virginia Board (1966) (voting equality); Reynolds v. Sims (1964); Anderson v. Celebrezze (1983); Bush v. Palm Beach County Canvassing Board (2000) (the earlier stay opinion).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Equal protection / election recount. Decided 2000. The ruling effectively resolved the disputed presidential election thirty-six days after the vote, in a decision the Court limited to the circumstances presented.
case.tldr: Florida ordered a manual recount with varying county standards in the 2000 election. The Court halted it under equal protection, effectively deciding the presidency for Bush.

case.title: Lawrence v. Texas
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. The statute criminalizing private consensual same-sex intimacy violated the Due Process Clause; Bowers overruled.
case.questionPresented: Whether a Texas statute criminalizing private consensual homosexual intimacy violates the liberty protected by the Due Process Clause, and whether Bowers v. Hardwick should be reconsidered.
case.facts: Harris County sheriff's deputies, responding to a reported weapons disturbance at John Lawrence's Houston apartment, entered and found Lawrence and Tyron Garner engaged in consensual sexual activity. Both men were arrested, held overnight, and charged with 'deviate sexual intercourse' under a Texas statute that criminalized sodomy only between persons of the same sex — the statute did not apply to opposite-sex couples. They were convicted on pleas of nolo contendere and fined. Lawrence challenged the statute as an unconstitutional invasion of the liberty to engage in private consensual intimacy and, because it targeted same-sex couples alone, as a denial of equal protection. Texas defended the law as a permissible expression of moral disapproval and relied on Bowers v. Hardwick's holding that no constitutional right to homosexual sodomy existed. The deputies entered on a reported weapons disturbance and found the men in private intimacy; the Texas statute criminalized sodomy only between persons of the same sex, not between opposite-sex couples.
case.proceduralHistory: Lawrence and Garner pleaded nolo contendere in the Harris County Criminal Court, preserving their constitutional challenge, and were fined. The Texas Court of Appeals sustained the convictions, relying on Bowers v. Hardwick to reject the due-process claim. The Supreme Court granted certiorari on whether the statute violated due-process liberty and equal protection and whether Bowers should be revisited.
case.evidence: The record established that the two men were adults engaged in private consensual conduct in a home, and that the statute criminalized only same-sex sodomy. The dispute was legal: whether liberty under the Due Process Clause encompassed private adult intimacy, whether Bowers had been correctly decided, and whether the statute's same-sex-only application denied equal protection.
case.plaintiffArguments: Lawrence argued that the Constitution protects an adult's right to private consensual intimate conduct as an aspect of liberty, and that Bowers had wrongly framed and rejected that right. He contended the statute criminalized conduct central to personal dignity and autonomy, that it applied only to same-sex couples in violation of equal protection, that moral disapproval alone was not a legitimate state interest, and that the law demeaned gay citizens' lives and relationships.
case.defendantArguments: Texas argued that Bowers correctly held there is no fundamental right to homosexual sodomy, that the statute reflected a rational legislative judgment about morality, and that states have traditionally regulated sexual conduct. It contended the statute promoted morality and public decency, that any change should come from the legislature, and that criminalization of conduct long subject to legal prohibition was within the state's police power.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment (liberty in private intimate conduct); the Equal Protection Clause; Texas's Homosexual Conduct law; the stare decisis question whether Bowers v. Hardwick (1986) remained sound.
case.precedents: Bowers v. Hardwick (1986); Griswold v. Connecticut (1965); Eisenstadt v. Baird (1972); Romer v. Evans (1996); Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992) (stare decisis).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Liberty / sodomy laws. Decided 2003. The decision both invalidated the remaining sodomy statutes and overruled Bowers, marking a turning point in constitutional protection for gay citizens.
case.tldr: Two men were convicted under Texas's ban on same-sex intimacy. The Court reversed, holding private consensual conduct is protected liberty and overruling Bowers.

case.title: Grutter v. Bollinger
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. The law school's narrowly tailored, individualized consideration of race to achieve diversity survived strict scrutiny. Effectively overruled by SFFA v. Harvard (2023).
case.questionPresented: Whether the University of Michigan Law School's consideration of race as one factor in a holistic, individualized admissions process to achieve a 'critical mass' of minority students satisfies strict scrutiny under the Equal Protection Clause.
case.facts: The University of Michigan Law School used race as one factor among many in a highly individualized, holistic review of each applicant, seeking a 'critical mass' of underrepresented minority students to obtain the educational benefits of diversity. It had no quota and no separate track. Barbara Grutter, a white applicant with strong credentials who was rejected, sued, arguing the school's use of race was a disguised quota that violated the Equal Protection Clause and Title VI. The law school defended the policy on the ground that student-body diversity was a compelling interest and that its individualized, non-quota consideration of race was narrowly tailored, as Justice Powell's opinion in Bakke had permitted. The case asked whether race-conscious admissions could survive strict scrutiny without crossing into forbidden quota territory. The law school sought a 'critical mass' of minority students through individualized review without quotas; Grutter's credentials were strong, and the contest concerned whether race operated as a decisive plus.
case.proceduralHistory: Grutter sued in the Eastern District of Michigan, which found the policy unconstitutional as a functional quota. A divided en banc Sixth Circuit disagreed, sustaining the policy as narrowly tailored to the compelling interest in diversity. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, deciding the case alongside Gratz v. Bollinger, which struck the undergraduate point-based system.
case.evidence: The record included expert testimony and data on the law school's admissions process — the individualized review, the 'critical mass' goal, the absence of a quota, and the comparative treatment of minority and non-minority applicants — as well as evidence about the educational benefits of diversity. The contest was over whether the policy was a disguised quota or genuinely holistic, and whether diversity was a compelling interest.
case.plaintiffArguments: Grutter argued that the 'critical mass' goal was a disguised quota, that race operated as a decisive factor for minority applicants, and that the policy was not narrowly tailored because race-neutral alternatives existed and individualized review could not mask a systematic racial preference. She contended that diversity was not a compelling interest sufficient to survive strict scrutiny, or that the policy's implementation was too broad and undefined to qualify.
case.defendantArguments: The law school argued that student-body diversity was a compelling educational interest recognized by Bakke, and that its policy was narrowly tailored because it used race only as one 'plus' factor in an individualized, holistic review with no quota or separate track. It contended the flexible approach satisfied strict scrutiny, that race-neutral alternatives could not achieve genuine diversity, and that the educational benefits of a diverse student body justified the limited use of race.
case.applicableLaw: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; Title VI; strict scrutiny of racial classifications; the 'narrowly tailored' requirement and the diversity rationale from Justice Powell's Bakke opinion.
case.precedents: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978) (Powell's opinion); Gratz v. Bollinger (2003) (striking the point system); United States v. Virginia (1996); Adarand v. Peña (1995).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Affirmative action. Decided 2003. The decision sustained holistic race-conscious admissions while a companion case struck a mechanical point system, defining the constitutional boundary for decades.
case.tldr: Grutter challenged Michigan Law School's holistic use of race in admissions. The Court upheld it as narrowly tailored to the compelling interest in diversity.

case.title: Kelo v. City of New London
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Taking private property for a comprehensive economic development plan qualifies as public use under the Fifth Amendment.
case.questionPresented: Whether a city's exercise of eminent domain to take private property for a comprehensive economic development plan — transferring it to private parties — satisfies the Fifth Amendment's public-use requirement.
case.facts: The City of New London, Connecticut, facing economic decline, adopted a development plan to revitalize its Fort Trumbull neighborhood by assembling land for a research facility, offices, a hotel, and housing, using eminent domain to acquire properties whose owners refused to sell. Susette Kelo and other homeowners sued, arguing that taking their non-blighted homes for transfer to private developers served a private rather than public use, violating the Fifth Amendment. The city argued the comprehensive economic-development plan served a public purpose — jobs, tax revenue, and revitalization — and that courts had long deferred to legislative judgments about public use. The homeowners contended economic development alone, taking from one private party to give to another, was not a public use within the constitutional meaning. The neighborhood was not blighted; the city sought the homes for a comprehensive redevelopment plan designed to generate jobs and tax revenue, transferring the land to private parties for development.
case.proceduralHistory: The homeowners sued in Connecticut state court to enjoin the condemnation. The trial court enjoined some takings; the Connecticut Supreme Court sustained the takings as a valid public use, finding economic development a legitimate public purpose. The homeowners petitioned the Supreme Court of the United States, which granted certiorari.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the development plan, the city's findings of economic distress and public purpose, and the character of the neighborhood — not blighted but targeted for economic revitalization. The legal question was whether the public-use clause permits takings justified solely by the projected economic benefits of transferring property to private entities under a comprehensive plan.
case.plaintiffArguments: The homeowners argued that the public-use clause means what it says — that government may take property only for actual public use like roads or facilities, or to eliminate blight — not to transfer property from one private owner to another for economic development. They contended the projected benefits were speculative, that allowing such takings would disproportionately harm poor and minority communities, and that deferring to any asserted public purpose read the public-use limitation out of the Constitution.
case.defendantArguments: New London argued that courts had long interpreted public use broadly to include any legitimate public purpose and had deferred to legislative judgments, citing urban-renewal and land-redistribution precedents. It contended the comprehensive development plan served a public purpose — economic revitalization, jobs, and tax base — that the takings were part of an integrated plan rather than a private benefit, and that property was taken for public benefit even if private parties would implement the plan.
case.applicableLaw: The Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment ('nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation'), applied through the Fourteenth; Connecticut's eminent-domain statute; the doctrine deferring to legislative judgments of public purpose.
case.precedents: Berman v. Parker (1954) (blight/urban renewal); Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff (1984) (land redistribution); Ruckelshaus v. Monsanto (1984); the broad public-purpose doctrine.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Takings / public use. Decided 2005. The decision provoked widespread backlash and led most states to enact reforms restricting eminent domain for economic development.
case.tldr: New London condemned homes for private economic development. The Court upheld the taking, ruling economic revitalization qualifies as public use.

case.title: Hamdan v. Rumsfeld
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. The military commissions violated the UCMJ and the Geneva Conventions; Hamdan could not be tried before them as constituted.
case.questionPresented: Whether the President had authority to convene military commissions to try Guantanamo detainees, and whether the commissions' procedures complied with the Uniform Code of Military Justice and the Geneva Conventions.
case.facts: Salim Ahmed Hamdan, a Yemeni national, was captured in Afghanistan in 2001 and detained at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. The Bush administration designated him an enemy combatant triable by a presidentially created military commission for conspiracy to commit terrorism. Hamdan petitioned for habeas corpus, challenging the commission's legality on the ground that the President lacked authority to convene it absent congressional authorization and that its procedures — which permitted conviction on evidence the accused could not see, no independent review, and denial of protections required by the Geneva Conventions — violated the Uniform Code of Military Justice and Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. The government argued the President had inherent and statutory authority to convene the commissions and that the Geneva Conventions did not apply to al Qaeda detainees. The commission rules permitted conviction on evidence the accused could not see and confined review within the executive; Hamdan contested both the President's authority and the procedures' legality.
case.proceduralHistory: Hamdan petitioned for habeas corpus in the Western District of Washington; the case was transferred to the D.C. district court, which found the commission procedures unlawful. The D.C. Circuit disagreed, sustaining the commissions and holding the Geneva Conventions inapplicable to al Qaeda. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and heard the case with the Chief Justice recused.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the military order establishing the commissions, their procedural rules — permitting hearsay, classified evidence unavailable to the accused, and limited appellate review within the executive — and Hamdan's status as a detainee charged with conspiracy. The dispute centered on statutory authorization (the UCMJ, the Authorization for Use of Military Force, and the Detainee Treatment Act) and the applicability of Common Article 3's procedural guarantees.
case.plaintiffArguments: Hamdan argued that the President lacked inherent authority to establish military commissions and that neither the Authorization for Use of Military Force nor the UCMJ authorized commissions with procedures so deficient. He contended the commissions violated the UCMJ's uniformity requirements and Common Article 3's guarantees of a regularly constituted court affording all judicial guarantees, and that conspiracy was not a triable law-of-war offense, so he could not lawfully be tried before such a body.
case.defendantArguments: The government argued that the President's authority as Commander in Chief, reinforced by the AUMF and the Detainee Treatment Act, permitted him to convene military commissions to try enemy combatants. It contended the Geneva Conventions did not apply to al Qaeda as a non-state actor, that the commission procedures were adequate for unlawful enemy combatants, and that courts owed deference to the executive's judgment on the conduct of the war on terror.
case.applicableLaw: Article II's Commander in Chief power; the Authorization for Use of Military Force (2001); the Uniform Code of Military Justice; Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions; the Detainee Treatment Act of 2005; habeas corpus jurisdiction.
case.precedents: Ex parte Quirin (1942) (military commissions); Hamdi v. Rumsfeld (2004) (detention and due process); Rasul v. Bush (2004) (habeas jurisdiction over Guantanamo); In re Yamashita (1946).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Military commissions / war powers. Decided 2006. The ruling invalidated the Guantanamo commission system and prompted Congress to enact the Military Commissions Act later that year.
case.tldr: A Guantanamo detainee challenged trial by military commission. The Court ruled the commissions violated military law and the Geneva Conventions.

case.title: District of Columbia v. Heller
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. The Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep a handgun in the home for self-defense; D.C.'s ban was unconstitutional.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defense unconnected to militia service, such that the District of Columbia's ban on handgun possession in the home and its trigger-lock requirement are unconstitutional.
case.facts: The District of Columbia banned the registration of handguns — effectively prohibiting private handgun possession — and required that any lawfully owned firearms kept in the home be unloaded and disassembled or trigger-locked. Dick Heller, a D.C. special police officer who carried a gun on duty, applied to register a handgun for home self-defense and was denied. He sued, arguing the Second Amendment protected an individual right to keep a functional firearm in the home for self-defense, and that the ban and trigger-lock requirement violated that right. The District defended the laws as permissible gun regulation, arguing the Second Amendment protected only a militia-related collective right or, alternatively, that the laws were reasonable even under an individual-right reading. The ban effectively prohibited private handgun possession and required other firearms to be kept nonfunctional; Heller, who carried a gun on duty, had been denied registration of a handgun for home defense.
case.proceduralHistory: Heller sued in the District of Columbia federal courts; the district court dismissed his complaint, holding the Second Amendment did not protect an individual right. The D.C. Circuit ruled for Heller, finding an individual right and striking the handgun ban and trigger-lock requirement. The District petitioned the Supreme Court, which granted certiorari on the individual-right question.
case.evidence: The case was decided on the constitutional text and history rather than contested facts: the record consisted of the statutes, the denial of Heller's registration, and extensive briefing and amicus submissions on the Second Amendment's text, original meaning, and the militia versus individual-right interpretations. The dispute was over the Amendment's scope and whether the regulations were permissible under it.
case.plaintiffArguments: The District argued that the Second Amendment's militia clause limited its scope to arms bearing connected to militia service, and that its handgun ban and storage requirements were reasonable regulations permissible under any view of the right. It contended the handgun ban addressed gun violence in an urban area, that long guns remained available, and that the Court should not invalidate a democratically enacted public-safety measure.
case.defendantArguments: Heller argued that the Second Amendment's operative clause — 'the right of the people to keep and bear arms' — protects an individual right unconnected to militia service, including self-defense in the home. He contended the handgun ban effectively eliminated that right for the most commonly owned defensive firearm, that the trigger-lock rule rendered firearms useless for immediate defense, and that the laws were unconstitutional under any standard of review once an individual right was recognized.
case.applicableLaw: The Second Amendment; the D.C. handgun-registration ban and safe-storage requirements; the debated collective-right versus individual-right interpretations; the standard of review for gun regulations (left unresolved beyond rejecting rational-basis and interest-balancing).
case.precedents: United States v. Miller (1939) (limited precedent on the right's scope); Presser v. Illinois (1886); United States v. Cruikshank (1876); founding-era sources and state constitutional analogues.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Second Amendment. Decided 2008. The case was the Court's first substantial interpretation of the Second Amendment in seventy years and established an individual right to keep arms for self-defense.
case.tldr: Heller was denied a permit to keep a handgun at home in D.C. The Court struck the ban, holding the Second Amendment protects an individual right to armed self-defense.

case.title: Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed in part. Limits on independent political expenditures by corporations and unions violate the First Amendment; disclosure requirements upheld.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act's ban on independent expenditures by corporations and unions for 'electioneering communications' near an election violates the First Amendment.
case.facts: Citizens United, a nonprofit corporation, produced 'Hillary: The Movie,' a critical documentary about then-Senator Hillary Clinton, and sought to distribute it through video-on-demand during the 2008 primary season. The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act barred corporations and unions from using general treasury funds for 'electioneering communications' — broadcasts referring to a candidate shortly before an election — and required disclosure. Citizens United sued for declaratory and injunctive relief, arguing that the ban on corporate independent expenditures suppressed core political speech based on the speaker's corporate identity. The FEC defended the statute under campaign-finance precedents permitting regulation of corporate election spending to prevent corruption and the distortion of elections by accumulated corporate wealth. The film was a feature-length critical documentary offered for video-on-demand; the statute barred corporate electioneering communications near an election while exempting media corporations from its reach. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Citizens United sued in the District of Columbia district court, which rejected its challenges and sustained the electioneering-communication provisions. The Supreme Court noted probable jurisdiction, heard argument in March 2009, then ordered reargument specifically on whether Austin v. Michigan Chamber of Commerce — which had sustained corporate expenditure limits — should be reconsidered. It decided the case in January 2010.
case.evidence: The record included the film's content, its planned distribution as an electioneering communication, the statute's corporate-expenditure ban and disclosure provisions, and submissions on whether corporate independent spending corrupted or distorted elections. The constitutional question turned on whether the government could suppress political speech based on the speaker's corporate form.
case.plaintiffArguments: Citizens United argued that the First Amendment protects political speech regardless of the speaker's corporate identity, and that the ban on independent expenditures was a content-based suppression of core speech. It contended independent expenditures by definition are not coordinated and cannot corrupt, that corporations — like media corporations exempted from the ban — may speak on politics, and that the differential treatment of corporate and individual speakers was unconstitutional discrimination among speakers.
case.defendantArguments: The FEC argued that Congress could regulate corporate election spending to prevent corruption, the appearance of corruption, and the distortion of the political process by the immense aggregations of wealth corporations accumulate in the economic marketplace. It contended corporate treasury funds did not reflect shareholder political support, that the ban was justified under Austin and McConnell, and that disclosure and PAC alternatives left ample channels for corporate political expression.
case.applicableLaw: The First Amendment; the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act's electioneering-communication and corporate-expenditure provisions; the distinction between contributions and independent expenditures from Buckley; the speaker-based discrimination doctrine.
case.precedents: Buckley v. Valeo (1976); Austin v. Michigan Chamber of Commerce (1990) (sustaining corporate limits); FEC v. Wisconsin Right to Life (2007); First National Bank of Boston v. Bellotti (1978).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Campaign finance / corporate speech. Decided 2010. The decision invalidated limits on corporate and union independent spending and is closely associated with the rise of super PACs in subsequent elections.
case.tldr: Citizens United was barred from airing a film criticizing a candidate. The Court struck limits on corporate independent expenditures as violations of free speech.

case.title: National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed in part, reversed in part. Individual mandate upheld as a tax (not under the Commerce Clause); Medicaid expansion's funding threat was unconstitutionally coercive.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate is within Congress's Commerce or taxing power, and whether the Medicaid expansion's conditioning of existing funding on state participation is unconstitutionally coercive.
case.facts: The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010 required most Americans to obtain health insurance or pay a penalty collected as a tax — the 'individual mandate' — and expanded Medicaid eligibility, conditioning states' continued receipt of all Medicaid funding on participation. The National Federation of Independent Business, twenty-six states, and individuals challenged the Act, arguing the mandate compelled individuals to engage in commerce (buying insurance) rather than regulating existing commerce, exceeding the Commerce Clause, and that threatening to withdraw all Medicaid funds coerced states in violation of federalism limits on the spending power. The government defended the mandate as regulating the uninsured's inevitable participation in the health-care market and the Medicaid expansion as a permissible condition on federal spending. The mandate's penalty was collected through the tax code, while the Medicaid expansion conditioned all existing federal Medicaid funding on states' participation in the broadened eligibility rules. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Multiple suits were filed in federal courts immediately after enactment. The Eleventh Circuit in the NFIB case struck the mandate and left the rest of the Act; other circuits reached differing results on severability and the mandate. The Supreme Court consolidated review and heard six hours of argument over three days on the mandate, severability, Medicaid, and the Anti-Injunction Act.
case.evidence: The dispute was constitutional rather than factual: the record included the Act's text — the mandate's penalty structure and the Medicaid funding conditions — and submissions on whether the uninsured's inactivity in the insurance market could be regulated as commerce, and whether the threat to withdraw all Medicaid funding crossed from inducement to coercion.
case.plaintiffArguments: The challengers argued that the Commerce Clause permits Congress to regulate existing economic activity but not to compel individuals to enter commerce by purchasing a product, so the mandate exceeded federal power. They contended the Medicaid expansion was coercive — a gun to the head — because states could not realistically refuse and lose all Medicaid funding, amounting to commandeering of state governments in violation of the spending power's limits.
case.defendantArguments: The government argued that everyone participates in the health-care market and that the mandate regulated how that participation is financed, a matter substantially affecting interstate commerce within Congress's power. It alternatively defended the penalty as a valid exercise of the taxing power. On Medicaid, it argued the expansion was a permissible condition on the receipt of federal funds under Spending Clause precedent and that states remained free to decline.
case.applicableLaw: The Commerce and Necessary and Proper Clauses; the Taxing Power; the Spending Clause and its coercion limits; the Anti-Injunction Act's bar on pre-enforcement tax challenges; the ACA's individual mandate and Medicaid expansion provisions.
case.precedents: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824); Wickard v. Filburn (1942); United States v. Lopez (1995) (activity/inactivity); South Dakota v. Dole (1987) (spending conditions); New York v. United States (1992) (anti-commandeering).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Affordable Care Act. Decided 2012. The case was the centerpiece challenge to the 2010 health-reform law and redefined the limits of the commerce and spending powers.
case.tldr: States and businesses challenged the Affordable Care Act. The Court upheld the individual mandate as a tax but struck the Medicaid expansion's funding threat as coercive.
