case.title: Shelby County v. Holder
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Section 4(b)'s coverage formula was unconstitutional as based on decades-old data; preclearance became inoperative.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Voting Rights Act's Section 4(b) coverage formula, which subjected certain jurisdictions to federal preclearance of voting changes based on decades-old data, exceeded Congress's enforcement powers under the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments.
case.facts: Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act required jurisdictions with histories of voting discrimination — determined by a Section 4(b) formula using 1964–1972 data on tests and minority turnout — to obtain federal preclearance before changing voting laws. Shelby County, Alabama, sued for a declaratory judgment that Sections 4(b) and 5 exceeded Congress's power, arguing the coverage formula was based on obsolete data, treated states unequally, and departed from the constitutional principle of equal sovereignty among the states. The government defended the formula and preclearance as still necessary to prevent voting discrimination in covered jurisdictions, noting Congress's 2006 reauthorization had retained the coverage formula after extensive findings of continuing discrimination. The coverage formula rested on 1964–1972 data concerning tests and turnout; Congress had reauthorized it in 2006 after compiling findings of continuing discrimination in the covered jurisdictions. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Shelby County sued in the District of Columbia federal courts; both the district court and the D.C. Circuit sustained the statute, finding Congress had ample evidence to reauthorize it. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to decide whether the coverage formula remained constitutional and whether preclearance could continue to rest on it.
case.evidence: The record included the 2006 reauthorization's legislative findings of continuing voting discrimination in covered jurisdictions, the decades-old statistical basis of the coverage formula, and comparative data showing current minority registration and turnout in covered jurisdictions. The legal question was whether the formula's reliance on old data and disparate treatment of states remained congruent and proportional to constitutional violations.
case.plaintiffArguments: Shelby County argued that Section 4(b)'s formula was based on obsolete 1960s-70s data that no longer distinguished covered from uncovered jurisdictions, so preclearance imposed extraordinary federal oversight without current justification. It contended the disparate treatment of states violated the principle of equal sovereignty, that current data showed covered jurisdictions had equal or better minority turnout, and that Congress's reauthorization failed to justify the formula under congruence-and-proportionality review.
case.defendantArguments: The United States argued that Congress had compiled an extensive record of continuing voting discrimination in covered jurisdictions and had reauthorized the formula in 2006 for twenty-five more years, warranting deference under the Fifteenth Amendment's enforcement power. It contended preclearance remained necessary because case-by-case litigation had proven inadequate to stop discriminatory voting changes, and that the formula, though old, targeted the jurisdictions with the worst records.
case.applicableLaw: The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments and Congress's enforcement powers; Sections 4(b) and 5 of the Voting Rights Act; the congruence-and-proportionality standard for enforcement legislation; the equal-sovereignty principle among states.
case.precedents: South Carolina v. Katzenbach (1966) (upholding preclearance); City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) (congruence and proportionality); Northwest Austin v. Holder (2009) (warning of constitutional doubts).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Voting Rights Act. Decided 2013. The decision effectively ended preclearance until Congress could update the coverage formula, prompting new voting-law litigation across formerly covered states.
case.tldr: Shelby County challenged the Voting Rights Act's preclearance formula. The Court struck the coverage formula as outdated, rendering preclearance inoperative.

case.title: Riley v. California
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Police generally need a warrant to search the digital contents of a cell phone seized incident to arrest.
case.questionPresented: Whether police may, without a warrant, search the digital contents of a cell phone seized from an arrested person as a search incident to arrest.
case.facts: David Riley was arrested after a traffic stop; police seized his cell phone from him and searched its contents at the station, finding photographs and messages linking him to a gang and a shooting. He was convicted on gang-related and firearms charges. In a companion case, police searched Brima Wurie's cell phone call log incident to arrest. The government argued that searching a phone's contents was a lawful search incident to arrest, permitted to protect officer safety and prevent destruction of evidence. Riley argued that cell phones contain vast quantities of private digital information, that a phone's contents pose no threat to officer safety, and that a warrantless rummage through a phone was a far greater intrusion than the physical searches incident to arrest the doctrine was built on. The phone's photographs, messages, and call logs tied Riley to a gang and a shooting; the government characterized the search as incident to arrest, like examining a wallet or address book.
case.proceduralHistory: Riley was convicted in California state court; the California Supreme Court denied review. The companion federal case produced a First Circuit ruling requiring a warrant. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in both cases to resolve whether the search-incident-to-arrest exception extends to digital data on cell phones.
case.evidence: The record established that police searched the phone's digital contents — photographs, messages, and call logs — without a warrant after seizing it incident to arrest. The legal question concerned the two rationales for search incident to arrest (officer safety and evidence preservation) and whether they could justify searching digital data, given the immense storage capacity and privacy interests of modern phones.
case.plaintiffArguments: Riley argued that a cell phone's digital contents implicate unprecedented privacy interests — holding the privacies of life — and that neither rationale for search incident to arrest applied: data poses no danger to officers, and the risk of remote wiping could be addressed by seizing and securing the phone pending a warrant. He contended that allowing warrantless searches of phones would permit the government to reconstruct a person's entire private life from a device carried everywhere.
case.defendantArguments: California and the United States argued that the search-incident-to-arrest exception had long permitted warrantless searches of items on an arrestee's person, that cell phones should be treated like wallets, address books, and purses, and that the need to preserve evidence — including remotely wiped or encrypted data — justified immediate inspection. They contended a categorical warrant requirement would impede lawful investigations of evidence already lawfully seized.
case.applicableLaw: The Fourth Amendment; the search-incident-to-arrest exception and its two rationales (Chimel/Gant); the distinction between physical items and digital data on cell phones.
case.precedents: Chimel v. California (1969); United States v. Robinson (1973); Arizona v. Gant (2009); Weeks v. United States (1914).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Fourth Amendment / cell phones. Decided 2014. The ruling required warrants to search cell phones, recognizing that digital devices raise privacy concerns qualitatively different from physical searches.
case.tldr: Police searched Riley's cell phone without a warrant after arrest. The Court ruled police generally need a warrant to search a phone's digital contents.

case.title: Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc.
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Affirmed. Under RFRA, closely held for-profit corporations could not be required to provide contraceptive coverage contrary to their owners' religious beliefs.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Affordable Care Act's contraceptive-coverage mandate, as applied to closely held for-profit corporations whose owners object on religious grounds, violates the Religious Freedom Restoration Act.
case.facts: Hobby Lobby Stores, a closely held for-profit arts-and-crafts chain owned by the Green family, objected on religious grounds to four FDA-approved contraceptives it regarded as abortifacients. The Affordable Care Act required employers' health plans to cover contraception without cost-sharing; refusal exposed Hobby Lobby to substantial fines. The Greens and the company sued, arguing that the mandate substantially burdened their exercise of religion under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which prohibits the federal government from substantially burdening religious exercise unless the law is the least restrictive means of serving a compelling interest. The government argued that for-profit corporations could not exercise religion and that the mandate served compelling public-health interests. The Greens objected to four contraceptives they regarded as abortifacients; the mandate exposed the company to large fines, and the government's existing nonprofit accommodation stood as an alternative mechanism. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Hobby Lobby sued in the Western District of Oklahoma, which denied a preliminary injunction. The Tenth Circuit, sitting en banc, disagreed and permitted Hobby Lobby to sue under RFRA. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and consolidated the case with Conestoga Wood Specialties' similar challenge.
case.evidence: The record included the corporation's ownership and governance by the Green family, their sincere religious objection to the four contraceptives, the mandate's requirements and penalty structure, and the existence of the government's accommodation for nonprofit religious employers — allowing insurers to provide coverage directly — as evidence of a less restrictive means. The sincerity of the religious objection was not disputed.
case.plaintiffArguments: The government argued that for-profit corporations cannot exercise religion under RFRA, that the mandate furthered compelling interests in public health and gender equality, and that it was the least restrictive means of ensuring contraceptive access. It contended that recognizing corporate religious exemptions would let employers impose beliefs on employees and undermine uniform statutory schemes, and that the accommodation for nonprofits showed the mandate could not be further relaxed without harm to third parties.
case.defendantArguments: Hobby Lobby argued that RFRA protected the religious exercise of closely held corporations and their owners, and that the mandate substantially burdened their sincere belief by forcing them to facilitate contraceptive coverage or pay enormous fines. It contended the government had a less restrictive means — the existing nonprofit accommodation or direct government provision — so the mandate failed RFRA's strict test, and that protecting employee access did not justify forcing owners to violate their faith.
case.applicableLaw: The Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 (strict scrutiny for substantial burdens on religious exercise); the ACA's contraceptive mandate; the definition of 'person' under RFRA and whether it includes for-profit corporations.
case.precedents: Employment Division v. Smith (1990) (pre-RFRA free-exercise rule); Sherbert v. Verner (1963); Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972); City of Boerne v. Flores (1997).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Religious freedom / RFRA. Decided 2014. The decision extended RFRA protections to closely held for-profit corporations and shaped subsequent disputes over religious exemptions from generally applicable laws.
case.tldr: Hobby Lobby's owners objected on religious grounds to covering contraception. The Court exempted closely held corporations from the mandate under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act.

case.title: Obergefell v. Hodges
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. The Fourteenth Amendment requires states to license and recognize same-sex marriages.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Fourteenth Amendment requires a state to license a marriage between two people of the same sex and to recognize a lawful same-sex marriage performed in another state.
case.facts: James Obergefell and his partner John Arthur, a same-sex couple, were legally married in Maryland because Arthur was terminally ill; when Arthur died in their home state of Ohio, the state refused to list Obergefell as the surviving spouse on the death certificate because Ohio did not recognize same-sex marriage. Their case was consolidated with challenges from Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio, and Tennessee by same-sex couples seeking to marry or to have their lawful out-of-state marriages recognized. The couples argued that denying them marriage violated the Due Process Clause's protection of the fundamental right to marry and the Equal Protection Clause's prohibition on discrimination. The states defended traditional marriage definitions as matters for democratic decision and argued the right to marry did not encompass same-sex couples. The consolidated cases involved couples married legally elsewhere or seeking licenses at home; Ohio would not list Obergefell on his husband's death certificate despite their lawful out-of-state marriage.
case.proceduralHistory: The consolidated plaintiffs sued in their respective federal courts; district courts ruled for the couples, but the Sixth Circuit disagreed, sustaining the state marriage bans and creating a circuit split with four other circuits. The Supreme Court granted certiorari on both the licensing and recognition questions.
case.evidence: The record included the couples' circumstances, the state constitutional and statutory definitions of marriage, and submissions on the history and nature of marriage, the harms of nonrecognition to couples and children, and the trajectory of liberty and equality doctrine. The legal question was whether the fundamental right to marry extended to same-sex couples and whether excluding them served any legitimate purpose.
case.plaintiffArguments: The couples argued that the right to marry is a fundamental liberty protected by due process, that excluding same-sex couples demeaned their dignity and denied equal protection without legitimate justification, and that the states' asserted interests — tradition, procreation, democratic choice — could not justify denying marriage rights. They contended the Court's privacy and sexual-liberty precedents, along with its Windsor decision, compelled recognition that same-sex couples seek the same marital commitment and legal protections as opposite-sex couples.
case.defendantArguments: The states argued that marriage has historically been defined as the union of a man and a woman, that the Constitution does not compel a redefinition of that institution, and that the question belonged to democratic debate rather than judicial decree. They contended the state had rational interests in linking marriage to procreation and child-rearing, that the fundamental right to marry as historically understood did not include same-sex couples, and that judicial recognition would short-circuit ongoing democratic deliberation.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment; state constitutional and statutory marriage definitions; the fundamental-rights doctrine on marriage and the equal-dignity analysis from Windsor.
case.precedents: Loving v. Virginia (1967); Griswold v. Connecticut (1965); Lawrence v. Texas (2003); United States v. Windsor (2013) (striking federal nonrecognition).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Same-sex marriage. Decided 2015. The decision resolved a fast-moving national transformation in which same-sex marriage had gone from unrecognized to lawful in most states within a decade.
case.tldr: Same-sex couples challenged state marriage bans and nonrecognition. The Court ruled states must license and recognize same-sex marriages nationwide.

case.title: Carpenter v. United States
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Acquiring historical cell-site location records is a search generally requiring a warrant.
case.questionPresented: Whether the government's warrantless acquisition of historical cell-site location information from a wireless carrier constitutes a Fourth Amendment search requiring a warrant supported by probable cause.
case.facts: Timothy Carpenter was suspected of participating in a series of armed robberies. Without obtaining a warrant supported by probable cause, the government obtained court orders under the Stored Communications Act — which requires only 'reasonable grounds' — directing wireless carriers to produce Carpenter's historical cell-site location information. Those records placed his phone near the robbery locations over more than four months, mapping his movements via the cell towers his phone contacted. Carpenter was convicted of robbery. He argued that acquiring detailed location records that track a person's movements over months was a Fourth Amendment search requiring a warrant, while the government contended the records were business records held by third parties, subject to the third-party doctrine under which a person loses expectation of privacy in information shared with others. The Stored Communications Act order required only 'reasonable grounds,' not probable cause; the carrier records mapped the phone's location across 127 days of tower connections.
case.proceduralHistory: Carpenter was convicted in the Eastern District of Michigan after the cell-site records were admitted over his Fourth Amendment objection. The Sixth Circuit sustained the conviction, applying the third-party doctrine of Smith v. Maryland and United States v. Miller. The Supreme Court granted certiorari.
case.evidence: The contested evidence consisted of the historical cell-site location records obtained from carriers under a Stored Communications Act order short of probable cause, which mapped Carpenter's movements over 127 days. The dispute was whether the third-party doctrine governed such records or whether the deeply revealing nature of long-term location tracking required a warrant.
case.plaintiffArguments: Carpenter argued that cell-site location records reveal the privacies of life — a person's movements day and night for months — and that their acquisition was a search requiring a warrant, not a mere collection of business records. He contended the third-party doctrine should not extend to information automatically and continuously generated by a phone, that users do not meaningfully share location data, and that the depth and breadth of modern surveillance demanded constitutional protection.
case.defendantArguments: The United States argued that the records were the carriers' business records, which Carpenter had voluntarily conveyed to the third-party providers, so under Smith and Miller he had no reasonable expectation of privacy in them. It contended the Stored Communications Act's reasonable-grounds standard sufficed, that a warrant requirement would impede investigations of a tool merely revealing general location, and that the third-party doctrine should govern uniformly.
case.applicableLaw: The Fourth Amendment; the Stored Communications Act's court-order standard; the third-party doctrine and its limits as applied to digital-era location data; the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test.
case.precedents: Smith v. Maryland (1979) (pen register); United States v. Miller (1976) (bank records); United States v. Jones (2012) (GPS tracking); Riley v. California (2014).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Fourth Amendment / cell-site data. Decided 2018. The ruling extended the digital-privacy trajectory of Riley and Jones to records held by third parties.
case.tldr: Police obtained months of cell-site location records without a warrant. The Court ruled acquiring historical location data is a search generally requiring a warrant.

case.title: Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. The Commission's proceedings showed hostility to the baker's religious beliefs, violating the Free Exercise Clause; the order against him was set aside.
case.questionPresented: Whether a state civil-rights commission's application of its anti-discrimination law to a baker who declined to create a wedding cake for a same-sex couple, in proceedings marked by hostility to his religious beliefs, violated the Free Exercise Clause.
case.facts: Jack Phillips, owner of Masterpiece Cakeshop in Colorado, declined to create a custom wedding cake for a same-sex couple, citing his religious opposition to same-sex marriage while offering other baked goods. The couple filed a complaint, and the Colorado Civil Rights Commission found Phillips had violated the state's public-accommodations law and ordered him to create such cakes and retrain staff. Phillips challenged the order, arguing that compelling him to create a cake violated his free exercise of religion and free speech rights, and that the Commission's process was infected by anti-religious hostility — including a commissioner's public comment comparing religious defenses to those used to justify slavery and the Holocaust, and the Commission's inconsistent treatment of bakers who refused to make cakes with anti-gay messages. Phillips offered other baked goods but declined the custom wedding cake; a commissioner's public comparison of religious defenses to those used for slavery, and disparate treatment of other bakers, fed the hostility claim.
case.proceduralHistory: The Commission ruled against Phillips; the Colorado Court of Appeals sustained the ruling, rejecting the free-exercise and free-speech claims. The Colorado Supreme Court declined review, and Phillips petitioned the Supreme Court of the United States.
case.evidence: The record included the Commission's adjudicatory proceedings, the commissioner's disparaging comments about religion, and the Commission's differential treatment of other bakers who declined orders for cakes bearing messages opposing same-sex marriage. The constitutional question focused on whether the adjudication was neutral and of general applicability or instead reflected hostility to Phillips's religious beliefs.
case.plaintiffArguments: Phillips argued that the Commission's order, issued through proceedings openly hostile to his religious beliefs, violated the Free Exercise Clause's requirement of religious neutrality. He contended that compelling him to create an expressive cake was compelled speech, that the Commission's inconsistent treatment of other bakers showed animus rather than neutrality, and that the state could not enforce its anti-discrimination law in a manner disparaging religion.
case.defendantArguments: The Commission argued that the state's public-accommodations law was a neutral, generally applicable prohibition on discrimination in commercial settings that applied to all businesses regardless of religious motive. It contended that a cake is a commercial product rather than protected speech, that exempting religious objectors would undermine anti-discrimination enforcement, and that the proceedings were a lawful adjudication of a discrimination complaint.
case.applicableLaw: The Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses of the First Amendment; Colorado's public-accommodations anti-discrimination law; the requirement of religious neutrality in adjudication under Employment Division v. Smith and Lukumi.
case.precedents: Employment Division v. Smith (1990); Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye v. Hialeah (1993); Obergefell v. Hodges (2015); Newman v. Piggie Park (1968).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Free exercise / anti-discrimination. Decided 2018. The decision resolved the case on the adjudicator's demonstrated hostility rather than the broader free-speech claim, leaving the underlying conflict open.
case.tldr: A baker refused a wedding cake for a same-sex couple. The Court set aside the state's order, finding its proceedings showed hostility to the baker's religious beliefs.

case.title: Bostock v. Clayton County
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Firing an employee for being gay or transgender is discrimination 'because of sex' under Title VII.
case.questionPresented: Whether Title VII's prohibition on employment discrimination 'because of sex' encompasses discrimination based on sexual orientation or transgender status.
case.facts: Gerald Bostock was fired by Clayton County, Georgia, shortly after he began participating in a gay recreational softball league; in consolidated cases, Donald Zarda was fired after mentioning he was gay, and Aimee Stephens was fired after informing her employer she was transgender and would begin presenting as a woman. The employers did not dispute the reasons for termination. Bostock sued under Title VII, which forbids employment discrimination 'because of sex.' The dispute was purely statutory: whether firing an employee for being gay or transgender necessarily discriminates 'because of sex,' since the same conduct or identity would be tolerated in an employee of the opposite sex, or whether sexual orientation and gender identity are separate traits Congress did not cover. The employers conceded that the terminations followed disclosure of sexual orientation or transgender status; the dispute was whether 'because of sex' in the 1964 statute reached those traits. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: Bostock sued in the Northern District of Georgia, and the Eleventh Circuit dismissed, holding Title VII did not reach sexual orientation. The Second and Sixth Circuits reached contrary results for Zarda and Stephens, creating a split. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and consolidated the cases to resolve whether 'because of sex' covers these claims.
case.evidence: The record was largely uncontested on the operative facts — the employees were fired for being gay or transgender. The dispute centered on the statutory text: whether the phrase 'because of sex' necessarily encompasses sexual orientation and gender identity under a but-for analysis, or whether congressional intent and the statute's original understanding excluded them.
case.plaintiffArguments: Bostock argued that firing someone for being gay or transgender is necessarily discrimination because of sex: an employer who fires a man for attraction to men but tolerates the same trait in a woman discriminates on sex, and firing someone for presenting as a sex different from their sex assigned at birth is discrimination because of sex. He contended that under Title VII's but-for causation standard, sex was a but-for cause, and that Congress need not have anticipated the application for the text to control.
case.defendantArguments: The employers argued that 'because of sex' in 1964 meant discrimination based on being male or female, not sexual orientation or gender identity, and that Congress had repeatedly declined to add those traits. They contended that firing both men and women equally for being gay could not be sex discrimination, that the term's ordinary meaning in 1964 did not reach the claims, and that expanding the statute was for Congress, not the courts.
case.applicableLaw: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 ('because of sex'); the but-for causation standard for statutory interpretation; textualism and ordinary meaning; whether sexual-orientation and transgender status are necessarily sex-based.
case.precedents: Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins (1989) (sex stereotyping); Oncale v. Sundowner (1998); Phillips v. Martin Marietta (1971) (sex-plus); the textualist methodology cases.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Title VII / sexual orientation. Decided 2020. The decision extended federal employment protection to gay and transgender workers as a matter of the statute's text, without relying on constitutional equality.
case.tldr: Employees were fired for being gay or transgender. The Court ruled such firings are discrimination 'because of sex' under Title VII.

case.title: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. The Constitution confers no right to abortion; Roe and Casey overruled; Mississippi's Gestational Age Act upheld.
case.questionPresented: Whether Mississippi's Gestational Age Act, prohibiting most abortions after fifteen weeks, is constitutional, and whether the Constitution confers a right to abortion at all.
case.facts: Mississippi's Gestational Age Act prohibited most abortions after fifteen weeks of pregnancy, before the point of viability. Jackson Women's Health Organization, the state's only abortion clinic, challenged the law on behalf of patients, arguing it was a pre-viability ban squarely forbidden by Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey. Mississippi defended the statute on the merits and went further, asking the Court to reconsider whether the Constitution protects abortion at all, contending that Roe and Casey were wrongly decided and that abortion regulation should be returned to the states. The case required the Court to decide whether the Constitution confers a right to abortion, and if so whether a pre-viability ban could stand. The Act barred most abortions after fifteen weeks — before viability — with narrow exceptions; Mississippi expressly asked the Court to reconsider the constitutional foundation of Roe and Casey. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: The clinic sued in the Southern District of Mississippi, which enjoined the Act as an unconstitutional pre-viability ban under Roe and Casey. The Fifth Circuit sustained the injunction, holding the law could not stand under governing precedent. Mississippi petitioned the Supreme Court, which granted certiorari limited to whether all pre-viability prohibitions are unconstitutional.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the statute's text, the undisputed fact that fifteen weeks precedes viability, and the parties' submissions on the constitutional status of abortion, stare decisis, and the viability line. There was no factual dispute about the law's effect; the contest was whether the Constitution protected the right and whether the governing precedents should stand.
case.plaintiffArguments: Mississippi argued that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion, that Roe and Casey were egregiously wrong and should no longer be followed, and that the issue should be returned to the democratic process. It contended the state's interests in protecting unborn life and maternal health sufficed to sustain the fifteen-week ban, that viability was an arbitrary line not grounded in the Constitution, and that even if a right existed, the ban was a permissible regulation.
case.defendantArguments: Jackson Women's Health argued that Roe and Casey's core holding — that the Constitution protects a right to abortion before viability — must stand under stare decisis, reliance, and fifty years of reaffirmation. It contended the fifteen-week ban was a flat prohibition before viability that the precedent squarely forbade, that overruling would strip women of a fundamental liberty, and that the state offered no justification for reversing settled law beyond the Court's changed membership.
case.applicableLaw: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; Mississippi's Gestational Age Act; stare decisis and the doctrine of fundamental rights; whether the right to abortion is 'deeply rooted' in history and tradition.
case.precedents: Roe v. Wade (1973); Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992); Washington v. Glucksberg (1997) (deeply-rooted standard); the states' abortion laws at the founding.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Abortion. Decided 2022. The case presented the most direct challenge to Roe in fifty years, argued before a Court whose composition had shifted after three appointments.
case.tldr: Mississippi banned most abortions after fifteen weeks. The Court upheld the ban, overruling Roe and Casey and returning abortion regulation to the states.

case.title: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. New York's proper-cause requirement for concealed carry violated the Second and Fourteenth Amendments; text-and-history test adopted.
case.questionPresented: Whether New York's requirement that applicants for a concealed-carry license demonstrate 'proper cause' — a special need for self-defense — violates the Second and Fourteenth Amendments.
case.facts: New York law required applicants for an unrestricted concealed-carry license to demonstrate 'proper cause,' meaning a special need for self-protection distinct from the general public's. The New York State Rifle & Pistol Association and two individuals who were denied unrestricted licenses sued, arguing that conditioning the right to carry a handgun in public for self-defense on a showing of special need violated the Second Amendment's individual right recognized in Heller. The state defended the law as a reasonable licensing requirement justified by a long tradition of regulating public carry and by the need to prevent gun violence in crowded areas. The case asked whether the right to bear arms extends beyond the home and what methodology governs Second Amendment challenges. New York required a special need beyond ordinary self-defense for an unrestricted carry license; most states required no such showing, and the individual applicants had been denied unrestricted licenses. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: The challengers sued in the Northern District of New York, which dismissed the complaint. The Second Circuit sustained the proper-cause requirement under intermediate scrutiny, finding it substantially related to public safety. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to decide whether the denial of public-carry licenses for lack of special need violated the Second Amendment.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the licensing statute, the denial of unrestricted licenses to the individual applicants, and extensive submissions on the history of firearms regulation in the founding era and later centuries. The legal question was whether the Second Amendment protects public carry for self-defense and whether the state's historical evidence justified the special-need requirement.
case.plaintiffArguments: The challengers argued that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to carry a handgun in public for self-defense, not merely to keep arms at home, and that conditioning that right on a special need to be approved by officials made it a privilege, not a right. They contended that under the text-and-history approach, the proper-cause requirement had no adequate historical analogue and that the vast majority of states did not impose such a requirement.
case.defendantArguments: New York argued that public carry had been regulated since the founding and that its proper-cause requirement was a permissible means of limiting the number of people carrying handguns in public, supported by an extensive Anglo-American tradition. It contended the law respected the right to armed self-defense while protecting public safety, that the individual applicants lacked a special need, and that the historical record supported discretionary licensing.
case.applicableLaw: The Second and Fourteenth Amendments; New York's proper-cause licensing requirement; the methodology for Second Amendment claims — whether tiered scrutiny or the text-and-historical-tradition approach announced in Heller.
case.precedents: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008); McDonald v. Chicago (2010) (incorporation); founding-era and later carry regulations debated; the Second Circuit's post-Heller intermediate-scrutiny cases.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Second Amendment / public carry. Decided 2022. The ruling extended the individual right to public carry and replaced interest-balancing with a text-and-history test for gun regulations.
case.tldr: New York required a special need for a concealed-carry license. The Court struck the requirement, recognizing a right to carry in public for self-defense.

case.title: Students for Fair Admissions v. President and Fellows of Harvard College
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Reversed. Race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard and UNC violated the Equal Protection Clause and Title VI.
case.questionPresented: Whether Harvard's and the University of North Carolina's race-conscious admissions programs violate the Equal Protection Clause and Title VI, and whether the Grutter framework permitting race as one admissions factor should stand.
case.facts: Students for Fair Admissions sued Harvard College and the University of North Carolina, alleging their holistic admissions programs discriminated against Asian American applicants by using race as a determinative 'tip' or plus factor. At Harvard, SFFA argued that statistical evidence showed Asian American applicants were admitted at lower rates despite stronger credentials, and that the university's 'personal rating' penalized them; at UNC, the challenge similarly targeted the consideration of race. The universities defended their programs as narrowly tailored efforts to achieve the educational benefits of diversity under Grutter, denying any intentional discrimination or quotas. The case asked the Court to decide whether race-conscious admissions could continue and whether Grutter remained good law. SFFA pointed to statistical disparities in admission rates and to the 'personal rating' as evidence Asian American applicants were penalized; the universities insisted race operated only as one holistic factor. The parties' competing positions framed the questions of law the court was asked to resolve.
case.proceduralHistory: SFFA sued Harvard in the District of Massachusetts, which ruled for Harvard after a bench trial, and the First Circuit sustained. The companion case against UNC followed a similar path through the Fourth Circuit. The Supreme Court consolidated the cases and granted certiorari to reconsider the permissibility of race-conscious admissions under Grutter.
case.evidence: The record included extensive admissions data, statistical analyses of the treatment of applicants by race, evidence about the 'personal rating' and its alleged disparate treatment of Asian American applicants, and the universities' documentation of their holistic review and diversity objectives. The dispute concerned whether race functioned as a permissible holistic factor or an impermissible discriminatory tip.
case.plaintiffArguments: SFFA argued that race-conscious admissions discriminate against Asian American applicants, that the programs were not narrowly tailored because race operated as a significant negative factor and the universities lacked measurable diversity goals, and that Grutter had proven unworkable and should be abandoned. It contended the Equal Protection Clause forbids all racial classifications absent the most compelling justification, and that the evidence showed stereotyping and a floor on admissions rates for a disfavored group.
case.defendantArguments: Harvard and UNC argued that race was considered only as one factor in a holistic, individualized review aimed at the compelling interest of educational diversity, consistent with Grutter. They contended there was no intentional discrimination or quota, that Asian American admission rates did not reflect bias, that race-neutral alternatives could not achieve genuine diversity, and that decades of reliance on Grutter counseled against overruling.
case.applicableLaw: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment; Title VI of the Civil Rights Act; strict scrutiny and the narrow-tailoring requirement; the Grutter framework on diversity and race-conscious admissions.
case.precedents: Grutter v. Bollinger (2003); Regents v. Bakke (1978); Fisher v. University of Texas (2016); Brown v. Board of Education (1954).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Affirmative action. Decided 2023. The decision ended race-conscious admissions in higher education after nearly fifty years, framed by the Court as consistent with equal protection's colorblind command.
case.tldr: Students for Fair Admissions challenged race-conscious admissions at Harvard and UNC. The Court ruled the programs violated equal protection and Title VI.

case.title: Trump v. United States
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Vacated and remanded. Former Presidents have absolute immunity for core constitutional acts and presumptive immunity for other official acts, but none for unofficial acts; the lower court must sort the allegations.
case.questionPresented: Whether a former President is immune from federal criminal prosecution for official acts taken while in office, and how to distinguish official from unofficial conduct.
case.facts: A federal grand jury indicted former President Donald Trump on charges arising from efforts to overturn the 2020 election results, including allegations concerning his communications with Justice Department officials and state officials. Trump moved to dismiss the indictment, arguing that a former President has absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts within his constitutional responsibilities, and that the charged conduct consisted of official acts. The government argued that no immunity shielded a former President from criminal prosecution and that the alleged conduct — an effort to subvert the election — was unofficial campaign-related activity, not official duty. The district court rejected the immunity claim, and the case reached the Supreme Court on whether and to what extent a former President is criminally immune. The indictment alleged communications with Justice Department and state officials and pressure over the electoral count; the parties disputed whether each alleged act was official or unofficial conduct.
case.proceduralHistory: Trump moved to dismiss the indictment in the District of Columbia district court, which rejected the immunity defense. The D.C. Circuit sustained the denial of immunity. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and heard expedited argument on the scope of presidential criminal immunity for official versus unofficial acts.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the indictment's allegations — communications with Justice Department officials, pressure on state officials and the Vice President regarding the electoral count — and the competing characterizations of each as official or unofficial conduct. The legal question was categorical: whether immunity existed, its scope, and how courts should classify the allegations.
case.plaintiffArguments: Trump argued that the President cannot function without freedom from fear of criminal prosecution for official acts, so absolute immunity for acts within the outer perimeter of official responsibility — and at minimum presumptive immunity for official acts generally — was constitutionally necessary. He contended the charged conduct involved official duties like supervising the Justice Department and advising on election integrity, that impeachment was the constitutional check on presidential misconduct, and that criminal prosecution of a former President for official acts would cripple the presidency.
case.defendantArguments: The United States argued that no President is above the law, that executive immunity from criminal prosecution had never been recognized, and that the alleged conduct — conspiring to subvert election results — was private, campaign-related conduct not within official duties. It contended the public interest in enforcing criminal law outweighed any immunity, that the district court could filter official from unofficial acts, and that blanket immunity would place the President beyond accountability.
case.applicableLaw: Article II executive power and the separation of powers; the Nixon v. Fitzgerald civil-immunity framework and its extension to criminal prosecution; the Impeachment Clause; federal criminal statutes on obstruction and conspiracy.
case.precedents: Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982) (civil immunity); United States v. Nixon (1974); Clinton v. Jones (1997); Marbury v. Madison (1803).
case.additionalContext: Topic: Presidential immunity. Decided 2024. The case arose from the federal election-interference prosecution and was the Court's first ruling on criminal immunity for a former President.
case.tldr: Trump sought dismissal of his federal election indictment on immunity grounds. The Court ruled former presidents have immunity for official acts and sent the case back for sorting.

case.title: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo
case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.actualOutcome: Vacated and remanded. Chevron overruled; courts must exercise independent judgment on statutory meaning without deferring to agency interpretations.
case.questionPresented: Whether the Magnuson-Stevens Act authorized the fisheries agency to require fishing companies to pay for federal observers, and whether Chevron deference to agency statutory interpretation should be overruled.
case.facts: The National Marine Fisheries Service, under the Magnuson-Stevens Act, required Atlantic herring fishing vessels to carry federal observers and adopted a rule making the vessel operators pay the observers' costs, though the statute authorized such cost-shifting only for certain fisheries and was ambiguous as to herring. Loper Bright Enterprises and other fishing companies challenged the rule, arguing the statute did not authorize the agency to impose the costs on them. The lower courts deferred to the agency's interpretation under Chevron v. NRDC, which required courts to accept reasonable agency constructions of ambiguous statutes. Loper Bright argued Chevron was wrongly decided and asked the Court to overrule it, contending that interpreting statutes is the exclusive province of the judiciary under Article III and the Administrative Procedure Act. The Act expressly authorized industry-funded observers for some fisheries but was silent or ambiguous for Atlantic herring; the agency's rule shifted observer costs onto the vessel operators.
case.proceduralHistory: Loper Bright sued in the District of Columbia district court, which deferred to the agency's interpretation under Chevron and sustained the rule. The D.C. Circuit likewise deferred under Chevron. The Supreme Court granted certiorari specifically on whether Chevron deference should be retained or discarded.
case.evidence: The record consisted of the Magnuson-Stevens Act's text — which expressly authorized industry-funded observers for some fisheries but was silent or ambiguous for Atlantic herring — and the agency's rulemaking. The constitutional question was whether courts must defer to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes or exercise independent judgment, with the Court examining the APA's text and the history of judicial review.
case.plaintiffArguments: Loper Bright argued that Chevron deference was inconsistent with Article III and the Administrative Procedure Act, which assign statutory interpretation to the courts exercising independent judgment. It contended the statute did not authorize the agency to impose observer costs on the herring fishery, that deference had enabled agencies to rewrite statutes and made law unstable, and that the judiciary — not the agency — must say what the law is when statutes are ambiguous.
case.defendantArguments: The government argued that Chevron reflected a presumption that Congress intends agencies to resolve statutory ambiguities they administer, that deference had been embedded in the law for forty years and relied upon by Congress, courts, and regulated parties, and that agency expertise and accountability made agencies better suited to fill statutory gaps. It contended overturning Chevron would destabilize administrative law and that the observer rule was a reasonable construction of the statute.
case.applicableLaw: The Administrative Procedure Act's judicial-review provisions; Article III's assignment of 'the judicial Power'; the Magnuson-Stevens Act's observer provisions; the Chevron two-step framework and whether it should be retained.
case.precedents: Chevron v. NRDC (1984) (the precedent under review); Marbury v. Madison (1803); Skidmore v. Swift (1944); Kisor v. Wilkie (2019); statutory-interpretation canons.
case.additionalContext: Topic: Administrative law / Chevron overruled. Decided 2024. The case marked the end of four decades of Chevron deference, transferring interpretive authority over ambiguous statutes back to the courts.
case.tldr: Fishing companies challenged a rule making them pay for federal observers. The Court overruled Chevron, holding courts must interpret statutes without deferring to agencies.
